Who could Arsenal sign after missing out on Vinicius Jr?

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 20:32:37 GMT

Who could Arsenal sign next? Tottenham defender Cristian Romero, Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez and Juventus' Turkey winger Kenan Yildiz have all been linked with the Gunners

One big signing missed and one through the doors - it's been a mixed transfer window for Arsenal.

The Gunners were unsuccessful in what turned out to be a very public pursuit of Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr but did manage to bring in fellow Brazilian and Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes for £75m.

The signing of Guimaraes is another of the "win now" signings like Martin Zubimendi and Viktor Gyokeres last summer as he immediately raises the level and competition of the Arsenal squad.

Manager Mikel Arteta was asked if Arsenal supporters can expect more faces through the door before the deadline and the Spanish manager said: "Well, that's what we're trying to do. If we have the right player in the market to make us much better."

The Gunners are also going to be without two key defenders through injury in Jurrien Timber and William Saliba going into the start of this season, so it could be a busy few weeks in north London as they get set to try to defend their title.

Why Arsenal are signing Newcastle captain Guimaraes

Vinicius Jr and Real Madrid agree new six-year deal

Kenan Yildiz has been monitored by Arsenal as a potential signing

For Arsenal it is hard to find any winger who would bring the excitement levels as well as the elite numbers that Vinicius Jr can.

So what other options do the club and sporting director Andrea Berta have?

Arsenal have come into this window looking at bringing in one or two forwards and Arteta has made it clearthat any player that comes in this season has to take the club to the next level.

Arsenal signed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge to replace the outgoing Leandro Trossard, with the 24-year-old producing a remarkable 22 goals and 29 assists in all competitions last season for the Belgian club.

Replicating those numbers is unlikely but the Greek international has looked one of the brightest players during pre-season.

Arsenal have explored a move for Paris St-Germain winger Bradley Barcola, but Liverpool are also interested and the French side are demanding a fee of more than £100m for the forward.

Morgan Rogers, before he completed his move to Chelsea from Aston Villa for £117m, was a target but Arsenal were not willing to go above £80m for the England international.

Finding value in the market is hard and Berta is always looking to ensure that a deal represents value for the club.

Kenan Yildiz is one player from Europe who is on Arsenal's list in a hunt for a left winger.

The 21-year-old had a seriously impressive 2025-26 season for Juventus, scoring 11 goals and registering 10 assists in 47 appearances in all competitions.

The Turkey international can play across the frontline too which adds another dynamic, which may make him appealing to Arteta.

Like all good wingers he is unpredictable and can go on either the inside or outside, which means it is hard for defenders to know if he is going to cross the ball or shoot.

And stats from Opta show that, of all players in Europe's top five leagues last season, only Manchester United's Bruno Fernandes (98) and Werder Bremen's Romano Schmid (77) created more open-play chances than Yildiz, while it was only Vinicius (43) who created more chances after carrying the ball than Yildiz too (37).

However, Yildiz has just signed a new four-year deal and sources indicate that Juventus are unwilling to sell him.

Atletico Bilbao winger Nico Williams is another who has been looked at before by Arsenal and would add some spark to an attack which can be criticised as being too predictable at times.

The Spain winger has a contract until 2035 with the Basque club but there are reports which suggest there is a release clause in his contract.

Williams completed 43.8% of his 153 dribbles last season, scored six goals and registered three assists in a campaign that was disrupted by injury.

According to Opta, Williams averaged 8.2 dribbles per 90 minutes last season in La Liga with only Lamine Yamal, Kevin and Jeremy Doku averaging more in Europe's top five leagues.

Availability is a big thing for Arteta and with a potentially high price tag and after a season of broken game time, this may not be the player for the Gunners at this point.

Arsenal also have the option of continuing with Tzolis on the left while they also have Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke who can fill that role too, with Eze playing from the left in some of Arsenal's biggest games at the business end of last season.

Guimaraes can ignite something different in us - Arteta

Arsenal are going to start the season with half of their first-choice back four out injured which means that any defender they sign is going to be required to play straight away.

That is why the Gunners have been interested in a move for Aston Villa defender Ezri Konsa who, as well as being a reliable centre-back, can play at right-back too.

Konsa has become a starting option for England and, alongside his importance to Villa, that will be why he is valued at around £60m.

However, Konsa is not the only defender that Arsenal have on their shortlist of targets.

The Gunners are interested in a move for Cristian Romero who is the captain of their rivals Tottenham Hotspur.

If any move does materialise for Romero, it would be a sensational development and be another deal, following the one for Eze last season, which would present a chance for bragging rights for Arsenal fans.

Atletico Madrid are reported to be chasing Romero though and with Spurs unlikely to want to strengthen their rivals, this deal seems unlikely to come to fruition.

One of the big moves of last season's summer transfer window was when Arsenal signed Gyokeres.

The Sweden striker was chosen to get the Gunners over the line in their hunt for a piece of silverware.

Gyokeres achieved that and scored 21 goals in all competitions but it was not always smooth sailing for the 28-year-old.

There are questions over his technical ability and about how suited he is to this Arsenal attack.

Arsenal have held a strong interest in Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez for sometime and the Argentinian international wants to leave the LaLiga club.

Alvarez, who was already played in the Premier League for Manchester City, would present a huge jump in quality and there would be no debate that he would make the Arsenal frontline better.

But, like many of the targets Arsenal are looking, at there is interest in Alvarez from elsewhere.

Barcelona are pursuing the forward which could scupper any plans that Arsenal have.

The Gunners are also trying to balance the books with Gabriel Jesus, Gabriel Martinelli and Reiss Nelson all available for a move if there is an offer that matches the club's value.

Denmark midfielder Christian Norgaard has already departed for Everton while there is not yet a clear path for academy graduate Ethan Nwaneri.

Arsenal have added Guimaraes and Tzolis as well as former Leeds goalkeeper Illan Meslier as back-up as they look to build on their success of last season.

But whatever happens, it is going to be a busy period in north London as they look to get their business finalised before the deadline.

Forest firefighting to continue overnight as cars abandoned

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 20:24:05 GMT

A firefighting operation will continue into the night to quell a blaze which began on Sunday and has affected one square kilometre (250 acres) of the New Forest national park in Hampshire.

It began when a van caught fire on the A31 near Bratley Wood, forcing motorists to abandon more than 20 vehicles.

Lindsey Legg was with her husband and three children when they were forced to stop by police and leave their car. She said "women and children were walking with buggies" on the road and it had been "pretty scary".

National Highways said the A31 dual carriageway through the New Forest would remain closed in both directions until further notice.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service said more than 120 firefighters had been working "in challenging conditions" to contain the blaze.

Forestry England said the blaze was under control, but it expected the firefighting operation to continue for several days.

It said it was supporting the fire service with car park closures to make sure it had easy access to the area.

Spokeswoman Esta Mion added: "There are still flames on site... but it is under control.

"It's nowhere near as bad as it was at the height of the fire last night. But we are very much asking people to stay away... it's unpredictable."

The blaze was started by a van fire on the A31 which spread to Bratley Wood and the surrounding area, Forestry England confirmed.

Aerial footage of scorched vegetation showed how the fire funnelled outwards in a south-easterly direction as the wind fanned the flames.

Smoke from the blaze drifted across both sides of the Solent, prompting fire crews to urge people to keep doors and windows shut.

The fire service said an 8km (5-mile) hose had been laid from Hightown Lake, just east of Ringwood, to supply water to crews tackling the blaze.

In some areas, the hose crosses tracks and passes through private property and residents were urged not to drive over it to avoid causing damage.

Legg, who was travelling back to Bournemouth from Heathrow, told BBC Radio Solent: "We started seeing people abandoning their cars. Women and children were walking with buggies.

"Police told us 'you can't go any further'. We realised the fire was going through the field - it was pretty scary.

"We had to abandon the car and cross the central reservation to get away from the side of the fire. We thought the car was going to go up at one point."

New Forest National Park Authority said the impact on the forest ecosystem and rare species would be severe.

"It's rare heathland, which globally is more rare than rainforest," a spokesperson said.

"We have the highest concentration of lowland heathland in western Europe and it's internationally protected.

"It is home to all six UK native reptiles, Dartford warblers, nightjars, insects – it's devastating."

Police said the 23 vehicles left behind by motorists were moved so they could be collected by the owners later.

National Highways said there was significant damage to the road surface and crash barrier following the fire and oil spillage from the burnt out vehicle.

It said there was no estimated time for reopening the road, which is a main tourist route to Dorset and south-west England.

After Sky Sports chose Fulham v Chelsea for live Premier League broadcast on Monday, 24 August, the potential for a knock-on impact was clear.

With the two teams not in Europe, and thus entering the Carabao Cup in the second round, both faced playing two games in the midweek.

Ordinarily, that should mean the EFL Cup ties would be played on the Thursday, with 72 hours' rest.

That, too, would impact the Premier League's weekend schedule.

Fulham's match at Sunderland, which was not selected for TV broadcast, was switched to the Sunday.

Chelsea v Brighton, meanwhile, was chosen by Sky for the Sunday.

All good so far.

That was until both Fulham and Chelsea were drawn at home in the Carabao Cup - and they are not supposed to play at home on the same day. The police will have to make a concession, or the EFL will have to get creative.

But there is another knock-on effect - at very short notice for eight EFL clubs.

The opponents of Fulham and Chelsea - Wimbledon and Luton respectively - are in League One action on the Saturday after the ties.

If one or both Carabao Cup ties are scheduled for the Thursday, then the Saturday games would ordinarily move to the Sunday.

And there's another complication.

The following Tuesday there is a full programme of League One games - and that could impact a further four matches with the potential they might have to move to Wednesday.

Either teams will have to play two games within 48 hours, or supporters who have made travel arrangements are going to find games displaced.

New train service connects Finland and Sweden for first time in decades

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 18:28:11 GMT

A new passenger train linking Finland and Sweden has begun running, creating the first rail connection between northern Finland and southern Europe in nearly 40 years.

Shortly after 05:00 local time (04:00 BST) on Monday, a double-decker train set off from the coastal Finnish city of Oulu, rumbling its way across the border to Sweden.

As the inaugural service crossed the Torne river from Finland and pulled into Sweden's Haparanda station, it was met by crowds of people waving Finnish and Swedish flags.

The route was initially suspended in the late 1980s to the early 1990s, due to low passenger numbers and technical differences in the tracks between Finland and Europe.

Finland uses the same track widths as Russia, which are wider than the European standard - a holdover from when the Nordic nation was part of the Russian Grand Duchy in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

It is currently in the process of updating its track widths to match the European standard.

The new, twice-daily journey to Sweden's Haparanda takes 100-minutes as it hugs the west coast of Finland before crossing the border between the two Nordic neighbours.

Passengers travelling on from Haparanda will need to transfer onto a different train to continue southward.

But the service makes it possible to travel around 5,000km by rail from Portugal's Algarve to Finland's northernmost train station of Kolari - believed to be the longest train route in Europe.

It will also enable a 24-hour train journey between capitals Helsinki and Stockholm.

Finland's transport minister said the return of the cross-border service shows cooperation between the two countries was growing "all the time".

Elisa Markula, chief executive of Finland's state-owned railway operator VR, said she hopes the service will benefit from a "renaissance" in rail travel across Europe.

"Train travelling in all Europe is having a renaissance. Also in Finland, our passenger numbers are increasing a lot," Markula told AFP.

Russian court bars only anti-war party from standing in parliamentary elections

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 18:19:41 GMT

Russia's only liberal, anti-war party will not be able to take part in next month's parliamentary elections, a Moscow court has ruled.

Yabloko was the only registered party to oppose Russia's war on Ukraine.

The case against it was brought forward by Rodina, a pro-Kremlin nationalist party.

Hundreds of people - mostly very young - on Monday had stood outside the Moscow courthouse where the hearing was taking place in support of Yabloko, singing songs and waving flags.

Videos posted on social media showed that when news of the verdict spread among the crowd, many started chanting: "Shame! Shame!"

The lawsuit by the Rodina party accused Yabloko of publicly supporting an extremist organisation by publishing material on its website in support of the "international LGBT movement", which Russia's Supreme Court designated as extremist in 2023.

Rodina also said Yabloko was guilty of copyright infringement after a senior party member had quoted the lyrics of a Soviet-era song - "Let there always be sunshine" - in an interview.

At the hearing, Russia's financial monitoring service also claimed that Yabloko received money through third parties from foreign countries, including Germany and the US.

The Kremlin-controlled Central Electoral Commission had approved Yabloko's candidate list in late July.

But by then several party members had already been barred from running, including two deputy chairmen and deputy leader Maxim Kruglov, who was sentenced in June to seven years' imprisonment for social media posts about civilian casualties in Bucha, Mariupol and other Ukrainian cities.

And last week, Yabloko had suffered a cyberattack soon after launching a donations appeal for its election campaign fund.

It campaigned under the slogan "For peace and freedom! For a life without fear!" and advocated for a "ceasefire, diplomacy, and peace" and "for a Russia free from fear and political repression".

Hundreds gathered outside the Moscow courthouse, chanting "Russia" and "Yabloko" - the Russian word for "apple" - as the eight-hour hearing dragged on. Many carried apples as a sign of support.

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, any remaining opposition to the Kremlin has been crushed.

Public shows of dissent have been suppressed by wartime censorship laws and can trigger hefty fines or long prison sentences.

Because protests are no longer permitted, the Yabloko hearing offered a rare chance for likeminded Russians opposing the war to gather publicly. "For Yabloko. For freedom" was scribbled in chalk on the pavement outside the courthouse.

Yabloko has not won Duma seats since 2003 but has contested every election since.

Once led by presidential contender Grigory Yavlinsky, it later fractured with allies - expelling the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny in 2007 and criticising him even after he was eventually imprisoned ahead of his death in 2024.

Still, Yabloko remained Russia's most consistent anti-war voice, opposing Russia's war on Chechnya, the 2014 annexation of Crimea, and the invasion of Ukraine.

With ruling party United Russia's ratings down to 33% amid inflation, internet blackouts and drone strikes, Yabloko's support had been surging.

The Central Electoral Commission could have allowed Yabloko to contest the election and initially appeared to be leaning in that direction, potentially to use the party's marginal result in 2021 - when it won just 1.34% of the vote - to show how that the anti-war stance in Russia does not hold much sway.

But the government has now appeared to have changed its calculations, as signs of growing dissent over the war in Ukraine emerge.

Without a political force that clearly represents the opposition on the ballot, fewer people may be motivated to go to the polls. A low-turnout election, particularly among those who oppose the ruling party, would likely benefit the Kremlin.

All 10 other parties taking part in the election either support the war in Ukraine or do not openly criticise it.

And although United Russia's ratings appear to be in a deep dive, the Kremlin still has the resources to deliver the outcome it wants at the election.

Independent election watchdogs have been deprived of much of their ability to monitor and challenge the process.

Why has Araujo joined Liverpool and where did it go wrong at Barcelona?

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 18:11:48 GMT

Ronald Araujo joined Barcelona from Boston River in 2018 and has gone on to make 213 first-team appearances

Barcelona captain Ronald Araujo has arrived in Liverpool after joining the club on season-long loan, with the move including an option for the Reds to make the deal permanent for 55m euros (£47.1m).

For the Premier League side, it's an opportunity to bring in an experienced defender at a crucial time. For Araujo, it's a chance to make a fresh start away from Barcelona.

New Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola gave the move the go-ahead last week and spoke to Araujo via phone, before the Uruguay international travelled to England. Araujo has taken a pay cut for the coming season and Liverpool will cover his salary for the duration of his loan spell.

The structure of the deal reflects Liverpool's need to solve an immediate problem rather than make a long-term commitment - at this stage.

They wanted a defender who could operate both at centre-back and right-back, and Araujo's versatility and physical profile made him an attractive option.

The timing is particularly significant. Conor Bradley, Joe Gomez and Giovanni Leoni are all injured, while new signing Jeremy Jacquet has yet to feature in pre-season.

With Ibrahima Konate leaving for Real Madrid in the summer, Virgil van Dijk is Liverpool's only fit senior centre-back, making the need for reinforcements increasingly obvious.

Liverpool still believe that their stock of centre-backs will serve them well for the coming season and beyond. Jacquet, Leoni, Mor Talla Ndiaye and Ifeanyi Ndukwe are all emerging players in the position.

But Araujo, with his strength, pace and experience at one of Europe's top clubs, was viewed as a player capable of helping Liverpool through that period. His leadership capabilities were also seen as a positive factor. He will wear the number 33 shirt.

At Barcelona, not only did his acceleration allow them to defend a high line with confidence but, at 6ft 4in (1.93m) tall, his frame made him a formidable presence in physical contests and aerial duels.

Araujo joined Barcelona from his native Uruguay in 2018, made his first-team debut the following October and has since gone on to make more than 200 appearances for the Catalan club.

He finished last season as captain, making 38 appearances for Hansi Flick's side in the 2025-26 campaign.

"He is a very good person and an exceptional player, but our style of play is slightly different," Flick said in a recent press conference.

"He is a footballer with great speed and power, and he is good with the ball at his feet, too. I wanted to get him involved; I think he is eager to try new things, and I believe he has also been affected by what happened in the past.

"I said goodbye to him this morning and saw that he was happy. Liverpool is a great club, and I wish him the best. You have to accept it."

The "past" Flick may have been referring to includes a number of high-profile moments in which Araujo's mistakes came under intense scrutiny.

His red card against Paris St-Germain in the 2024 Champions League quarter-finals became one of the defining moments of his Barcelona career, with his dismissal helping turn the tie in PSG's favour.

He was also heavily criticised for mistakes in the second leg of the 2025 Champions League semi-final defeat by Inter, when Flick came out and publicly defended him.

Last season, in Barcelona's Champions League 3-0 away defeat by Chelsea, he was sent off just before half-time after receiving a second yellow card for a foul on Marc Cucurella.

A week after, he was granted a leave of absence to prioritise his mental health and received professional support and treatment to "take care of himself emotionally".

He returned a month later and made 23 appearances over the second half of the season, starting six matches.

There is also a financial benefit for Barcelona.

The club have been looking to generate a significant sale to help ease their financial pressures and, although this is only a loan with an option to buy, Liverpool will cover Araujo's full salary for the season. As one of Barcelona's highest earners, that represents a significant saving for the Catalan club.

For Araujo, though, he arrives at Anfield with an opportunity to reset his career and rediscover the confidence that once made him one of the club's most highly regarded defenders.

We are chasing Ebola virus - it is ahead of us, WHO warns

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 17:50:29 GMT

The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo began at least three months before it was officially declared - meaning the health authorities are still playing catch-up, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned.

More than 1,900 people have died from the virus since that declaration on 15 May, making this the second-worst Ebola outbreak ever.

Infection rates are still high, adding to the concern that the authorities are struggling to get to grips with the spread of the disease.

The epicentre of this outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, is in the east of DR Congo where insecurity has hampered control efforts.

There is also no approved vaccine or any recognised therapeutic drugs, making treating Bundibugyo harder.

"We are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," WHO Africa director Dr Mohamed Janabi said at a news conference in the city of Bunia, which is at the heart of this outbreak.

He cited research showing that the virus started spreading in February and was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid.

Janabi also said that, in part because of insecurity, health workers are only reaching about 30% of the cases with the rest dying at home.

Traditional burial practices – where mourners touch the deceased's body - and a suspicion of health authorities in some communities have also made things difficult.

But there are now several dedicated treatment centres in the east of DR Congo and people are getting diagnosed much more quickly.

So far there have been 4,294 confirmed cases and 1,960 deaths, DR Congo's health ministry has said.

The largest recorded outbreak was in West Africa between 2014 and 2016 when 11,325 people died.

More than two-thirds of England now in drought

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 17:41:39 GMT

Drought officials have declared 71.3% of England is now in drought, after the nation recorded its driest July since records began in 1836.

The East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs moved into drought status on Monday, joining half of England and the whole of Wales.

The National Drought Group – made up of regulators, government officials, water companies and agricultural bodies - made the decision after a meeting on Monday.

A total of 45 million people are now living in a drought area in England, with more than 27 million facing water use restrictions.

It comes after an exceptionally hot and dry summer, with heatwave conditions set to return for many this week.

Chair of the National Drought Group, Tony Grayling, said that drought conditions will continue to worsen until "significant and sustained rainfall".

The week ahead is forecast to remain mostly dry, as the fifth heatwave of the year intensifies, although there are signs of some rain coming into the UK on Sunday.

"We know the hot and dry weather is taking a real toll on farming and there will be long-lasting impacts on our environment," Grayling said in a statement, adding that "we need everyone's help in using a little less water to make sure our current water reserves last".

The National Drought Group said most of England is now experiencing a flash drought, which "develops very quickly" and is "brought about by a combination of very low rainfall and higher temperatures."

Yorkshire and north-east England have been moved to "prolonged dry weather" status, which is the stage before drought.

Nowhere in England is now under a "normal" status.

Hot weather is continuing, with the UK Health Security Agency issuing amber heat health alerts for all of England apart from the North East from Tuesday at 09:00 BST until Friday at 21:00 BST.

An amber alert means significant impacts "are likely" across health and social care services due to the high temperatures.

The continued hot and dry conditions increase the risk of wildfires. Dozens of firefighters are currently battling a fire in the New Forest, which earlier on Monday was estimated to be the size of 140 football pitches (247 acres).

Scotland and Northern Ireland have not been experiencing drought conditions and are expected to see spells of heavy rain over the week ahead.

Scotland does not declare drought, but monitors "water scarcity".

While conditions have improved in some parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some eastern areas remain in the two most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.

Last month, England and Wales saw the driest July since records began in 1836 - while for southern England, it was the driest month ever recorded.

South-east England received 1% of the expected average rainfall for July, while some parts of Hampshire, Isle of Wight and West Sussex have not had a rain day for 59 days.

All of England is experiencing pressure on water resources, the National Drought Group said.

Farmers have reported reduced output after their earliest harvests in 20 years, with the National Farmers Union (NFU) warning that continued dry weather could lead to some food shortages.

NFU president Tom Bradshaw said yields of wheat and oats were "very, very poor" this year and warned livestock farmers have had to use their winter feed rations because they have been unable to grow grass.

Water Minister Emma Hardy said the government is working to make it easier for farmers to build more on-site irrigation reservoirs, which capture and hold water.

Only 14% of England's rivers are considered to be at normal levels, while 22% are "exceptionally low" - including the River Avon in south-west England and the River Ely Ouse in eastern England.

The Environment Agency has warned that low water levels have resulted in potential navigation issues for boats on the Thames, Lark and Ouse.

Reservoir levels have also continued to decline, with almost all across England below normal and five classed as "exceptionally low", according to the agency.

Warmer water is putting fish under "severe stress," Head of Fisheries at the Angling Trust Mark Owen said, as it holds less dissolved oxygen.

Emma Pinchbeck, chief executive of the Climate Change Committee, said the UK is "not prepared at all" for the prolonged dry weather.

"We're seeing right now with the impacts on farming from this drought and the extreme heat we're experiencing, our infrastructure, our agricultural sector and lots of areas of the economy are not really ready for the weather we now have and how that weather will change up to 2050," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

What has been striking about this summer is not any single record, but the way weather extremes are piling up.

Climate change does not cause every heatwave or drought, but it does shift the odds.

By raising average temperatures, it makes extreme heat more likely and, when rain fails, increases evaporation and dries soils faster.

That creates a feedback - dry ground cools the air less, allowing temperatures to climb still higher.

The UK is now seeing the kind of hotter, drier summers climate scientists have long projected, part of a global pattern of heat.

There have been three droughts in the past five years – in 2022, 2025 and now 2026.

This year, there have been 34 days with temperatures that have reached 30C or above somewhere in England, including 13 consecutive days in July.

Heat extremes are becoming more likely and more intense due to human-caused climate change, the Met Office says.

Meanwhile, El Niño - the recurring climate pattern in which unusually warm Pacific Ocean waters can affect weather around the world - is giving global temperatures an additional, natural boost.

The World Meteorological Organisation, the UN agency for climate and weather, says a strong El Niño event is developing and is expected to "dominate global climate patterns" in the coming months.

MSP apologises for hurt caused by rape 'demonisation' comments

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 17:22:18 GMT

A newly-elected MSP has apologised for the hurt caused by comments in which they talked of the "demonisation" of rape.

Scottish Green Party politician Q Manivannan has also faced criticism for suggesting rape is a "spectrum of things" during a podcast recorded before they were elected to the Scottish Parliament.

Earlier, the Scottish Rape Crisis Alliance (SRCA) - which represents four rape crisis centres - said there is "no hierarchy of rape" and warned the MSP not to minimise sexual violence.

In a statement, Manivannan said clips from the podcast had been "selectively edited" but said they were "sorry" for the upset, and insisted they would never seek to diminish a rape survivor's experience.

The comments, which were made during The Subjective Space podcast recorded last year, sparked fury after they re-emerged online at the weekend.

Manivannan, who identifies as non-binary and uses they/them pronouns, was being interviewed about care and carers in society, when host Sindhu Rajasekaran raised the rehabilitation of criminals, saying she could have no empathy for rapists.

The Edinburgh-based former writer and academic said there was a "myth of the monster rapist" and "a demonisation of rape in the sense of it is a spectrum".

They continued: "It is a spectrum, none of which is any less or worse, but it is a spectrum of things that constitute one homogenised word 'rape'".

Manivannan went on to argue that the idea of a rapist as a "big burly man" was understandably a source of fear.

But the MSP told Rajasekaran that "any individual is capable of rape, including yourself and me, and I think that scary thought is the hardest to contend with".

The comments have been widely criticised by survivors groups and political opponents who said they downplayed the seriousness and lasting trauma of rape.

The SCRA, which comprises support groups in Glasgow, Lanarkshire, Ayrshire and the Western Isles, said the impacts of rape can last a lifetime, and the crime should never be reduced to a theoretical debate.

In an open letter the alliance said: "We are not demonising rape. We are naming it."

The authors strongly opposed the idea of rape existing on a "spectrum", insisting "there is no hierarchy of rape" and that no survivor should feel compelled to ask whether their experience was serious enough."

The letter urged politicians "not to normalise" rape or sexual violence, and "not create hierarchies of harm".

While not naming Manivannan, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Violence against Women and Girls, Reem Alsalem, posted on X that rape should never be spoken about in terms of it being a spectrum.

Scotland's Children's Minister Siobhan Brown told the BBC's Sunday Show Manivannan's words were misjudged.

Scottish Labour and the Scottish Liberal Democrats have also been critical, while the Scottish Conservatives called on the Scottish Greens to suspend the MSP.

Meghan Gallacher, the party's equalities spokeswoman, said: "It is deeply alarming that anyone, but especially an elected representative, would ever seek to minimise the seriousness of rape and suggest that there is a spectrum of offences."

In a statement issued on Monday afternoon, Manivannan said they were "horrified" that the comments had been "selectively edited in order to mislead people and misrepresent me".

"I also accept that my language was abstract in the first place and for that I take full responsibility and am sorry," they said.

The MSP said that during the interview they had categorically stated that every rape in every context is equally serious and harmful but this had been "maliciously" left out of clips.

They added: "I recognise that the words in the clip shared, without the full context of the conversation, have caused considerable upset.

"For that I apologise. I will always stand with and for victims and survivors."

Manivannan said they were themselves a survivor of sexual violence and understood the enduring trauma of such an experience.

"I would never seek to diminish or dismiss any survivor's experience, or to make anyone feel that their pain was not heard or understood," they added.

"I am genuinely sorry to everyone who has been distressed, hurt or triggered by the clips, and by the discussion and coverage that has followed.

"Words matter, particularly when speaking about something as deeply personal and painful as sexual violence, and I regret this hurt caused."

Manivannan, who was elected as a list MSP representing Edinburgh and Lothians East under Scotland's proportional representation system, said they would welcome the opportunity to meet survivor and advocacy groups to listen to their perspectives.

30 years later, a former gang member will stand trial for Tupac's murder

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 16:52:47 GMT

It's been three decades filled with mystery, conspiracies - and anger.

The drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 changed the trajectory of hip-hop and elevated the rapper from the face of the genre to a cultural icon.

His killing became one of popular culture's great mysteries, with countless theories but no arrests until 2023, when Duane "Keffe D" Davis was unexpectedly charged with murdering the famous rapper.

The 63-year-old former gang boss is due to stand trial in Las Vegas, where he is accused of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. He's pleaded not guilty. If convicted, he faces life in prison without parole.

The trial is likely to unravel the intricacies of the bitter and deadly East Coast vs West Coast rap rivalries and turf wars between the Bloods and the Crips street gangs that were immortalised in rap lyrics and news reports in the 1990s.

It could also include several celebrity witnesses - including Suge Knight, the former CEO of Death Row Records, who has been thought of as the last surviving witness to Shakur's death.

But the complicated case hinges almost exclusively on one key piece of evidence: a book co-authored by Davis that he has argued is partially a piece of fiction.

Jury selection in the case began on Monday, with opening arguments slated to start on 17 August.

To understand how the case became so mythologised, you have to go back to rivalries that grew larger than the men at its centre.

In the Los Angeles gang landscape of the 1990s, there was a vicious turf war between the Bloods, often represented by the color red, and Crips, who often wore blue. But that territorial dispute spread through the airwaves as part of a bigger national rivalry - East Coast vs West Coast rap. The genre dispute was represented by two rival record companies that defined 1990s hip-hop: Knight's Death Row Records and Sean "Diddy" Combs' Bad Boy Records.

"The funny thing about it is Tupac is actually an East Coast rapper," said Jeff Pearlman, author of Only God Can Judge Me: The Many Lives of Tupac Shakur.

Born in New York City, Tupac moved to northern California as a teenager. He became known as a Southern California rapper after signing with Death Row Records, which included acts like Snoop Dogg and Dr Dre.

Santi Elijah Holley, author of An Amerikan Family: The Shakurs and the Nation They Created, says the Death Row persona never told the whole story.

Tupac's mother Afeni was a Black Panther and he grew up around the Black liberation movement. Holley says his music became his politics: "His activism was his art, his lyrics."

He acted in a number of Hollywood movies, and released hip-hop's first double album, All Eyez on Me, which sold over 5,000,000 copies. That album, which debuted months before his death, cemented his place in the cannon of gangsta rap, a genre that celebrated the violent life of street criminals and drug dealers.

After he was shot in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996, he became immortalised as a kind of martyr for the lifestyle he helped make famous.

That fatal night began when Tupac and Knight attended a boxing match between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon at the MGM Grand.

After the match, surveillance footage captured Tupac and members of his entourage, who police have said were associated the Mob Piru Bloods street gang, attacking a man named Orlando Anderson, an alleged member of the South Side Compton Crips.

About three hours after the attack, Tupac was riding in the passenger seat of Knight's BMW driving through Las Vegas when a white Cadillac pulled alongside them and opened fire.

Tupac was hit four times and died six days later.

For nearly three decades, the killing remained one of America's most famous unsolved murders. There is no single explanation why.

Las Vegas police have long said witnesses refused to cooperate. Members of Tupac's entourage said police initially treated them like suspects and failed to follow important leads.

Within weeks of the shooting, investigators had identified Anderson from the MGM footage and questioned him.

He denied involvement and was never charged; he was killed in an unrelated shooting in 1998.

Over the years, police say they pursued thousands of tips, but the case stalled amid disappearing witnesses, many of whom were also killed in gang-related shootings, limited physical evidence, and a street code that forbade cooperation with police.

It was years later when Anderson's uncle, Davis, started talking and according to police, blew the case wide open again.

It was ultimately the death of another legendary rapper that helped unravel Tupac's shooting death.

Months after Shakur was gunned down, Biggie Smalls, or the Notorious BIG, was killed in a drive-by shooting in Los Angeles.

Both rappers were the stars of their respective rival record labels - Shakur with Death Row Records and Biggie with Bad Boy Records.

Biggie's case has remained unsolved, with no arrests or suspects.

In the mid 2000's the Los Angeles Police Department reopened the investigation and spoke with Davis, who was at a party with Biggie before the fatal shooting. While Davis said he didn't have information about Biggie's death, he did have knowledge in Tupac's case and shared that he was in the car when the rapper was shot and killed. He told police the information in exchange that he not be charged.

That deal stuck until years later, when Davis went public with his knowledge.

He co-authored a memoir in 2019 titled Compton Street Legend, that claimed he not only was inside the vehicle when Tupac was shot but also he was the person who "tossed" the gun used to kill him into the backseat of the Cadillac. He never claimed to be the person who opened fire.

Davis also elaborated on the shooting to the media, detailing information to reporters in interviews.

Las Vegas police said his public statements had "reinvigorated" the investigation. Over the next couple of years they spent time corroborating Davis' account and then in 2023, searched his home and seized multiple computers, two tubs of photographs and a slew of Tupac-related material, including a Vibe magazine.

He was arrested later that year.

Prosecutors have alleged that Tupac's killing was in retaliation for the beating of Davis' nephew - Orlando Anderson - just hours before the shooting.

They claim that Davis was the architect of the crime, who ordered the shooting and supplied the deadly weapon to further gang criminal conduct.

Nevada prosecutors argued that by publicly talking about what happened on the night of Tupac's death and writing a book where he claimed to have supplied the gun, Davis had broken the agreement he entered with law enforcement. A judge later sided with the prosecutor's argument, opening the door for Davis's arrest.

Davis and his defence team have argued that the book was co-authored and sections were embellished or fictionalised to make a profit, and they should not be viewed as direct admissions. In an interview last week with a local TV news station, Davis denied being in Las Vegas when Tupac was killed and distanced himself from the memoir that lists him as an author.

"I did not write that book," Davis told Fox 5. "A ghost writer wrote that."

He also said he might take the stand and testify at his trial. "If I have to, I will."

"This is what makes this case so fascinating. The two biggest pieces of evidence against Keffe D came from Keffe D," trial attorney Shaun Kent told the BBC. "Keffe D has the right to take the stand and say 'I made all this up. I lied to sell copies of the book. I lied to the police. I'm a liar but I did not murder Tupac.'"

Davis has also publicly stated multiple times that Bad Boy Records head Sean "Diddy" Combs had offered him $1m to kill Death Row Records rivals Tupac and Knight.

Combs is currently serving a 50-month prison sentence after being convicted for two counts of transportation for the purposes of prostitution in New York. He has repeatedly denied allegations that he was involved in Tupac's death.

Prosecutors have released a list of potential witnesses who could be called to testify, with over 200 names, including members of Tupac's family, former mayor of Las Vegas Oscar Goodman and former Los Angeles police Detective Greg Kading.

Prosecutors have also named Knight, although it's unclear if the rap impresario will testify, as he's previously said he would not.

"This would be huge as he has never offered law enforcement any information that would lead to the conviction of anyone," Kent said. "This trial is going to be a legal scholar's Super Bowl."

Get all the latest trial updates on the BBC Sounds 'Fame Under Fire: The Tupac Murder Trial' podcast available wherever you get your BBC podcasts.

Treasury contributed to woman's death, inquest hears

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 16:50:50 GMT

The death of a Treasury worker who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers was "materially contributed" to by her employers, an inquest has heard.

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Surrey Coroner's Court heard the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy which would have made clear that if the allegations were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

A spokesperson for the Treasury said it was "considering the findings carefully".

In a statement to the press, Moffat's family said they believed the Treasury failed in its duty of care.

"When she needed support, reassurance and fair treatment, she was left frightened, isolated and convinced her career and reputation had been destroyed," they added.

The inquest, in which a conclusion of suicide was recorded, heard that on 19 May Moffat went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

She was told of allegations she had shared sensitive personal information about colleagues, obtained as part of her job.

Moffat, from London, denied this.

She was informed that no final decision had been taken as to how the allegations would be handled but that it may be by way of a formal investigation or disciplinary meeting.

On asking if she would lose her job, assistant coroner Anna Crawford said the senior manager told Moffat she "could not predict the outcome at this stage".

Shocked and upset, Moffat cried, and it was agreed she did not have to work for the rest of the day.

She texted a friend, the court heard, to say she thought she would be sacked.

Moffat then spoke to her mother on the phone, who tried to reassure her, and it was decided she would stay at her parents' house.

The next day she took her own life.

Crawford said if written policy had been followed, instead of attending the 19 May meeting, Moffat would have been sent a letter which would have advised the likely penalty, if the allegations were proven, was a written warning.

During the inquest, evidence was heard that the fact-finding meeting was standard practice at the Treasury and other departments, which Crawford said was a "matter of concern".

She said she would be sending a Prevention of Future Deaths (PFD) report to the Treasury, the head of the civil service and Acas.

Moffat's family said: "Our hope has always been that some good can come from this tragedy.

"We therefore welcome any recommendations made by the coroner aimed at preventing other families from experiencing the heartbreak we have endured."

The family said it hoped a PFD report would lead to "meaningful changes" in how disciplinary processes are conducted and how employees' welfare is safeguarded.

"Nothing will bring Chloe back. She was a much-loved daughter, sister and friend, and the loss we feel every day is immeasurable," they added.

The Treasury said: "We continue to mourn Chloe's passing as a colleague and friend. Our thoughts remain with her family and friends.

"We take the coroner's concerns extremely seriously and recognise it is important to act quickly. We are now considering the findings carefully.

"We have introduced improvements to guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements but recognise we must continue to take action to prevent this happening again."

If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

From Dubai to a Dublin court - how alleged cartel boss Daniel Kinahan returned to Ireland

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 15:43:59 GMT

Armed police took up positions at the entrances to the Special Criminal Court in Dublin, as the plane carrying Daniel Kinahan approached the city.

On the steps of the building, journalists from Irish and international media tracked the flight online.

The Irish government had sent its jet to Dubai.

It is usually used to transport ministers, but it left the United Arab Emirates (UAE) with a suspected crime boss on board.

The doors of the court opened around half an hour after the aircraft landed at a military airfield nine miles (14km) away.

As reporters went through security, we heard the sound of sirens outside - indicating the arrival of the accused.

The courtroom filled up over the next 45 minutes - as detectives, prosecutors, and some members of the public took up seats along with the media.

From the moment Kinahan entered the dock, until he was led out 13 minutes later, almost everyone was looking towards him - and the proceedings were accompanied by constant typing from the press benches.

Complex international investigations, and diplomacy, had led to this moment.

Kinahan was charged with a single offence - directing the activities of a criminal organisation between October 2015 and April 2017.

He did not have to enter a plea at this stage of the court process.

But his lawyers have previously told the BBC that the allegations he is a crime boss are false and have no evidential basis.

They also said he had no criminal record or convictions.

Law enforcement agencies on both sides of the Atlantic believe he is a leading figure in the Kinahan Organised Crime Group.

The gang began as a street drug dealing operation in Dublin in the 1980s. From there, it became an international player in organised crime.

It has been linked to drug trafficking, money laundering, and murder.

The former deputy director of the UK's National Crime Agency, Roy McComb, said the group had grown globally because it had the "ambition and drive" to do so.

McComb told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the Kinahan group had created links with other organisations from South America, Eastern Europe, Pakistan and Afghanistan, who were involved in the "wholesale distribution" of drugs.

He said the cartel became "the go-to organised crime group to move large quantities of narcotics around Europe".

McComb explained they were "seen to be a threat to the stability of the US dollar", because they were trading in the currency.

In 2022, the US offered a reward of $5m (€4.3m; £3.7m) for information about Kinahan, his father Christopher Senior and brother Christopher Junior.

The organisation had previously come to more widespread global media attention in 2016, as the result of a vicious feud with another Irish gang known as the Hutch organisation.

During that year, Kinahan was targeted by gunmen at a boxing weigh-in at a hotel in north Dublin.

Mobile phone footage of the shooting captured the chaos and brutality of the violence.

One man was murdered in that incident. During months of gangland violence, 18 people were killed.

Kinahan left Ireland shortly after the attempt on his life.

The Irish government put a major diplomatic effort into negotiating an extradition treaty with the UAE, which was signed in 2024.

Kinahan is the second person to be brought to Ireland under the terms of the agreement.

The first was Sean McGovern, who was described by a judge to be a "senior lieutenant" in the Kinahan group.

In June, McGovern was sentenced to 24 years in jail after pleading guilty to two charges of directing a criminal organisation.

Kinahan rose to his feet, with his hands clasped in front of him, when a court official read his charge to him on Sunday.

I was sitting about three metres from Kinahan.

His appearance was slightly different compared with the well-known photographs of him.

He wore plain clothes, including a black hoodie, and glasses.

He spoke several times during the hearing, when one of the three judges addressed him directly.

His tone was polite.

He indicated he would decide later whether he would come to court in person for the next hearing on 5 October, or appear via video link from prison.

Outside the court, a crowd of more than 100 people were waiting to see a police convoy carry him away at speed.

The prosecution has formally commenced.

From Stonehenge to the Serpentine - satellite images show impact of hot, dry summer

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 15:36:33 GMT

With more parts of England set to join Wales as being officially declared to be in drought, BBC Verify has been gathering satellite imagery showing the impact of this year's extreme summer heat.

From historic sites and parks to reservoirs and golf courses, the hot, dry weather has changed how large parts of the UK usually look.

This year's consecutive heatwaves and above-average temperatures have had a noticeable effect - even compared with last summer which was the UK's warmest on record.

According to the UK government, almost all reservoirs in England and Wales are officially classed as having water levels below normal or low.

Five are exceptionally low - among them Clywedog reservoir in Powys which provides water supplies for parts of the West Midlands.

These satellite images show how more of the banks of the reservoir are visible this August compared with the same month last year.

Low reservoir levels have not been the primary cause of recent hosepipe bans and drought declarations - which are ultimately triggered by a lack of rain - across large parts of England and Wales.

The Environment Agency has reported that reservoir storage is now at 69% in England, which is below the long-term average of 82% for the time of year but higher than during last year's drought.

However, in its latest report the agency says water storage levels are above those recorded during similar periods in 2022 and 2025.

While Scotland has not been as badly affected as England and Wales, July's rainfall was below average for the south and east of the country, with many areas seeing less than half the long-term average for the month.

This has led the Scottish Environment Protection Agency to warn of "significant" water scarcity in the Borders and "moderate scarcity" in areas on the eastern side of Scotland.

Hard and dry fairways were a key talking point at golf's Open Championship which was held at Royal Birkdale on Merseyside last month.

A side-by-side comparison shows how much greener the fairways appeared in summer 2025 compared with this year.

As the BBC reported earlier this month while domestic users face hosepipe restrictions the rules for commercial users - including golf courses - vary.

When hosepipe bans are in force sports grounds can use hoses or sprinklers - but only to water grass areas "actively used for play". For golf courses this means the greens and tees can be irrigated but the fairways cannot.

Right in the heart of the UK capital, Hyde Park's famous Serpentine lake was closed for swimming on Monday because of high levels of blue-green algae.

Blue-green algae occur naturally, but warm, sunny and settled conditions can help blooms develop. Some can be harmful to people and animals.

A similar issue is affecting Killington Reservoir in south Cumbria. Satellite images show a visible change in the water between 24 May and 8 August, where a blue-green algal bloom has been confirmed.

Looking at the rest of Hyde Park and what is one of London's prime green spaces is now mostly brown following consecutive heatwaves since May.

It's a similar sight in south Wiltshire where the usually green rolling fields surrounding the ancient stone circle at Stonehenge have become almost as pale as the path around the prehistoric site.

As BBC Verify previously reported parts of the country are suffering from "vegetation stress" where the development and growth of plants, grass and crops can be severely affected.

Vegetation turning brown, even on this scale, does not mean the plants have disappeared or died, as grass, shrubs and some trees can recover once rainfall returns, provided their root systems remain intact.

Experts have said the combination of next-to-no rainfall and prolonged hot weather is likely to cause significant issues for the farming industry and could have an impact on agriculture and food prices in the coming months.

And perhaps counter-intuitively, prolonged dry weather can raise the risk of flash flooding when it eventually does rain. That is because parched, rock-hard ground may struggle to absorb water at first, so some rainwater may simply run off the surface instead.

Scientists also warn the UK is facing a growing risk of water shortages in the decades ahead, driven by human-caused climate change and increased demand.

Graphics by Tom Shiel

The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 15:34:56 GMT

Enes Kanter Freedom played 11 seasons in the NBA

The WNBA is still in the midst of its 2026 season and yet it is next year's Draft for North America's top women's basketball league that is dominating the headlines.

Why? Because some former men's NBA players have declared they will enter for selection - citing the current eligibility guidelines, or lack of, for transgender women players.

"I'm officially declaring myself a WNBA prospect," said Enes Kanter Freedom, who played 11 seasons in the NBA.

It is the latest development in a story ignited by a comment made by Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham, who said she wanted to protect young girls "who shouldn't have to go against biological men" in sport.

Her words have instigated protests - albeit not grand in scale - on both sides of the argument, and once again catapulted the debate around transgender women in sport into the spotlight.

Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN, external in which the conversation turned to the topic of "protecting" women's sports.

The Indiana Fever guard said she had received criticism from people who believed she "hated" transgender people, something she denied.

She said she wanted to "extend love" to everyone, but added: "I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

She later doubled down on her comments, saying it was "common sense", external to bar transgender athletes from competing in women's sports.

Her words quickly moved beyond basketball and into a wider political debate in the United States.

President Donald Trump expressed his support for Cunningham, while vice-president JD Vance said she was "inspiring".

Though the 29-year-old later said she is "not a very political person", her remarks have followed her around the country. Competing rallies from critics and supporters were organised at Indiana's games, along with small-scale protests.

The scale of the debate in the media, online and in politics was striking given no openly transgender woman is due to play, or has ever played, in the WNBA.

Sophie Cunningham is playing in her eighth WNBA season

The WNBA operates under a collective bargaining agreement (CBA), a deal negotiated between the league and its players association (WNBPA), setting rules on matters including player salary caps, revenue sharing, benefits and overall league operations.

On player eligibility, the CBA states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA."

The WNBA has yet to comment publicly on the row since Cunningham's comments but league commissioner Cathy Engelbert reportedly sent a memo to teams last week in which she said the matter would be discussed at an upcoming pre-arranged meeting with team presidents.

In the memo, seen by the Associated Press, external, Engelbert said the league would "always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league".

She added: "Our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities."

However, the lack of detail in the league's eligibility criteria has been brought to light by Kanter Freedom, who finished his playing career with the Boston Celtics in 2022.

"If simply declaring who you are is all that's required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," he wrote on Instagram, external.

Kanter Freedom, who has previously spoken out about human rights violations in China and Turkey, among other issues, added: "I know my presence on the court will stir up strong opinions. I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices.

"I'm simply asking that the current rules be applied equally to everyone - the rules that represent the very values many WNBA players and coaches have publicly advocated for."

A day after Kanter Freedom's 'announcement', Royce White - who made three appearances in the NBA as a player and is now a Republican Senate candidate - said he would also declare for the Draft, adding: "I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball."

Whether the vagueness of the rules are by design to leave it open to transgender women or a sign of an oversight that genuinely needs tightening up is not clear.

BBC Sport has contacted Cunningham's representatives, the WNBA and WNBPA for comment.

Demonstrators protest before the WNBA matches between Minnesota Lynx and Indiana Fever earlier in August

Cunningham's comments have become a flashpoint inside a league which has a long history of player activism on issues including race, gender equality and LGBTQ+ rights.

The players' association did not mention Cunningham by name when it eventually addressed the debate.

In a statement the WNBPA denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" and reaffirmed its commitment to "justice, equity, diversity and inclusion".

It called on fans to report abusive behaviour at games and added that it would continue to have "hard" conversations but it "will not be used as political pawns".

There is strong feeling on both sides of the argument. Minnesota Lynx head coach and president Cheryl Reeve, who said: "I come from a space of inclusion.

"The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."

Reeve wore a "Trans Kids Belong" T-shirt before Minnesota played Indiana earlier this month and was seen speaking to Cunningham on court before the game.

Cunningham later said the pair had exchanged their perspectives and that the conversation ended with "love and respect".

Cheryl Reeve wearing a 'Trans Kids Belong' t-shirt

Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams said she would welcome a transgender athlete "on my team or against my team, any time".

Last month, the WNBA suspended Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton from attending the team's next five home games after an exchange with two fans, who were sat courtside displaying signs thanking Cunningham for "speaking up for girls".

Keaton reportedly confronted the teenage fans and admonished them during the game. The Storm have since apologised.

As for Cunningham, the attention has increasingly become an unwelcome distraction.

Having defended her original comments, she said recently that she now wanted the conversation to return to what was happening on court.

"I want to get back to basketball, it's always been about basketball" she said, arguing that the standard of play in the WNBA was being overshadowed by issues away from the game.

But that may prove difficult, as pressure grows on the league to clarify exactly who is eligible to play.

In recent years, many governing bodies in sport have amended their rules about the inclusion of transgender athletes at the elite level, moving more towards restrictions.

Athletics, cycling and aquatics, for example, have implemented outright bans on transgender women taking part in women's events.

In March, it was announced that the women's category of Olympic sports will be limited to biological females from the LA Olympic Games in 2028.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) says eligibility will be determined by a "once-in-a-lifetime" sex test, which would prevent transgender women and those with differences in sexual development (DSD) who have gone through male puberty from competing.

In the United States, transgender women and girls are banned from competing in women's sports categories in schools, universities and the grassroots level.

That was part of an executive order - titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" - signed by President Trump last year.

It does not cover professional sport.

New weight-loss pill approved for use in UK

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 15:25:07 GMT

A daily weight-loss pill made by the drug firm behind the Mounjaro jab has been approved for use in the UK - the first country in Europe to do so.

Foundayo, made by Eli Lilly, is for treating obesity and type 2 diabetes.

But while people will be able to buy it privately with a prescription, the approval by the Medicines and Healthcare productors Regulatory Agency does not automatically mean it will be made available on the NHS.

Foundayo is a form of GLP-1 medication that blunts appetite, and comes after the MHRA approved a pill version of a similar weight-loss drug, Wegovy, in June.

Eli Lilly said while it could immediately be used by the NHS for type 2 diabetes, it would be making an application to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence in England for it to be recommended as a weight loss treatment as well.

Dr Simon Cork, from Anglia Ruskin University, said while the weight-loss benefits of Foundayo were less than other treatments, patients could still expect to see "significant, clinically meaningful changes to their weight".

And he said a key advantage was that it was likely to be cheaper than other weight-loss treatments, which have tended to be tightly restricted by the NHS.

University of Glasgow expert Prof Naveed Sattar agreed it was "good news".

He said another benefit was its convenience, pointing out that unlike the Wegovy pill, which has to be taken on an empty stomach, this pill could be taken at any time of the day.

"The arrival of another effective oral option is a positive development and should help more people access treatment that best suits their needs and preferences," he added.

Experts believe it could help people coming off weight-loss jabs remain slim.

Trials found that patients who had used weight loss jabs and then been given the tablet, also called orforglipron, every day for a year avoided regaining much of the weight they had lost - a known risk when coming off GLP-1 injections.

People on weight loss medication are also advised to eat a healthy diet and get enough exercise.

And, like any medication, there can be side effects to using Foundayo, including nausea, diarrhoea, constipation and vomiting.

Record 230 people cross Channel in one small boat

BBC News Mon, 10 Aug 2026 14:51:06 GMT

A small boat has crossed the English Channel carrying 230 people, the largest number to make the journey in a single vessel.

It breaks the previous record set in July, when 165 people made the crossing on a single vessel.

The boat arrived in the UK in the early hours of Monday.

A picture taken off the coast of northern France showed the inflatable boat was so full many passengers had to dangle their legs in the water as it entered the busy shipping route.

A Home Office spokesperson said this latest incident demonstrated the "reckless and dangerous tactics employed by criminal gangs... who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people onto unseaworthy vessels".

French rescuers said the 15m (49ft) boat was "buckling" in the water and could have led to a "tragedy".

The boat was already carrying about 50 people when it was seen heading towards a beach to pick more passengers up, the crew in Berck-sur-Mer added.

French maritime officials said 30 migrants were left stranded by the tide during a boarding attempt at Berck beach in northern France.

They were brought to safety by maritime and land-based rescue services, the statement from France's Channel and North Sea Maritime Prefecture said.

The boat carrying 232 people continued its journey, before two passengers requested assistance and were taken to Calais by a French Navy rescue ship, the statement added.

There are signs smugglers have been putting increasing numbers of people into each boat.

In 2018, there was an average of seven people per boat - but last year, that had risen to 62.

Last Tuesday, 173 migrants had to be rescued from a single boat, which caught fire.

Some 258 migrants arrived in the UK in four boats on Saturday, according to Home Office figures, with 423 arriving in five boats on Sunday.

However, the number of crossings overall is on course to be lower this year.

The provisional total for the number who have made the crossing so far in 2026 is 15,242, which is down by 43%, while the number of boats that have successfully crossed is down by 49%.

Last month, the Home Office recorded the lowest number of crossings in July since 2020.

Officials think this is partly because they have managed to disrupt the supply of small boats and engines to the people smugglers, with 1,100 seized since Labour came to power.

Officials claim that with the sophisticated surveillance and reconnaissance operation now operating over the Channel, "unintercepted" beach landings have ended.

All boats that make it across the halfway point in the Channel are met at sea by Border Force, which then brings the migrants safely ashore for processing.

There is still clear demand for the crossings as the number of people waiting in camps in northern France has not reduced.

At the same time, weather conditions have not been significantly different this year.

Officials believe this shows their work to disrupt the smuggling gangs is beginning to show results.

Despite this, concerns persist about the numbers still able to make it to the UK.

Ten people have been sentenced for endangering lives at sea since a new law designed to target people who pilot small boats came into force in January.

A spokesperson for the prime minister said: "We've seen today some appalling images... of young babies being put into these unseaworthy craft... shocking images, and they show the reality behind the ruthless smuggling gangs that are prepared to risk human lives for profit..."

"As the prime minister has said, we're not complacent and we are bearing down on these crossings, and that's reflected in the joint action that's prevented 47,000 attempted crossings since the election."

The English Channel is one of the most dangerous, and busiest, shipping lanes in the world.

Many migrants come from some of the poorest and most chaotic parts of the world, and ask to claim asylum once they are picked up by the UK authorities.

On a recent visit to Dover, the prime minister pledged his government would be "relentless" in curbing the number of small boat arrivals.

Andy Burnham said enforcement officers tackling people-smuggling gangs had been doubled on both sides of the Channel, but "a system that offers safe routes for people" needed to be built as well.

In April, the UK and France struck a £662m (773m euro) deal aiming to address the issue.

The three-year agreement included plans to send riot-trained police to French beaches to tackle violence and "hostile crowds", as well as France deploying millions of pounds worth of drones and two helicopters as part of a system to intercept people smugglers and illegal migrants.

On X, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "At 2.30am this morning a boat carrying 230 people was taken into Dover.

"This is a record number in a single vessel.

"It's yet more proof that this illegal invasion is a national security emergency."

Earlier on Monday, a Home Office spokesperson said: "We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.

"But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches."
