Directly south is the North Water Polynya, open water that is the most biologically productive place in the Arctic and a crucial hunting ground for the Inuit. Ice arches help keep ice out of the polynya in winter.

“To go, ‘well, it’s inevitable what’s going to happen’… that’s not the world I want to live in,” says Evatt.

At the same time, power demand can jump by around 20 per cent during a heatwave, due to a spike in air conditioning use.

Finally, low wind speeds have dampened output from turbines.

Solar has been the one bright spot, with clear skies and sunny weather delivering record levels of generation across the European Union in June 2026, according to Ember. In Hungary, for instance, solar has provided as much as 80 per cent of the country’s power during the day. But without battery storage, solar is of little use for the evening peak, when long, hot evenings mean people keep their air conditioning running into the early hours.

“These levels have never been really seen before. The Paks nuclear plant in Hungary, to my understanding, hasn’t been switched off before. It’s never seen sort of levels of production as low as they currently are,” he says. “There are people [in Hungary] saying, how are we going to meet this electricity demand? Normal prices would be between €100 and €150 per megawatt hour.

I would expect hydropower to remain at very low levels into August as well,” says Chris Rosslowe at Ember. The key outstanding question, he says, is how power demand may shift. “We just don’t know whether we’ll get some relief from these high temperatures. So I think a lot could depend on that.”

So far, European nations have avoided having to impose power rationing, rolling blackouts or other more severe curbs on demand during severe heatwaves. A mathematical measure of surprise explains why we fall for clickbait

New Scientist August 07, 2026

This one weird trick allows journalists to grab your attention! This kind of clickbait works because it promises information without actually delivering it – in fact, clickbait headlines go out of their way to be as uninformative as possible. A headline such as “Trump wins election” contains more information than “You’ll never believe who just won the election”, despite the latter containing far more words.

The man who ruined mathematics

It might seem paradoxical that more information can be conveyed using fewer words, but there is a mathematical framework that explains exactly why this is the case. And this so-called information theory, first developed in 1948 at the dawn of the computer age, paved the way for how much of the modern world works.

The theory was born when Claude Shannon, a mathematician working at Bell Labs in New Jersey, was trying to solve a problem that plagues us even today: how to communicate when you have a bad signal. Bell Labs was then the research arm of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, better known today as AT&T. It was very much the Google of its time, inventing everything from the transistor and solar panels to lasers – civilisation-altering stuff.

Advertisement

Shannon’s creation, while far more theoretical, is easily as important as those three. His mathematical breakthrough was to realise that the specific meaning of a message is irrelevant when attempting to communicate it. Or, as he put it in his famous paper A mathematical theory of communication, “semantic aspects of communication are irrelevant to the engineering problem”.

Instead, what matters is how surprising a message is – to put it in mathematical terms, the probability of a specific message being selected for transmission. It might seem strange to think of messages as having probabilities, but because they are built from a limited alphabet, in principle we can calculate them.

To take a very simple example, imagine we want to transmit the outcome of a coin flip as either H for heads or T for tails. Assuming the coin is fair, there is a 50 per cent chance of either outcome. If we land on H or T, either way, we will get new information with each flip. But what if the coin is doctored to always land on heads? In that case, we will transmit H 100 per cent of the time and T 0 per cent of the time, meaning that whatever happens, we aren’t communicating any new information.

Extremely basic AI prompt cracks decades-old maths problem

Shannon’s insight was that we can perform this calculation for any message, and so quantify the information transmitted, using a formula now called Shannon entropy. It states that the entropy H is equal to -∑p(x)log(p(x)). Stick with me, let’s unpack this.

We have x, which is simply the message that we want to transmit, so in the coin example, this is either H or T. And the p(x) is the probability of message x occurring. If every message is equally likely, this is simply 1 divided by the number of possible message, but there can also be more complicated cases that I will ignore for this explanation.

Next, we need to take the logarithm of the probability. What is a logarithm? It’s like a reverse exponent: for example, if 23 = 2*2*2 = 8, then log 8 = 3, in base 2. Finally, ∑ tells us that we should perform these calculations for all possible values of x and add them together.

That might seem complicated, but understanding the power of logarithms is key to information theory. In his paper, Shannon explained that your choice of base – the number of digits a system uses to represent numbers – determines the unit for measuring information. He proposed using base 2, as in the example above, resulting in a unit called binary digits, or “bits” for short – a name he took from his colleague, John Tukey. It is these bits, typically represented by a 0 or a 1, that underpin all our digital communications today.

Free newsletter

To go back to the coin example, for a fair coin we have a probability of 0.5 for either heads or tails, and log(0.5) = -1. Plugging this into Shannon’s formula, we get –(0.5*-1 + 0.5*-1) = 1. In other words, a fair coin communicates 1 bit of information. For the doctored coin, the outcome is 0. It offers no surprises, so it can’t transmit information.

What does all of this have to do with clickbait? Well, surprise, or novelty, is the currency of journalism. There’s a saying that “dog bites man” isn’t news – it’s too commonplace an event – but “man bites dog” is worth a story. This is exactly the same intuition that drove Shannon’s mathematical formulation of information, but there are important moments when maths and journalism diverge. Remember, Shannon wasn’t concerned with the meaning of messages, but merely with the probability. Crucially, this says nothing about whether the information is accurate or meaningful.

The most famous example of this might be a headline published a few months after Shannon’s 1948 paper. The US presidential election that year was between the incumbent Harry S. Truman and his opponent Thomas E. Dewey. On the eve of the election, the Chicago Daily Tribune found itself in the unfortunate position of having to go to press for its early edition before the results were finalised. Based on polling at the time of press, the paper predicted that Dewey would win, running the headline “Dewey Defeats Truman”.

From Shannon’s point of view, this is information communicated perfectly. With two possible outcomes, and a roughly equal chance of either candidate winning, the headline communicates around 1 bit of information, very similar to the fair coin. The only problem is that, in reality, the polling was wrong and Truman had won, leading to one of the most gleeful pictures ever published of someone reading the news.

The paper’s error was unfortunate, but it also provided an early warning sign that Shannon’s theory doesn’t encompass the value we place on one piece of information over another – the semantic meaning that he was so dismissive of. In the 21st century, this gap became weaponised in the form of clickbait.

A clickbait headline has a single job to do: to get you to click it. This is a very different job to traditional print headlines like “Dewey Defeats Truman” (or indeed the correct “Truman Defeats Dewey”), which are designed to convey the maximum amount of information in the smallest possible space, constrained as they are by the realities of print. Shannon would strongly approve of this effort at efficient communication.

By contrast, the more information a clickbait headline provides, the worse it is at its job. To go back to the example at the start of this article, “Trump wins election” tells you everything you need to know. You might choose to click through and read the particular details, such as the vote share, but in the 2024 contest between Donald Trump and Kamala Harris, these three words efficiently communicate around 1 bit of information (you could even shorten it to just “Trump wins”).

The rise of Google and, more importantly, ad-funded online publications changed the calculation. The goal became for publishers to attract as many visitors to their website as possible to maximise advertising revenue. To do this, publications, whether knowingly or not, hacked Shannon’s information theory to exploit our attention. The headline “You’ll never believe who just won the election” primes us for information without delivering it, like a coin that is mid-toss. Only by clicking can you complete the communication as Shannon originally envisaged it. If it turns out to be an unsurprising, low-information article, too bad – the publication already got your click.

That’s not to say Shannon’s work isn’t useful today – far from it. As I said earlier, Shannon was attempting to figure out how to communicate in the face of bad signal, or as he put it, over a noisy channel. His entropy formula showed that, by studying the probability distribution of possible messages, we could encode them in such a way as to preserve them in the face of noise, giving rise to everything from streaming video to space travel. No one denies that Shannon’s information theory made the modern world, but what it can’t do is solve our modern information overload.

National MP Chris Bishop is not denying there is appetite for leadership change within the party, refusing to comment on speculation Christopher Luxon’s time may soon be up.

“I am not going to comment today on media stories like that,” Bishop said when asked about conversations within the party, as first reported by the Herald last night.

He said, “briefing to media anonymously like that... is unhelpful and not what caucus members should be doing.”

“I am not going to comment on anonymous briefings.”

Bishop said the briefing “indicates a couple of people who are prepared to talk to media are unhappy about it.”

The minister said he retained confidence in Luxon.

Bishop, who has been speculated as a potential contender though has denied such ambitions, spoke to reporters at the opening of Te Mahia Station level crossing in Auckland.

Asked whether there had been calls amongst MPs about the party’s leadership, Bishop responded: “I don’t talk about calls that I have with my caucus colleagues.”

Bishop said he spoke with MPs on the phone regularly, as is normal when MPs are out of Wellington during a recess week.

“It’s a recess week, people are out and about. I think I’m in about four different cities in the next four days, so of course people are talking on the phones.”

The MP confirmed National’s caucus would be meeting virtually this week, but said this was prescheduled. He didn’t believe Luxon’s leadership was on the agenda.

He was unsure why his name continued to come up amid leadership speculation.

“I am just getting on with the job.”

Bishop described himself as “very optimistic about the future of this Government.”

It follows revelations from the Herald last night that discontented National MPs were hitting the phones on Monday about a potential leadership change.

One MP said, “there’s going to be change” in the top job, but it was a “question of who is going to be it”. They cited senior National MPs Bishop and Erica Stanford as potential front-runners.

Both Bishop and Stanford have previously denied ambitions for the leadership, though caucus sources have said they believe both MPs are contenders despite their public statements.

Other National MPs spoken to expressed openness to change, but did not say they were definitively in either camp, while an MP in Luxon’s camp disagreed with change.

Concern over Luxon’s leadership has been rumbling away all year, with the leader forcing a confidence vote on himself in April, which he survived.

The Herald has been told by MPs that they believe the margin of that vote was 27 to 22 in favour of Luxon; however, the figure is kept confidential to the party whips.

When the Herald put that vote margin to Luxon on Saturday, he responded: “All I know is I have the support of my caucus ... I just say to you I have the support of my caucus.”

The latest round of speculation appears to have been triggered by the leader’s out-of-the-blue announcement last week that he wanted a referendum on the country’s electoral system if re-elected.

That came as a surprise to his own MPs, who gave differing answers afterwards as to whether it was party policy.

It also followed Luxon belittling the concerns of business at a Rotorua event – for which he later apologised – and a story from the Herald revealing he’d used a Defence Force plane to get home from a National Party fundraiser.

On Sunday, Luxon and his finance spokeswoman Nicola Willis fronted a press conference to talk about the party’s fiscal rules, which included keeping taxes low, but couldn’t rule out increasing taxes.

Luxon less than 24 hours later clarified potential tax increases were limited to fuel excise, an accommodation levy, and a tax on banks.

Solar panels for 13 Gisborne schools in $30m Government project

New Zealand Herald August 10, 2026

Gisborne Boys' High School is one of 13 Gisborne Schools receiving solar panels through a government-funded programme. Photo / Imogen Brophy.

Thirteen Gisborne schools are to be included in a government-funded $30 million solar panel project.

The Solar on Schools project will provide panels to 500 schools nationwide over three years.

In Tairāwhiti, Lytton and Gisborne Boys’ high schools will each receive 30 panels while Ruatōria-based Ngata Memorial College will get 20.

The remaining 10 schools, including Tolaga Bay Area School, Muriwai School and Te Kura Kaupapa Māori ō Whatatutu, will each receive 10 panels.

East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick said the scheme would help schools reduce electricity costs while strengthening their resilience.

“Schools are facing the same pressures as households and businesses when it comes to rising operating costs, so finding practical ways to reduce their power bills makes good sense.

“On average, larger schools are expected to save around $8000 a year on electricity. That is money that can stay within our schools and be put towards what matters most – supporting our students and teachers in the classroom.”

Schools were selected based on energy efficiency, higher energy costs, resilience needs and upcoming gas or diesel boiler replacements, Kirkpatrick said.

“I’m looking forward to seeing this programme move from announcement to installation and seeing the benefits delivered in schools across the East Coast.”

Gisborne Boys’ High School principal Tom Cairns welcomed the decision.

“We’d taken out our gas heating a year or two ago, so we were in a position where we’re going to be running on electricity and running air conditioning.”

The installation would help with “exorbitant” cost increases and he hoped it would provide long-term savings for the school and Ministry of Education.

Gisborne Boys’ High and Ngata Memorial College had previously explored solar installation, but the cost of independent installation was too high.

Ngata principal Peter Heron said the Government initiative was “awesome”.

“It’ll cut costs in terms of our own bills, but more importantly, it’s going to increase resilience because with the weather events that come through we can have issues with power and connections up here.”

When power lines were damaged or power outages occurred, Heron said the school would be able to function as usual and key facilities like toilets would be unaffected.

While many students lived remotely and used solar, he said the panels would help the school promote clean energy to its ākonga [students].

Full details about installation and providers are yet to come, but site assessments are expected from December.

Heron said he hoped students would be able to learn about the impact the panels had on the school’s electricity through app-recorded data.

Native planting project grows into three nurseries on Clifton dairy farm

New Zealand Herald August 10, 2026

Sandra Campbell stands in one of her drone-seeded gullies. The plants have taken to the environment well. Photo / RNZ, Anisha Satya

By Anisha Satya of RNZ

Clifton farmer Sandra Campbell tries not to take life too seriously, so there was room to experiment when she began planting the gullies on her dairy farm with native shrubs.

“Inevitably this improves water quality because no one’s putting stock in here ... it should improve bird life at some stage,” she said.

“There’s offsetting of emissions. There’s all sorts. [But] we’ve just had a heap of fun along the way.

“We’ve met a heap of people, and it’s made farming a little bit more exciting.”

What began as an attempt to beautify some land has grown into three nurseries, a fridge full of seeds, and a blue Bedford named Beryl.

Campbell has documented her and her husband Chris’ “water care journey” on Instagram, taking viewers through the challenges and triumphs of harvesting native seeds and growing them.

She was inspired to try her hand at growing seedlings through her role as a catchment group facilitator.

“Covid happened, and we were not in the financial position to buy lots of trees, so I figured that I could give it a go,” she said.

“We started with one nursery, and then it extended to the other side of the shed and became a second nursery, and then it ended up in the tractor yard as a third nursery.

“We now grow about 4000 trees in the nursery on-farm as a hobby.”

There is a DIY spirit about the nursery: seedling houses made from pallets, an old water line and windbreak, a garden sprinkler and timer setup found on Temu.

Even the storage for the foraged seeds – the hand-collected jewels of the Campbells’ operation – is a repurposed fridge.

“You used to come in here, and it just smelled like mice,” Campbell said.

“Granny’s fridge broke down, so it got moved down here.”

Containers full of southern rātā, ake ake (Dodonaea viscosa) and more seed sit alongside paper bags and pillowcases of mixed seeds, and a tub of unprocessed mānuka branches.

“Seed collecting takes over the shed normally, and also sometimes my house, because I’m drying a lot.

“There’s a period of time between December to April that I’m very busy seed-collecting; I try and make weekends away to Te Anau or the Catlins so I can collect seed, and everybody I know who has ever holidayed with us has gotten roped in to helping.”

Some seeds get potted for the nursery, to be hand-planted in the gullies, or donated to other farmers who want to start their native planting journey.

The seed mixes were used for drone seeding, which was not commonly done when planting natives, but Campbell said it was cost-efficient.

“You could solely drone seed and not plant.

“If we did that, we could probably almost do it for free, bar the first drone visit.

“But it’s quite patchy... so it works well with the planting.”

Drone seeds take time to “strike”, some popping up years after they’ve been spread, but the plants that want to grow will, Campbell said.

“I just think nature sorts that out.

“If I plant something that shouldn’t be [there], it’ll die, and then we try something else.

“And when you’re growing it yourself, you get a bit less picky about things dying because you just haven’t [gone] and spent $10 on a tree for it to die.”

Aside from efficiency, Campbell said drone-seeded plants often passed the hand-planted ones, likely because they had not had their root structure handled.

She said six hectares of gully had been planted – but there were many more to go.

“It’s satisfying to see it grow and improve the farm.

“It’s like putting up a new fence if your fence line’s been awful.”

Bay of Plenty photographer David Hall has described a terrifying ordeal after being caught in a powerful earthquake that killed more than 100 people in Colombia.

Hall and his wife were in the town of Salento, about an hour south of the city of Pereira, when the magnitude 7.4 quake struck early on Tuesday morning local time.

Speaking while travelling by bus to Medellín, Hall said the shaking lasted several minutes and was so severe he struggled to stay on his feet.

“It went on for about three minutes in full ‘can’t stand up’ mode.”

Hall said they had been travelling through Central and South America for the past six weeks.

“Today’s our last day - going out with a bang.”

The couple were due to fly out of Pereira, near the epicentre, later that day but instead joined others seeking to leave the affected region.

“Currently on a six-hour bus to Medellín to escape,” he said in an email to SunLive.

Hall said early reports indicated significant damage in Pereira, while Salento appeared to have escaped the worst destruction.

“Salento damage is mostly collapsed roofs rather than whole buildings.”

Initial reports placed the quake’s epicentre in the country’s west at a depth of about 100km.

Hall said the earthquake was a “real wake-up call”.

He said it started as a light shake that felt like a standard New Zealand rumble, but it quickly intensified.

“We had to get out of the house, which, let’s face it, was probably quite badly constructed, given we’re in rural Colombia.

“Once outside, we clung to each other on the road for what seemed like ages. Power lines were swaying, buildings were rocking, and fortunately none of the structures near us came down.”

Hall said Salento was relatively unscathed, with mainly roof tiles knocked loose, but when they eventually reached Pereira it was a different story.

“There was massive damage, with power, phone and internet services down, and damaged buildings everywhere.

“The most amazing thing was seeing people already inside those buildings, starting to clean up. It clearly wasn’t remotely safe.”

Colombian authorities later declared a state of emergency as the death toll climbed.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said at least 111 people had died and dozens more had been injured, with the toll expected to rise as rescue crews searched damaged and collapsed buildings, AFP reported.

The hardest-hit areas were reported to be the coffee-growing Risaralda region and Valle del Cauca department, while major damage was also reported in cities, including Cali and Manizales.

News footage showed collapsed buildings, rescue operations and residents gathering in the streets after the quake, which was felt across neighbouring Ecuador, Panama and Venezuela.

Hall said the experience was unlike anything he had encountered before.

“More of a travel anecdote than a story, but it’s been a bit of a day.”

Authorities warned the number of casualties could increase as emergency teams continued searching through rubble and assessing damage across western Colombia.

The quake also disrupted transport infrastructure, with several airports suspending operations and communications outages reported in some areas.

For Hall, the priority was simply getting to safety as rescue efforts continued around the quake zone.

Waiuku murder trial: Witness says defendant was jovial after killing Judith Cunniffe in rural South Auckland

New Zealand Herald August 10, 2026

A man with name suppression accused of having murdered Judith Cunniffe in Waiuku in April 2025 appears in the High Court at Auckland. Photo / Michael Craig

WARNING: DISTRESSING CONTENT

“I sorted that c*** out once and for all.”

That is what a Waiuku man charged with murder is alleged to have told a witness the same night he beat a chicken hoarder to death amid a long-running meth-fuelled feud over her animals and his chook-chasing English bulldog.

David Moutray initially didn’t take the statement seriously because of the “blase” way in which the defendant said it, he told jurors in the High Court at Auckland yesterday as the third week of the murder trial began.

“He seemed happy enough,” the witness said, describing the defendant’s mood through the rest of the night as “quite jovial”.

“He wasn’t too deterred about anything,” he said.

The defendant, who has name suppression, has acknowledged through his lawyers that he beat Judith Rose Cunniffe, 53, to death on the evening of April 10 last year outside the rural South Auckland boarding house where she lived.

But they say the 51-year-old had no murderous intent and should instead be found guilty of manslaughter.

The witness, who wore a long black Western-style duster coat and styled the back end of his grey mullet into a bun as he sat in the witness box, said he “had a little puff” of methamphetamine with the defendant and others in the home not long after the “sorted out” comment.

Moutray said he asked about the whereabouts of some methylated spirits that had been in another bedroom and the defendant explained he had used the cleaning solution to wipe blood off a car.

“I didn’t really think that much of it either,” Moutray said.

About an hour or so later he finally realised it had been no joke when the defendant showed him Cunniffe’s body stuffed into her own car, he told jurors. The revelation came about, he said, when he asked the defendant how Cunniffe was getting along with a possum trap she had put in a nearby tree.

“Oh, I’m not sure but I’ve got a big possum in the back of that car,” he recounted the defendant saying before he opened the back door to Cunniffe’s car and her limp hand spilt out.

The victim had been stuffed upside down in the back, with her head in the footwell behind the driver’s seat, Moutray recalled. She was still wearing the colourful gloves she always put on to feed her chickens, he said.

Prosecutors said at the outset of the trial that Cunniffe and the defendant had clashed repeatedly over his dog chasing her chickens, to the point that the defendant had been trespassed.

Cunniffe was described by prosecutors as an animal lover whose interest in chickens had crossed the line to hoarding as her methamphetamine usage increased. She would often sleep in her car at the property while chickens stayed in her room, jurors were told.

“If you knew Judy Rose, you don’t get near her ducks or her chickens and cause any harm to them; otherwise, you’re in the s***,” said Moutray, who figured he knew both Cunniffe and the defendant for “30-odd years”.

He had arrived at the property at around lunchtime that day and had used a connection to get the defendant a half gram of methamphetamine for $150, he recalled.

Shortly after the drug was delivered, Cunniffe came into the room and pushed another woman who lived there off of her chair, the witness said, explaining that Cunniffe was livid because she thought the other woman had put her chooks in cages then neglected to feed them.

“Calm down, Judy Rose, and have a puff,” Moutray recalled telling her.

Cunniffe initially declined but then took the pipe and smoked all of the remnants, he said. Then she took what was left in the bag after finding out the defendant had paid for it, he said.

“He’s ripped me off enough - I’m taking that bag,” he recalled her saying as she left.

After realising the defendant was at the house, Cunniffe said she was going to ring the police and get his dog destroyed, the witness said.

Police did show up at the house later looking for the defendant, but he hid under a bed with his dog and police never found them, Moutray said.

He recalled leaving the house at about 6.30pm to do chores in Pukekohe, including picking up a methadone prescription for the other female resident. He saw Cunniffe sitting in her car as he left, he said.

“I know he’s in there, Davey,” he recalled her telling him. “When he comes out I’m going to take a photo and send it straight to police. I’ll see you when you get back.

“She seemed quite happy, knowing that he was there and she was going to snap him.”

He returned to the home about five hours later and smoked more meth before going inside, at which point he said the defendant first mentioned the killing then showed him the body.

“Something to do with her head didn’t look right,” he said. “To me, it looked like a soccer ball that was flat and pushed in. I didn’t look too much harder.”

After that point, he said, “things turned a little surreal” and “got a little bit fragmented” as he spent the rest of the night with the defendant and others until sunrise, continuing to use drugs.

“I thought, ‘Oh, he might have a gun or something like that,’” he said of not calling 111. “I just wanted to make sure he was gone and everyone was safe.”

Defence lawyer Sacha Norrie pointed to numerous inconsistencies between Moutray’s testimony and the three statements he gave police in the weeks following Cunniffe’s death. His testimony also differed at points with two other witnesses who were there that night.

“I didn’t see any obvious injuries and I didn’t see any blood,” he initially told police of Cunniffe’s body, mentioning nothing about a football.

Norrie suggested her client was “quiet and subdued” that night. She cited one of Moutray’s own police statements.

She also suggested that the witness was lying about hearing the defendant say he “sorted that c*** out” or making a joke about a possum in the back of the car.

“You have a good reason to exaggerate or put the boot in - to cover your own backside,” Norrie told the witness, suggesting that he was the one repeatedly suggesting ways to dispose of the body while her client remained quiet that night.

“That’s hideous,” he replied. “I don’t agree at all.”

Norrie called him the “ideas man” after discovering the body. He had his own violent history with Cunniffe, she suggested, and didn’t want the body found because it could lead police to suspect him.

“You invented or amped up the things [the defendant] had said,” she suggested.

Annoyed, the witness said he wasn’t going to justify the question with an answer. Justice Simon Mount said he had to.

“Bull****,” the witness muttered eventually in response to the question. “What was there to amp up?”

Moutray’s testimony lasted all but the last 30 minutes of the day. Prosecutors then called witness Miriam Snook, who met Moutray the day after Cunniffe’s death.

“He was distraught,” she said of Moutray. “He was just crying a lot - freaking out.”

She recalled Moutray saying the victim’s “face was caved in” and how the defendant seemed “proud of it”.

That same day she tried to reach her nephew, who is a police officer, she said. She went to police in person later that day, encouraging Moutray to go with her but he never showed, she said.

The trial continues today.

Craig Kapitan is an Auckland-based journalist covering courts and justice. He joined the Herald in 2021 and has reported on courts since 2002 in three newsrooms in the US and New Zealand.

Police didn’t know child victim’s name in reopened abuse case, documents reveal

New Zealand Herald August 10, 2026

Emails released to RNZ reveal how senior staff at Oranga Tamariki had concerns the agency could be "a bit over reliant on police's view" in the Child Protection Protocol process. Photo / NZ Herald

By Sam Sherwood of RNZ

A review into how police handled 40 child protection complaints has already triggered nine reports of suspected abuse or neglect. A series of documents obtained by RNZ reveal NZ Police did not know the name of a child victim whose case they had reopened, and that Oranga Tamariki was unaware of the major investigation until media began asking questions.

Eleven days before Oranga Tamariki was told of a major police investigation that involved the reopening of 40 child protection complaints, police sought its help to identify a child linked to one of the cases under review.

Five days later, on June 30, Oranga Tamariki (OT) replied saying it would grant access to the information request but, because of high demand, expected to provide the information by December.

Police responded saying staff were “taking another look at an older file we believe holds risk for both police and OT”.

“It has come to our attention because of a sensitive matter which I can’t elaborate on at this time.”

Internal police emails reveal the request was urgent because investigators needed information that would help identify the victim including the names and details of children placed in a person’s care.

Police warned that waiting until December for the information “is going to create significant problems in addressing this risk”.

The documents do not reveal what action, if any, OT took in response. It was not until July 6 that the agency was formally told about what police had dubbed Operation Hark.

More than 100 pages of emails released to RNZ under the Official Information Act reveal how Oranga Tamariki first learned of the investigation, its scramble to assess dozens of affected cases, and senior staff’s concern the agency could be “a bit over reliant on police’s view” in the Child Protection Protocol process.

RNZ can also reveal that nine reports of concern have been created as a result of the NZ Police and Oranga Tamariki review of the identified cases.

Operation Hark began after concerns were raised in May about Detective Inspector Kevan Verry’s handling of a historical sexual abuse case in Northland that had sat for a couple of years with no investigation. The initial case sparked a further review where another 13 cases were identified as requiring re-investigation.

Police also carried out a rapid review of about 1000 files which were under Verry’s oversight, with a further 40 cases identified for re-investigation. A team of specialist child protection and adult sexual assault investigators had been pulled together to work on the re-opened cases.

On June 25, police sent the information request to Oranga Tamariki. Five days later they got a response from OT saying they would grant their request.

“As we are currently receiving more requests than anticipated, we are experiencing delays in processing these.”

OT said it would supply the information by December 7.

A police staffer, whose name is redacted from the OIA, sent an email that went to Detective Superintendent Uraia Vakaruru and another staff member asking if they had any way of fast-tracking the request.

One of the recipients asked what the file related to and said they would follow up with their contact at OT.

The staffer replied with information about the case (this information is redacted in the OIA).

“I have attached the IR that I submitted to OT – I did request a lot of information from them but the most important part was the names and details of children placed in her care as that would help us identify the victim.”

One of the staff then emailed a staff member at OT saying they were taking another look at an older file “which we believe holds risk for both police and OT”.

“It has come to our attention because of a sensitive matter which I can’t elaborate on at this time.

“What I can say is that this IR relates to [redacted] so there is obvious risk and additional scrutiny attached to this.”

Police asked for the request to be “escalated in the priority queue”.

“The estimated response time of December 2026 by OT is going to create significant problems in addressing the risk.”

On July 6, OT chief social worker Nicolette Dickson sent an email to six staff including deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan and national commissioner north Alison Cronin advising them she had just been contacted by an assistant commissioner at NZ Police who was managing a “conduct issue” relating to one of their Child Protection Protocol (CPP) investigators.

“It appears that this information in quite significant detail has been leaked to media …” Dickson said.

An urgent meeting was being set up for OT and police staff that afternoon.

“One of the key issues for me is that the CPP process is a joint process and we will need to assure ourselves that we took appropriate steps for at least the 30 cases where gaps have been raised.

“We can be a bit over-reliant on police’s view in the CPP process so we will need to check we took appropriate steps from a child safety/wellbeing perspective.”

Ronan later emailed Assistant Commissioner Tusha Penny asking to have a chat before a meeting that was planned for later in the week as OT needed to do “some assessment work off the back of it”.

Penny cc’d in Assistant Commissioner Corrie Parnell who was in charge of investigations and asked him to have someone forward details relating to each child protection case to OT.

Later that evening, a member of the police’s media team emailed OT’s media team with a copy of a statement that would be sent to media about Operation Hark.

The statement included a line that said police were “working with Oranga Tamariki, IPCA and other agencies, as we progress this matter”.

OT chief of staff Stephanie Short replied in an internal email querying the line about working with OT and asked whether that referred to the meeting that was scheduled to take place later that week or the initial call that Dickson received earlier that day.

“I’m also concerned from our minister’s office perspective about what and when we knew about this issue when the police media response indicates we are working together.”

On July 7, an email was sent to a group of OT staff about the operation in Te Tai Tokerau relating to concerns about CPP work.

The staffer who sent the email – whose name is redacted – said they had told chief adviser Simon Harding that the group of staff would be happy to be part of any work OT undertakes to look at the cases that have been identified so far.

“I noted we will have been across lots of these and we have noted some cases where delays occurred or decisions to not take actions.

“I will let you know when I hear more, it is great to see police moving to address the concerns and responding publicly as a team we have seen how serious things have been up in TTT for some time.”

That morning RNZ approached OT with questions about Operation Hark.

Ronan emailed police and said media requests had been received and OT hoped to get the case details from police “as soon as possible”.

A police staffer said two staff were assigned to sorting the information and hoped to have it completed by the following day.

In a separate email exchange on July 7, Harding emailed some staff about the list of cases that was coming on July 8 and said they would need a “structured spreadsheet or template” to use to inform the reviews.

He then listed a series of possible things to cover including did OT know, and what actions OT took.

“Possibly something about what the Police told us? (unsure about this one, I am getting at the potential issue we may find of Police telling us things are fine when there is insufficient information to take that at face value, or perhaps that was about prosecution and we used it as the reason to close without considering safety and wellbeing more broadly? This could instead be a consideration under other areas).”

Harding also suggested questions around safety.

“I. e. is there evidence to show we considered safety risks and (if needed) either addressed them or were satisfied they were addressed? Are you worried about child safety after taking a look??”

Ronan told RNZ OT had completed a review of all cases identified by police as potentially impacted and which involved children, all of whom were under-18 at the time of reporting to police.

“We did not identify any cases requiring urgent intervention to keep children safe.

“However, we continue to work with police locally to consider each case, share information, and determine any further actions required.”

Asked how many of the CPP cases required further action by OT, Ronan said the agency had worked with police on most of the cases identified thus far to determine what further response was appropriate. This included engaging with children and families.

“Nine reports of concern have been created as a result of the police and Oranga Tamariki review of the identified cases,” he said.

A report of concern is a notification to Oranga Tamariki about suspected abuse, neglect, harm, or wellbeing concerns for a child or young person.

RNZ also approached police for comment on the OIA including why the victim’s name was not known and why Oranga Tamariki was not informed of the investigation before July 6.

In response, Detective Superintendent Keith Borrell said police had made specific inquiries with OT “during an early and sensitive stage of our investigations”.

“During the initial assessment phase of Operation Hark we were working to understand the scale of the situation. We have shared more fulsome information once it was appropriate to do so with OT.”

Borrell said police were “not in a position to comment on specific cases that are in the re-investigation phase”.

Christchurch man fined $255 after parking unregistered Mazda at mechanic, despite having what he says is a good defence

New Zealand Herald August 10, 2026

When Christchurch man Liam Senior returned from a year living abroad, one of the first things he wanted to do was get his beloved Mazda MX-5 back on the road.

What he didn’t anticipate was a $255 fine after parking the unregistered car outside a mechanic while taking it in for a warrant of fitness – despite New Zealand vehicles having to pass one before they can even be registered.

Senior had put the car’s registration on hold while overseas. After returning to New Zealand, he began the renewal process and booked the car in for a warrant of fitness on February 4.

He was unable to pull into the mechanic’s carpark, and parked outside the building.

“I parked on the side of the road directly outside of their driveway and then went to check in with them,” Senior said.

While the car was parked, a parking warden ticketed it for not having a registration.

Senior later discovered the fine when the bill arrived in the mail.

He contacted the Christchurch City Council parking compliance team to explain what happened.

“I’d sort of explained my situation that I was overseas, which is why the registration was so far out of date, that I was taking it to a mechanic to be repaired,” he said.

Senior said he also provided a copy of the mechanic’s invoice as evidence of the inspection.

However, he said the compliance team declined to void the fine.

“[Parking compliance] doesn’t consider that I’ve directly taken the car to a place of repair or inspection because it was parked on the road and vehicle inspections do not take place on the road,” Senior said.

Senior said he was also told “businesses aren’t allowed to use the road as an extension of their business” before being informed the team would not respond to further correspondence.

Under section 77 of the Land Transport (Motor Vehicle Registration and Licensing) Regulations 2011, a person commits an offence if they operate an unregistered motor vehicle.

However, under the same legislation, taking a vehicle for repairs is a valid defence for a stationary or moving vehicle.

Senior believes that defence applies to him.

“It seems to be a pretty common practice, and there’s lots of mechanics that will, once they’ve finished working on it, will take them out of their yard and park them on the side of the road for customers to collect,” Senior said.

“I would hope that most people would agree with me in saying that parking directly outside of the entrance to a mechanic because you weren’t able to directly drive in is still effectively directly bringing it to a mechanic.”

The dispute continued for seven months, with Senior also contacting local MPs to challenge the fine.

At the end of July, he received a “Notice of Court Fine” in the mail instructing him to pay $255.

For Senior, the fine has become more than a parking dispute.

He said it was “disappointing” that after a year overseas, his first few months back in New Zealand were spent disputing the fine.

“At the moment, we have lots and lots of Kiwis leaving [for] overseas because it’s quite difficult for living in New Zealand at the moment with the cost of living,” he said.

“I’ve recently returned, and I feel like I’ve been treated very badly, and I feel like I was treated much better overseas in Japan.

“I think most people would just pay the fine rather than deal with it.

“It seems that I might be forced to do that myself as well because at this point I’m not sure what other course of action I have.”

He wanted other Kiwis who had been overseas and were looking to return to know that “New Zealand is perhaps not what it once was”.

“It feels like this society that I once enjoyed has now become a whole lot meaner and less forgiving, and it’s really disappointing.”

The Herald approached Christchurch City Council for comment on why Senior’s appeal was declined, whether staff had considered his defence, and whether the council believed it was being fair.

The council said it was “satisfied with the decision made in respect to this matter”.

Jazlyn Whales is a multimedia journalist based in the Christchurch newsroom.

Solar panel fears: The shadow of a fight over Napier’s six-storey high-density future

New Zealand Herald August 10, 2026

Lyndon Watson (inset) says his family are working to protect the rights of people investing in clean energy across New Zealand.

A Napier family who spent $110,000 on a premium solar power system for their home have fears the sale of a $9 million Kāinga Ora residential property opposite them could cast a literal shadow over their investment.

Lyndon Watson, who is the family trust’s managing trustee, said they had installed a 44-panel residential photovoltaic network – with LG NeON 2 panels and three Tesla Powerwalls – at their Hall St property in October 2020.

The installation required structural work under the house to install heavy-duty pilings and foundation reinforcements to support the weight of the battery bank vault, switchboard upgrades for the family’s main house and cottage, improved property earthing and network connection and inspection fees.

But the family now fear the system could be overshadowed by future development.

Napier City Council has proposed allowing non-notified six-storey developments on dozens of streets near the central city and Taradale under its new District Plan, which is currently going through 12 separate Environment Court appeals.

One of the 1595 properties proposed to be opened up for six-storey development is a 39-home complex opposite the Watsons’ home, owned by Kāinga Ora.

In June, Kāinga Ora regional director for East North Island Graeme Broderick said the units in a “high-value area” had reached the end of their life as social housing and it now made financial sense to sell them.

The complex, opposite Napier Health on Wellesley Rd with entrances and homes facing Hall St and Nelson Cres, has a capital value (CV) of nearly $9m.

Watson said he feared his family’s fully decoupled, asset-protected residential micro-grid was now at risk of being ruined by a developer swooping in, buying the Kāinga Ora complex and building a six-storey, 19.5m-high high-density housing development in its place.

He said a development of that size, if allowed under the District Plan, would block the sun during the home’s peak power-generating hours.

“This home represents our entire, multi-generational family estate and our lifetime investment into renewable energy resilience,” Watson said.

“Every dollar went directly into bringing this integrated infrastructure online. My parents knew (and I knew), that I would not be able to afford electricity once they were gone, once I went on superannuation, which I did last year,” he said.

“A high-rise built anywhere within that massive site will project a sweeping shadow that completely jumps the tight road gap, burying our infrastructure in darkness.”

Harrison’s Solar Hawke’s Bay owner Laura Duncan provided Watson with an updated return-on-investment assessment, based on a situation where a six-storey apartment building was built approximately 10m north of the existing dwelling.

In it, Duncan wrote that in her professional opinion, a development would significantly diminish the performance and financial return of the system – from generation of 46.9 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of power a day to just 28.0kWh/day.

Duncan said the Watsons’ annual savings would drop from $5190 to $2850, with the payback more than doubling from 12-and-a-half years to 26 years.

Watson said his family were speaking out now to protect the rights of people investing in clean energy across New Zealand.

Watson said he had also approached the National MP for Napier, Katie Nimon, for help over his concerns.

Nimon said her office took the concerns seriously, making inquiries with the relevant agencies, raising the broader policy issues with the appropriate ministers and advocating on Watson’s behalf throughout the process.

“The specific situation remains hypothetical, as there is no confirmed development proposal and the property is not currently for sale,” she said.

“Without a defined proposal, there is limited scope for further action.

“While I appreciate the constituent is disappointed, MPs cannot intervene in individual property or planning matters or direct the decisions of government agencies.”

Watson said the issue was not going to go away.

“Eventually the property will be sold, as will others in the new high-density zones.

“It’s not just our family that will have to deal with huge buildings towering over our home, blocking out the sun.”

Watson said he wanted covenants, caveats or sale conditions to be placed on the site, mandating that any “private developer purchasing the site must step back, tier or design the northern facade of the future structure to preserve the existing solar path of 8 Hall Street”.

In correspondence seen by Local Democracy Reporting (LDR) between Kāinga Ora and Nimon’s office, Kāinga Ora’s manager, ministerial services, Emma Atkins, wrote: “Kāinga Ora will offer the property for sale and is not marketing it for any specific outcome, development type or future use.

“The tender process will not specify or require a particular development proposal.

“Consequently, Kāinga Ora is unable to provide information regarding any potential future development, site layout, building massing or associated shading effects.

“Assessing the property’s development potential and undertaking any related due diligence is the responsibility of prospective purchasers.”

Kāinga Ora regional director east North Island Graeme Broderick told LDR the agency understood that changes to neighbouring properties could create uncertainty.

“However, once a property is sold, Kāinga Ora has no role in, or influence over, how it may be developed in the future,” Broderick said.

Napier’s proposed District Plan is facing 12 appeals lodged with the Environment Court.

A spokeswoman for the Environment Court said some appeals against the plan had been resolved, but others were continuing.

“I am unable to say when the appeals will be heard, or if they will be at all,” she said.

“At this stage, no hearing time has been sought or directed. Consequently, I cannot advise when a decision [on the District Plan] is expected.”

They said numerous decisions resolving specific topics and appeals would likely be issued throughout the proceedings.

Napier City Council said its proposed District Plan – first proposed in 2023 and amended in 2025 – was not yet fully operative.

It said the proposed high-density residential provisions showed where buildings of up to six storeys could be built, but that didn’t mean every site would have a six-storey development.

“The council cannot comment on the potential impact of a hypothetical future development on an individual property or solar installation.

“Any future development would need to be assessed against the planning provisions that apply at the time.”

In a Talking Point in Hawke’s Bay Today on the proposed District Plan in November 2023, former Napier Mayor Kirsten Wise wrote that Napier had a housing problem.

She said the council would look to introduce medium- and high-density residential zones around commercial centres and main transport routes, away from natural hazards.

“We envisage high-density residential zones could be terraced homes and urban apartment living up to six storeys close to Napier city centre and Taradale town centre.”

Under Napier’s proposed District Plan, 1595 properties would be rezoned to allow high-density residential use on a non-notified basis.

The streets where the properties were located were:

Nelson Cres, Kennedy Rd, Higgins St, Georges Drive, Peddie St, Mckenzie Ave, Herrick St, Gloucester St, Avondale Rd, Devon St, Douglas Mclean Ave, Hammond Rd, Wellesley Rd, Eton Rd, Hastings St, Carnell St, Jull St, Church Rd, Gebbie Rd, White St, Oxford St, Puketapu Rd, Meeanee Rd, Devonshire Place, Roskilda Cres, Marine Parade, Hall St, Latham St, Murphy Rd, Elbourne St, Winifred St, McDonald St, Munroe St, Lee Rd, Gebbie St, Sale St, Owen St, Neeve Rd, Storkey Rd, Russell Rd, Thackeray St, Nuffield Ave, Wilding Ave and Weatherfield Mews.

Burnham to give councils more powers to block vape and betting shops

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 21:30:05 GMT

Vape shops in England and Wales to need planning permission while betting shop law change will also apply in Scotland

Councils are to be given powers to stop betting and vape shops taking over their high streets under new plans announced by Andy Burnham.

Local authorities will be able to reject new betting shops and adult gaming centres, while vape shops will be subject to planning permission under plans Downing Street said could be in place from the start of next year.

Burnham is promising to scrap the “aim to permit” rule in the Gambling Act 2005, which in effect requires councils to allow new gambling premises where applications meet licensing requirements.

This could mark a big shift from changes introduced by his predecessor, Keir Starmer, in April that gave councils more of an ability to consider the number of gambling premises already in an area but stopped short of scrapping the “aim to permit rule”.

As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called on Starmer to abolish the rule in January, alongside almost 300 other politicians and campaigners.

Burnham said communities should have much more control over their high streets where traditional shops, pubs and other services have disappeared while vape and gambling shops have expanded.

The push fits into Burnham’s attempt to make the first weeks of his prime ministership about tangible changes people can see in their everyday lives.

A No 10 source said the government was determined to crack down on vape and betting shops because they were two of the most visible signs of decline on high streets, and local people were genuinely concerned. A fast-tracked consultation on the new measures would take six weeks, with the aim of having the measures in place by the start of 2027.

“Local people will actually have more of an input into whether or not those shops should open in the first place, giving them a proper say about how their high streets should look,” they said.

The move comes after research suggested Labour would be “washed away in a tide of discontent” at the next general election unless it tackled the decline of Britain’s high streets.

Prof Will Jennings, who led the University of Southampton research, said Burnham’s targeting of vape and betting shops was “an important first step”. However, with nearly one in three retail sales in the UK now online, it was clear that the policy would “not solve everything”, he said. “But it is speaking to some real area of concern that impacts how people view their local area.”

Vape shops currently fall into the same planning category as shops, cafes and even banks meaning they can open without needing a new planning application. Ministers will consult on putting them into their own planning category so councils will be able to consider each new vape shop application individually and reject those they deem not appropriate for the area.

The government is also looking at tightening the definition of what a vape shop is, to prevent people saying they were opening a convenience store that had the primary function of selling vapes as well as provisions to specifically stop them opening near schools. Angela Rayner said the move addressed problems that had built up over decades. “That’s why we’re giving local leaders the power to say no to what doesn’t belong on their high street, and the tools to fix it themselves,” the communities secretary said.

Jennings said the government also needed to tackle opaque ownership structures of high street property, which allows some landowners “who aren’t necessarily that motivated to have shops in their property”.

The growth of vape shops is not evenly spread, with research from Health Equity North highlighting the most deprived communities had three times as many vape shops as the most affluent areas.

Burnham said high streets had become “unrecognisable” after decades of decline. “The rise of vape shops, betting shops and rogue operators have replaced the shops, services, and community spaces that people are crying out for.

“That’s not on. I said we would improve Britain’s high streets, and that’s exactly what we are starting to do.”

The measures are seen as a “first step” on a wider beautification of Britain’s high streets, with Westminster setting clearer expectations for the design and appearance of high street shopfronts.

Local leaders will be encouraged to look at blueprints for ideal high streets, and given examples of what works best and how they can improve the look of their own main shopping areas.

Dawn Butler, the MP for Brent East, who has campaigned on the issue, said: “It was a real shock to me to discover, during a previous visit to a high street with the Guardian, just how much money gambling machines can generate.

“Government analysis of Gambling Commission data found that B3 machines generated an average of £35,000 in gross gambling yield per machine each year. That figure really brought home to me the scale of the gambling industry’s presence on our high streets and why they would want multiple shops on the high street to maximise their profits.

“To put it in perspective, the national living wage for someone aged 21 or over works out at around £26,400 a year for someone working 40 hours a week. And in Brent the average wage is less than £35k. That experience underlined for me why urgent action was needed.”

Britain’s Amy Hunt powers to emphatic 100m European gold to thrill home crowd

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 21:29:49 GMT

24-year-old secures title in 11.00sec in Birmingham

Norway win 4x400m mixed relay, Britain second

Britain’s Amy Hunt sprinted to women’s 100m glory to take a brilliant gold at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham. The 24-year-old came into the event as favourite, having won world silver over 200m in Tokyo and 100m at the Commonwealth Games a fortnight ago – and she delivered in emphatic style.

Hunt is never the quickest starter. In truth, she started like a woman whose spikes had been superglued to her blocks. But she came through at the finish to win in 11.00sec. Ewa Swoboda of Poland took silver in 11.02 and Delphine Nkansa claimed bronze for Belgium in 11.06.

Moments earlier there was also a plucky silver for Great Britain’s mixed 4x400m relay team behind the gold medallists Norway. Britain’s team of Ben Jeffries, Charlotte Henrich, Toby Harries and Yemi Mary John all ran well. But a Norway team spearheaded by the 400m hurdles world record-holder Karsten Warholm and the fastest woman in Europe this year, Henriette Jæger, were too strong with a championship record of 3:09.62, nearly a second clear of Britain.

The only disappointment was that more people were not here to witness it given that the Alexander Stadium, which seats around 20,000, looked barely half full.

However, organisers told the Guardian 13,623 tickets had been sold for the Monday night – along with 170,000 tickets for the week – and that from Thursday night onwards the event was pretty much a sellout.

Britain’s Max Burgin was deeply puzzled after he bombed out in the Commonwealth Games in the semi‑finals 12 days ago – before realising later in the day that he was in the early stages of a nasty virus. The 24‑year‑old has barely run since, but he looked much more like his old self on Monday in winning a stacked 800m heat in 1min 45.80sec.

“The doctor said it was a virus so I had to take three or four days off, which I did, and when I got back into running after that I still felt rough so it just sort of dragged on for a bit longer than expected,” he said.

“Last week I’ve not managed to do too much running at all really and the bits that I have done haven’t inspired much confidence, so I really wasn’t too sure. I went into this heat just thinking I’d approach it a bit more conservatively. Sit off a little bit to start with, run a bit more traditional tactics. But we ended up being a lot faster than the Commonwealth Games heat.

“I was happy with how I ran it. Happy with my kick finish which is always good to know I’ve still got one. I don’t often see it. It was a good run out. I’m looking forward to the semis.”

Ben Pattison also made it through as the fastest non-automatic qualifier, finishing fourth in his heat but advancing with the fifth-fastest time overall in 1:45.40. “I tried to make a big move on the back straight and my legs weren’t really there, and then I kind of got caught up,” he said.

Ireland’s Mark English looked the best of the other qualifiers for the semi-finals on Wednesday, but his compatriot Cian McPhillips, who had reached the world 800m finals in Tokyo last year, is out after running far below his level because of a virus.

Asked whether she could challenge for a medal, she said: “Anything can happen in the final. I’m just taking it race by race. I think the semis will be very difficult, so my plan is to recover as best I can.”

“I am happy with how I performed no matter what happens,” Norris said. “I am not much of a morning person, I struggled with the early wake up. But I am proud of how I have been throwing and training has been going well.

“Today was a reflection of how well training has been going. I was disappointed with my performance at Commonwealths, it felt like I didn’t show my capability. Today I got it back.”

Trump demands Iran pay compensation for decades of US soldier deaths

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 20:45:52 GMT

US president’s statement is latest sign that negotations to end war and reopen strait of Hormuz have stalled

Donald Trump has said he will demand that Iran pay compensation for the deaths of thousands of US soldiers and Iran’s own civilians killed in recent decades in the latest sign his negotiations to end the war and reopen the strait of Hormuz have reached an impasse.

The US president is trying to end conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Lebanon, and his additional demands of Iran are likely to provoke anger in Tehran at the same time as Israel has rejected Trump’s terms for a 15-point roadmap to end the war in Gaza.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response to Iranian negotiators making similar claims for damages for the five-month war that has killed thousands and devastated Iran’s military and economy.

“Now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by Gen Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat,” he wrote on Truth Social.

“Additionally, compensation should be paid to the families of the hundreds of thousands of innocent protesters that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months.”

The demands are likely to be a nonstarter for Iran’s leaders in the careful peace negotiations aimed at reopening the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of global oil trade flowed before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in late February. Trump and other senior negotiators have claimed many times that a deal is imminent, although none has materialised.

The remarks followed a series of setbacks for Trump’s efforts to end several Middle East conflicts before the midterm elections in November, in which high oil prices and inflation will probably hurt fellow Republicans at the polls.

On Sunday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he rejected the Trump-backed Board of Peace’s 15-point plan to end Israel’s war in Gaza. Netanyahu had said Hamas must fully disarm before Israel would consider pulling out of Gaza, rather than the phased withdrawal proposed by the Board of Peace.

Netanyahu framed the decision as a rejection of US pressure on Israel to make peace in several wars in the Middle East. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said.

Trump has not replied to Netanyahu’s statement, which was a remarkably public break between the leaders of the US and its closest ally in the Middle East. But in response to a shouted question in the Oval Office on Monday, he said his relationship with Netanyahu was “very good”.

Trump has sought to increase pressure on Iran. An hour after his first post demanding war reparations from Tehran, he broadened their scope to include the victims of recent wars throughout the region.

“Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!” he wrote.

Ann Widdecombe police investigate whether accused had role in Farage incident

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 18:46:20 GMT

Police looking into whether Joshua Kerry linked to alleged attempted burglary last year at Reform leader’s then home

Police are investigating whether Joshua Kerry, the man charged with the murder of the former Reform UK and Conservative politician Ann Widdecombe, had any role in an attempted burglary last year at the then London home of Nigel Farage.

Kerry, 28, from Rotherham, was charged with the murder of Widdecombe, 78, who was killed at her Devon home in July, after an investigation by counter-terrorism police.

On Friday, police said they were reinvestigating an incident in April 2025 at a London address where Farage was living at the time, which they have said was an attempted burglary. Other sources describe it as an attempted arson.

Police attended the incident, which they initially recorded primarily as a burglary. The Guardian understands detectives are studying fingerprints taken from the scene, as well as video from CCTV cameras in the area and from devices such as video doorbells. They examined the scene to see if an accelerant, such as lighter fluid, was used.

On Friday, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said it had referred itself to the police watchdog over the initial investigation of the April 2025 incident.

It said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.

“In April 2025, the Metropolitan police received a report of an attempted burglary at an address in the Greater London area. Enquiries were carried out by the Metropolitan police, supported by Counter Terrorism Policing London. No arrests were made and the investigation was subsequently closed, pending any new lines of inquiry.

“Following the reopening of the attempted burglary investigation, Counter Terrorism Policing London identified a line of enquiry which was not identified and pursued by them at the time, which may have been relevant. As a result, to ensure their support to the initial investigation is thoroughly reviewed, Counter Terrorism Policing London made a mandatory conduct referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct today.”

On Monday, Farage said at a press conference: “It’s a great, great tragedy that it took the death of Ann for the security services in Britain to finally take seriously the safety and security of Reform politicians and Reform prominent figures.”

He said he now had confidence in counter-terrorism police and said they were not trying to cover anything up.

The Reform leader said of CTP’s decision to refer itself to the IOPC: “The fact they’ve done that shows you they’re not trying to cover up, they’re not trying to ignore, and I have to say I have met Laurence Taylor [the head of CTP] and I did feel a great, great confidence in it.”

Widdecombe’s body was found with “serious injuries” by paramedics at her home in Haytor Vale, Devon, at 11.40am on Thursday 9 July.

Kerry’s first court appearance in July heard that Widdecombe died after being hit on the head with a hammer 21 times in her home. Police have said they believed the 78-year-old former minister was attacked the day before her body was found.

The attack on Widdecombe has not yet been declared a terrorist incident. CTP took the lead in the investigation because of the possibility there may have been a political motive behind her killing.

Berger, who is Jewish, asked whether Bonehill-Paine’s new role could bring him to Westminster. She wrote on X: “Can I expect to come face to face with him on the parliamentary estate?”

Badenoch’s spokesperson said Bonehill-Paine would not have a parliamentary pass and would not be on the estate.

Berger’s intervention came after the Conservative party leader published a lengthy defence of Bonehill-Paine in the Times, describing questions over his suitability to stand as a councillor in Somerset as a “pile-on”.

Bonehill-Paine was set to stand as a Tory local councillor but announced last week that he had withdrawn from next year’s local elections after Badenoch offered him the advisory role.

Badenoch said: “People need to understand that the Conservative party under my leadership is now the party of personal responsibility and law and order. That means insisting on consequences by punishing wrongdoing and protecting the public, especially victims.

We should be tough enough to stand by our beliefs even when politically inconvenient, wise enough to recognise rehabilitation and consistent enough to apply the same principles to friend and foe.”

Berger said she had seen the piece late on Saturday night and “tried to ignore it” but after Badenoch shared the article on Monday, the former MP for Liverpool Wavertree accused her of giving insufficient consideration to Bonehill-Paine’s victims.

“It’s still not too late for Badenoch to listen to victims and reverse her decision.”

A spokesperson for Badenoch said Bonehill-Paine had served his time, completed Home Office Prevent (counter-terrorism) courses, and had gone into schools to teach about combatting antisemitism and extremism. But the party did not answer questions about what safeguarding checks it had carried out in relation to his appointment as an adviser, or why Badenoch had not contacted Berger.

The abuse Bonehill-Paine directed at Berger included calling her a “rodent” and an “evil money-grabber”. He also has a conviction for assaulting a police officer and burglary of a police station, and was convicted in 2014 of malicious communications over an anti-Islam hoax that led to death threats against the owners of a pub in Leicester.

Berger challenged Badenoch over what consideration had been given to safeguarding: “Badenoch’s article says she wants to safeguard the public and victims, but what safeguarding checks have she and the Conservative party carried out?”

If Badenoch or her team had reached out to her, Berger said, “I would say, I don’t think it is ‘harder politics’ for this man to be part of Kemi’s operation. I think it’s the wrong politics.”

She added: “I’m all for rehabilitation. But someone convicted of neo-Nazi misogynistic crimes is not suitable for public office less than a decade after his conviction. And neither should he be gifted a national advisory role, even closer to power.”

The Guardian view on the failed Gaza peace plan: Trump’s hollow claims are ignored in Jerusalem

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 17:47:44 GMT

Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has no interest in agreeing to a deal. For relief to come to Gaza, real US pressure must be exerted

At the end of July, Donald Trump announced that a “monumental” US-backed deal had been struck on Gaza, securing the phased disarmament of Hamas in parallel with Israeli military withdrawal. Three days later it was reported that another 18 people had died in Israeli airstrikes. Not for the first time, it appeared that Mr Trump’s rhetoric had only a distant relationship with the reality it purported to describe.

Such suspicions were duly confirmed yesterday. Under pressure from far-right members of his coalition, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, explicitly rejected the sequencing of a 15-point plan from the increasingly hapless Board of Peace – an international body set up by the US president – and poured scorn on “a wave of rumours of … Israeli withdrawals on all fronts”. In a direct message to the White House, Mr Netanyahu stated that “we know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary.”

In practical terms that will mean the continued, brazen violation of the terms of last October’s ceasefire agreement, since when close to 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli air assaults. Far from envisaging any withdrawal, the Israeli military has expanded its presence and now controls about 65% of the territory. Hemmed in towards the coast in the rest of the strip, much of the population faces an unrelenting daily struggle.

Formal schooling has not restarted, the healthcare system has been largely destroyed and the entry of medical and other humanitarian aid remains severely restricted. Reconstruction work has been blocked, while the first building contract issued by the Board of Peace has been for an outpost to host foreign troops. Meanwhile, the world’s attention has shifted to Mr Trump’s illegal and reckless war on Iran – a grievous miscalculation in which Israel’s prime minister also played his part.

In calling for complete Hamas disarmament before Israel makes a move, Mr Netanyahu is transparently playing for time. For two years he has relentlessly flattered the US president, and exploited his backing to pursue a scorched earth project of revenge following the Hamas massacre of October 7. But two months out from the first elections held since then, his priority now is appeasing the intransigent far-right forces who can keep him in power. Should Mr Netanyahu lose, he could face jail in relation to corruption charges first laid more than five years ago.

Despairing Palestinians can only hope that growing White House frustration with Mr Netanyahu’s forever wars will lead to a tipping point – one that should have been reached during the Joe Biden presidency. If he opted to use it, Mr Trump has the power to isolate the Israeli prime minister, call time on his temporising and manoeuvring, and compel a different approach. Board of Peace attempts yesterday to reassure the Israeli government over the verification process for disarming Hamas indicate that we are not close to that point.

Nevertheless, ahead of challenging midterm elections for the Republicans, pro-Israel sentiment may not be the political force that it once was. Recent polling suggests that traditionally high levels of US public sympathy with Israel are on the wane. Mr Trump has a choice: he can continue to accept being played by Israel’s prime minister, or he can exert the kind of pressure that could bring genuine relief to Gaza.
