The Guardian view on Meta’s smart glasses: regulators must get on the front foot

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 17:47:18 GMT

Privacy needs defending against invasive wearable gadgets. So far, businesses are ahead of the government

It is not yet clear to what extent Meta’s new smart glasses will live up to the nickname of “pervert glasses” – bestowed in recognition of the obvious appeal of wearable cameras to voyeurs. The past week has seen rising criticism of the devices, which in the UK have been banned by the pub chain Wetherspoons and the theatre group ATG, as well as restaurants, schools and members’ clubs. These organisations deserve praise for standing up for privacy. By contrast, regulators appear once again to be on the back foot.

There have, inevitably, already been reports of women being mistreated. Earlier this year the BBC spoke to several who had been filmed without their consent, with footage subsequently uploaded to social media. In one case, the content creator demanded a fee to remove it. In the year to March 2025, image-based sexual abuse and cyberflashing were responsible for more than half of an 11% increase in reported sexual offences in England and Wales. Normalisation of smart glasses would, clearly, make such offences easier to commit.

Worrying as this is, it is not the only reason to be concerned. Privacy has much wider significance and most people, as the businesses banning smart glasses from their premises have recognised, do not want to be filmed as they go about their lives. While videoing in public is not illegal, this does not give smart glasses wearers the right to place others under involuntary surveillance. An LED light that blinks when the camera is in use, and cannot be disabled, is not an adequate safeguard, whatever Meta might think. Pubs, parks, beaches and workplaces are not film sets.

Having invested $80bn in its latest product, Mark Zuckerberg’s company is unlikely to give up easily on its ambition to make the glasses, which have been likened to face-mounted smartphones, as ubiquitous as the handheld kind. More than a decade after the first smart glasses, made by Google, flopped, Meta has bet heavily on making its latest version more stylish, functional and affordable – with UK prices starting at £269. The choice of Kylie Jenner to front this summer’s advertising campaign, and the slogan “Never miss a moment”, aimed at parents of young children, appear calculated to dispel fears about how the glasses will be used by sexually predatory men.

Like most digital devices, these ones can be helpful as well as harmful. As aids for people who are blind or visually impaired, smart glasses that can read text or describe images have been described as life-changing. Any restrictions, in the UK or elsewhere, should be crafted so as to enable such uses to continue – just as guide dogs are exempted from rules about pets. But while the benefits that smart glasses offer to groups of people with specific needs should be recognised, this must not be allowed to distract from their potential to cause harm.

Tech regulation is difficult. But given the UK government’s recent moves towards restricting smartphone use among young people, and the public outcry regarding sexualised AI imagery, it is disappointing that ministers have so far had almost nothing to say about the rollout of wearable hidden cameras. While the tech companies market their products as tools to be used, one of the key lessons of the last two decades is that users are rarely, if ever, as in control as they would like to be. Ministers and regulators should be active, not passive, as Meta intentionally blurs the line between looking and filming.

Water companies circumventing bonus rules? What did ministers expect?

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 17:44:09 GMT

Door was left open to such behaviour because the regulator for England and Wales can only use the powers it was given by parliament

Thames Water’s £1m payout to finance chief is ‘unacceptable’, says government department

Anybody who followed the supposed “clampdown” on bankers’ bonuses after the great financial crash in 2008 knew what to expect when water company bosses became a similar target for a bash in the bonus department. We would see the waterbed principle in action: when you push down in one area of remuneration, such as the performance-related stuff, another tends to go up.

Back in the day, banks invented “role-based allowances” – salary top-ups – to “compensate”, as they put it, their top earners for being subject to EU caps on bonuses. No executive was seriously inconvenienced by forgoing the chance of an astronomical (but not guaranteed) bonus and getting a smaller (but still hefty) increase in fixed pay instead. Some even preferred greater certainty over what they would take home.

In water-land, the Labour government arrived in 2024 promising to “ban the payment of bonuses to polluting water bosses until they have cleaned up their filth”, which generated a few pleasing headlines. But the flaw in the resulting Water (Special Measures) Act 2025 was obvious. While the regulator for England and Wales, Ofwat, was given powers to block performance-related bonuses at the worst environmental and financial miscreants, it could do nothing formally about other payments.

Thus – surprise, surprise – salary increases, allowance awards and, most of all, retention payments have proliferated. After the English and Welsh companies published their annual reports last month, this newspaper found that overall reported pay packets rose by 1.5% to £25.3m for chief executives and chief financial officers for the year. It was the second year in a row that a bonus ban had resulted in higher overall pay across the sector.

One can usually rely on Thames Water to muddy things further, and its post-annual report contribution was the news that the chief financial officer, Steve Buck, who was paid £591,000 in the financial year to March, got a delayed £1m signing fee at the end of July. As for retention payments for other executives that were “paused” after a political kerfuffle a year ago, the company has “entered into 14 agreements” to “resolve its liability for any potential claims”.

The government is shocked, or pretends to be. “It is unacceptable that one of the worst-performing water companies is handing out huge payments to its executives when it should be focusing on improving performance and rebuilding public trust,” a spokesperson for the environment department said.

Again, though, one must ask: what did ministers think would happen? It’s easy to agree that executives of underperforming monopolies are grossly overpaid but it was fantastically naive on the part of politicians to think a ban on bonuses would not result in alternative wheezes. It was predictable.

Water companies in general have deployed the retention manoeuvre in less-than-transparent – or just shameless – ways, it should be added. Helen Campbell, the interim executive director of Ofwat, was clearly correct last month when she complained that customers’ trust is harmed when remuneration committees make decisions that “give the appearance of circumventing the rule” or aren’t explained.

The point, though, is that the government left the door wide open to such behaviour. If ministers were relying on remuneration committees to obey the “spirit” of their reforms, they were born yesterday. Restricting bonuses is not the same as restricting overall pay. And Ofwat can use only the powers it was given by parliament.

Flip-flopping Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan but cannot placate all his allies

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 17:27:54 GMT

Israeli prime minister faces incompatible demands from his far-right government ministers and from Donald Trump

Benjamin Netanyahu’s public rejection of a US-backed deal for Gaza drew scepticism in Israel, amid reports he was personally hammering out details of a pilot military withdrawal days earlier.

The Israeli prime minister is struggling to balance incompatible demands on Gaza policy from his key domestic and international allies.

The far-right Israeli politicians who prop up Netanyahu’s coalition government want to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and establish settlements inside the territory.

Donald Trump, who provides vital diplomatic and military backing for Israel, wants to move toward a permanent settlement and return to Palestinian control in Gaza, brokered by the Board of Peace that he created and chairs.

With an Israeli election looming in just over two months, Netanyahu appears to have opted to publicly placate domestic partners who are already on the campaign trail.

On Sunday, he rejected a new 15-point plan for Gaza, which included a Hamas commitment to give up its weapons, meeting a key Israeli demand. He also resisted US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in.

The remarks blindsided Israeli commanders, who had been discussing the implementation of the plan in meetings with Netanyahu and the IDF’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, days earlier, Israel’s Channel 12 television reported.

“We learned about it today from the media,” the station quoted a defence official as saying. “At the meetings that were held until now, the prime minister personally gave his consent to this plan and to a withdrawal from the points in Rafah.”

The meetings covered precise boundaries of three pilot areas in southern Gaza where a proposed international force – which has yet to be stood up – could take over from the Israeli military, and the interface between the two forces, the report said.

Netanyahu’s public attack on the Board of Peace plan seemed like a particularly pointed rejection of US goals because it was released soon after a reported visit by Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command.

He came to deliver in person the message that the Trump administration wants Israel to end its wars in Gaza and Lebanon, Israeli media reported. “The Americans’ message to the IDF was to move in the direction of shutting down all three theatres of operations,” a senior Israeli military officer told Channel 13 Television.

Defying Trump, who is notoriously thin-skinned and intolerant of dissent, is risky when Israel is internationally isolated and needs US military supplies.

But Netanyahu has a long track record of audacious political manoeuvring, both at home and internationally, undaunted even by ostensible power imbalances. Bill Clinton, after meeting him for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?”

In May 2024, the then US president, Joe Biden, announced an Israeli-backed ceasefire and hostage release plan for Gaza, only to have Netanyahu distance himself from the proposal and ultimately reject it.

For now the administration in Washington appears to have largely shrugged off Netanyahu’s comments as electioneering, perhaps encouraged by military decisions that indicate a far more attentive regard for Trump’s wishes.

Last week, Netanyahu scaled back Israeli airstrikes on Gaza by raising the threshold for authorising attacks. Targeted killings must now be approved by the chief of staff, rather than the regional commander, unless Israeli forces are in “imminent danger”.

Nor is this the first time he has bowed to US pressure to rein in wars that have the enthusiastic backing of his far-right allies, recently limiting the offensive in Lebanon, and last year ordering fighter jets heading for Iran to turn back at Trump’s demand.

Netanyahu’s combination of fierce domestic rhetoric and some conciliatory steps on the ground in Gaza may have bought him a bit of time but US patience may not last until polling day in late October.

Trump is weighing up election concerns of his own, as the US is holding midterms just a week after Israel votes.

Netanyahu’s visit to the White House last month was notably low profile for a leader who has repeatedly campaigned on his reputation as an international statesman and close relationship with the US president, Haaretz newspaper noted.

It ended without a joint statement, and strains caused by the Israeli prime minister’s competing political priorities have become increasingly evident. “That’s how it is when you try to juggle too many balls; you start dropping them,” the paper said.

The top envoy for the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, declined to comment on Netanyahu’s rejection of a deal that took months to hammer out. In an interview with Israeli media he said only that “discussions continue”.

Palestinians in Gaza have endured nearly a year of deadly limbo after Trump brokered a nominal ceasefire last October, that he said would halt fighting and pave the way for reconstruction.

Israeli attacks have continued, killing over 1,200 people, and Israel has blocked the entry of equipment, supplies and fuel needed for rebuilding homes, schools and medical infrastructure.

The majority of Gaza’s surviving population live in tent camps with little sanitation, and although hunger has diminished food shortages are still widespread, with over 70,000 children projected to need treatment for acute malnutrition to April 2027, food security experts have warned.

Netanyahu’s office rejected reports that he had discussed detailed withdrawal plans for Gaza.

Police use teargas on young Indians as government jobs protest escalates

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 17:16:28 GMT

Thousands of angry young job-seekers clashed with police in Jharkhand, one of India’s poorest states, on Monday as a weeks-long protest over alleged irregularities in recruitment drives for coveted government jobs escalated into a march on the state legislature.

Police fired water cannon and teargas and swung batons as they tried to stop flag-waving demonstrators from clambering over barricades and surging towards the assembly in Ranchi, the state capital. Some of the protesters responded by dancing and cheering as jets of water drenched the crowd.

The unrest comes just weeks after the Cockroach movement, a youth-led protest campaign – which began as an online joke and grew into a nationwide outcry over leaks in a national medical entrance examination – put the BJP-led national government under heavy pressure and led to the resignation of the education minister.

Both protesters and police officers were injured in the Jharkhand clashes, local media reported, although no official figures were released.

“The baton charge was barbaric. We were protesting peacefully, but the government used batons against us,” protester Piyush Kumar Soni told the Press Trust of India.

The demonstrators are demanding an investigation by the CBI, India’s premier investigative force, saying only an independent inquiry can get to the bottom of alleged wrongdoing in government recruitment examinations.

They accuse authorities of failing to prevent irregularities in public service exams, including test paper leaks and cheating, and say the alleged scandals have deprived young people of a fair chance.

Jharkhand has long struggled with high unemployment, making government jobs highly sought after. Competition is intense for civil service and other public sector posts, which offer job security, health and pension benefits.

Government recruitment drives routinely attract hundreds of thousands of applicants, and many young people spend years preparing for examinations. In one recent Jharkhand recruitment exercise, nearly 640,000 applications were received for 2,025 posts. In another, more than 322,000 candidates competed for 510 vacancies.

The state government, led by a regional party allied with the opposition Congress, has sought to defuse the crisis through talks. Officials say most of the protesters’ demands have been accepted and that they are open to more negotiations.

Mental health: one step forward and two steps back?

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 16:46:30 GMT

Dr Kate Martin is encouraged by the new network of community clinics, while Prof Dr John R Ashton says the forthcoming mental health strategy is an opportunity to grasp the nettle, while Marjorie Wallace expresses concerns about plans to cut mental health jobs in the NHS

It’s very encouraging to hear the announcement about the new network of community mental health clinics in England (Editorial, 6 August). The focus on early intervention is crucial, as it means that people can access treatment as early as possible, rather than waiting for their mental health to reach a crisis point. The centres should improve access, reaching people where they are. The government should make sure that they meaningfully involve people with lived experience of mental health problems to ensure the centres are co-designed and co-led with them.

As your editorial says, parity between mental and physical healthcare became a policy goal in 2011. Mental health is an issue that unites us. According to new research, which we commissioned from More in Common, nearly three-quarters of the public believe that mental health is as important as physical health, most people are comfortable talking about it, and support for early intervention is high across the political spectrum. Three-quarters also say the government should do more to improve services.

The centres are an important step forward, but the government needs to make sure that people can access the many new and improved mental health interventions that have the potential to transform lives. New evidence-based mental health treatments must be rigorously evaluated, adopted and made available across the NHS. This will help people get the right treatment at the right time, and lead fulfilling lives. Dr Kate MartinHead of field building and lived experience, Wellcome Trust

While the announcement of a new initiative on early access to mental health care must be welcomed, there is a danger that without a parallel programme on mental health promotion, it could compound an already disastrous situation by uncovering massive further unmet need.

A public health approach to mental health is long overdue. I refer to one which takes its cues from the history of tuberculosis, the “captain of the men of death” that was brought under control not by pharmaceuticals alone, but by paying attention to the environmental conditions that predisposed to transmission.

The initial prescription for action was written 60 years ago by the Manchester psychiatrist Gerald Caplan, who identified how those with psychiatric training might best be deployed to build population-level mental health resilience through their support in the community, school, places of work and recreation; in Caplan’s blueprint, clinical work was only one aspect of the daily round of the psychiatrist and their team.

The forthcoming mental health strategy is an opportunity to grasp this nettle; for too long these opportunities have been missed. Prof Dr John R AshtonFormer president, Faculty of Public Health

Your report (NHS mental health trust plans £25m in cuts to jobs and services, 3 August) is concerning. As the NHS faces yet another reconfiguration, patients and staff can only look forward to an uncertain future as not only this trust but other mental health trusts are expected to make savings to already impoverished levels of care. This is in stark contrast to the recent announcement of a major expansion of community mental health support in England.

Successive governments have insisted that mental health should be given the same priority as physical health, yet each year psychiatric services undergo ever more cuts to funding, services and beds. This has left people with minimal help and nowhere to go in times of loneliness or crisis. Marjorie WallaceChief executive, Sane

Katriona O’Sullivan’s story of growing up in poverty is one that we can all learn from

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 16:46:25 GMT

Adrian Chiles’s emotional response to Poor by Katriona O’Sullivan really resonated with me (I’d never cried during a live broadcast – then three poignant words had me sobbing, 30 July). I read it and my heart both sobbed and cheered for Katriona’s younger self and the woman she has become.

With its linear narrative, rich cultural references and “rags-to-riches” form, it might be taken for a tale of “that was then but this is now”. However, the defining part of the book is the epilogue, making clear that Katriona’s account of growing up in grinding, abject poverty is a story of then and now. Every day, countless Katrionas enter schools with “pissy pants” and empty bellies, their nervous systems on high alert, in fight, flight or freeze.

School is a place to survive, not thrive. I know, because I have worked in a primary school for over 20 years. I provide mental health support to vulnerable children and their equally vulnerable and disadvantaged families.

My job is not to educate, but to help make children feel seen, heard, cared for and valued – to try to reduce the stigma attached to being poor ie, the misconception that having less means being less.

Reading Poor reinforced the vastness and complexity of poverty as an issue – it can feel “too big”. But that doesn’t prevent each of us from treating others with dignity, respect and kindness, noticing when someone is struggling, is hungry, dirty or alone, and offering a supportive hand.

Pollyanna-ish? I don’t think so. It was heart-warming and affirming to read about the lasting, positive impact certain school staff had on Katriona. When school reopens in September, my copy of Poor will be available in the staffroom – anyone who works in a school (or indeed anyone at all) should read it. Sarah SchofieldWhitefield, Greater Manchester

The cricket fiction of Sassoon and De Sélincourt isn’t in a ‘bucolic dreamworld’

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 16:46:18 GMT

There are serious political and societal messages to be found in some of the best-known fictional accounts of village cricket, argues Rod Edmond

Your leader (The Guardian view on sporting fair play: it was never quite cricket, 30 July) recycles the persistent caricature of Siegfried Sassoon’s, Hugh de Sélincourt’s and AG Macdonell’s cricket fiction as existing in a “bucolic dreamworld”.

Sassoon’s The Flower Show Match is set against the background of the Boer war, with recurring references to the relief of Ladysmith. The home umpire is also suspected of using his wooden leg to make dents in the pitch.

In De Sélincourt’s The Cricket Match, a war profiteer has felled the fir trees surrounding the Tillingford ground to have them sawn into pit props. The club is struggling to recover from the war, and there’s a feeling of “melancholy certainty that each season must surely be the last”. There are passing references to the Russian Revolution, and the hope expressed by the lady of the manor that village cricket will ease class antagonism is contradicted by the contempt the team’s fast bowler, a labourer, feels for her public-school son who also plays for Tillingford.

Macdonell’s England, Their England is pervaded with the after-effects of the first world war. Three-quarters of England in drought as summer’s fifth heatwave looms

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 16:32:53 GMT

Four more regions given drought status, putting 27 million people under restrictions on water use

Almost three-quarters of England is now in drought, as much of Europe braces for its fifth climate crisis-driven heatwave this summer.

Four more regions of England have officially been declared to be in drought: the East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and East Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs.

They join seven regions already under drought status since last month: East Anglia, Hertfordshire and London, Thames Valley, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, Devon and Cornwall, the West Midlands, and Wessex (covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire and south Gloucestershire).

Farmers have reported their earliest harvests in 20 years, with reduced yields, while reservoir levels have fallen to 69% – 11.6% lower than expected for this time of year.

Yorkshire and the North East have joined Cumbria and Lancashire and Greater Manchester, Merseyside and Cheshire in prolonged dry weather status – the stage before drought – meaning nowhere in England is deemed to be in normal status.

This flash drought, which developed quickly because of very low rainfall and higher temperatures, means 27 million people have restrictions on their water use.

Prof Liz Bentley, chief executive of the Royal Meteorological Society, said it was a “stark reminder that climate change isn’t just about rising temperatures – it’s making droughts develop faster and hit harder.

“With three droughts in the past five years, we’re seeing the growing influence of a changing climate. We need to adapt to more frequent periods of extreme heat and drought while taking action to reduce the emissions driving these changes.”

Southern Water has applied for two drought orders. The first is to maintain normal abstraction rates from the River Test even during low river flows and the second is for a non-essential use ban. These are both under consideration by the government. South East Water said last week supplies in its area were “critically low” and warned customers they might lose supply unless demand for water in the area dropped.

The drought announcement comes as England braces for its fifth heatwave of the summer, with temperatures possibly exceeding 36C in some places. This year has so far seen 34 days where temperatures have reached 30C or above somewhere in England, including 13 consecutive days in July.

Rivers, reservoirs and groundwaters are also continuing to decline, with 22% of rivers now classed as exceptionally low.

Glenn Watts, director of water science at the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, said river flows across England and Wales were approaching or worse than previous records set in 1976.

The record temperatures and extremely dry weather are having wide-ranging impacts: 245 wildfires have been recorded on the country’s most protected sites this year alone and the government said important wetland and sensitive peatland habitats were drying out.

Paul Tompkins, the deputy president of the National Farmers’ Union, said that with no meaningful rain forecast in the coming weeks, the situation for farmers was increasingly concerning.

“Many farmers have completed the earliest harvest on record, with poor yields in key crops reported in some areas of the country. Livestock and dairy farmers are already using winter feed because grass has stopped growing, while growers are working hard to keep fruit and vegetables watered, but many are struggling to access the water they need,” he said.

The government said it was considering ways to give more support to the farming sector. The water minister, Emma Hardy, said this would include making it easier to build on-farm reservoirs.

River temperatures are rising, reaching 28C on the River Misbourne, a chalk stream in Buckinghamshire, 27C on the Hampshire Avon and 27C on the River Trent – around 2C higher than to be expected.

England is on track to record its highest number of heat-related deaths this summer, after the UK Health Security Agency announced that an estimated 2,877 people died in the May and June heatwaves.

The UKHSA has updated heat health alerts for nine regions in England, warning that rising temperatures this week may increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.

The National Drought Group, whose members include the government, water companies, the National Farmers’ Union, the Met Office and conservation experts, met on Monday to assess the situation across England.

Many other parts of Europe are also bracing for another heatwave. The French national weather agency said on Monday that temperatures in the south-east could reach 35C, spreading further across the country, while Italy and coastal Croatia are already experiencing extreme heat. Countries including Slovakia, Austria and Hungary have registered record temperatures in recent days.

Reform backer Arron Banks urged to set out extent of surveillance of journalists

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 16:30:47 GMT

Industry body says use of private investigators against reporters is ‘attack on our democracy’ after Banks apparently admitted doing so

The businessman and Reform UK backer Arron Banks is facing calls to lay out the extent of his surveillance of journalists, described by an industry body as an “attack on our democracy”.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents regional and national media, raised concerns after Banks appeared to admit over the weekend to hiring private investigators to spy on a Sunday Times journalist.

The revelation, first reported in the New Statesman, has led to fears that other journalists examining the funding of Reform and Nigel Farage, including those at the Guardian, could have been targeted.

When asked over the weekend whether he had commissioned investigators to surveil reporters at the Guardian, Banks, a Reform UK member and former mayoral candidate, said he was “not really interested in the Guardian” but declined to comment further.

The Guardian, along with the Sunday Times, has broken a series of stories in recent months revealing how cash has been given to Reform and Farage personally from donors and wealthy benefactors.

Theo Bamber, the chief executive of the NMA, said aggressive attempts to deter journalistic inquiry were at risk of becoming normalised.

He said: “Using private investigators to try to deter journalists from making legitimate inquiries about public figures is an attack on our democracy. Sadly, intimidation and abuse of local and national journalists is increasingly used as a weapon to limit scrutiny and deflect attention away from matters of public interest. This must not become normalised.

“Ministers must wake up to this threat to our democracy and do much more to protect the independent journalism which underpins our democratic way of life.”

According to the New Statesman, Banks instructed Precision Risk and Intelligence, a private investigations company he once owned, to examine Gabriel Pogrund, the editor of the Sunday Times’ Insight investigations team.

In response to inquiries, Banks told the magazine: “We believe the Sunday Times used hacked information and that was an area of interest. We do have an investigative arm that’s got advanced capabilities.”

The Sunday Times has strongly rejected Banks’s suggestion.

Banks, when asked directly by the New Statesman whether he had paid investigators to look into Pogrund, responded: “When you live by the sword, you die by the sword.”

Jemimah Steinfeld, the chief executive of Index on Censorship, said Banks should be open and transparent about the extent of his surveillance of journalists.

She said: “I really, really hope that it’s not happening to other journalists. But my fear is that it will be, because Gabriel is not the only one who’s asking the right questions about Reform.

“These tactics are often used to just stop the questions, to stop accountability, and that can have hugely detrimental effects on our democratic structure.”

Reform UK has denied any knowledge of Banks’s alleged use of investigators.

Gawain Towler, a member of Reform’s board and a former head of press for Ukip, said he was uncomfortable with the development but there were legitimate questions as to where journalists were sourcing private information.

“Personally I don’t like it,” he said. “But truly how in the light of the situation does one ask questions with a possibility of getting an answer …

“I think the issue with Banks is that there was actually silence about this possible collusion with the [National Crime Agency and journalists] … It would be ridiculous of us not to ask questions. So how do you ask questions?”

Nicky Morgan, a former Conservative secretary of state for culture, media and sport, said such intrusions in press freedom were “not compatible with an open democracy”. She said: “Investigating a journalist can only be intended to have a chilling effect on free speech.”

Lisa Smart, the Liberal Democrats’ Cabinet Office spokesperson said: “Hiring private investigators to target journalists who are simply doing their jobs is a desperate attempt to dodge accountability.

“Anyone who uses or condones these tactics demonstrates complete contempt for a free press and should have no business in British public life.”

Banks, who helped run the pro-Brexit campaign group Leave. EU, is reported to have previously hired what he described as “ex-MI5 and SAS” operatives to surveil political opponents in the run-up to the EU referendum.

Included among those was Matthew Elliott, a Conservative peer who was the chief executive of the rival Vote Leave campaign. He has warned that such tactics will “drive out the decent people we need in public life”.

Ukraine drone strike on oil refinery deep inside Russia kills at least 13

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 16:25:30 GMT

Attack hundreds of miles from border would be among deadliest of war as Kyiv aims to strangle Russian economy

A Ukrainian drone strike on an industrial city deep inside Russia has killed at least 13 people, according to the local mayor, as Kyiv steps up its campaign of long-range strikes on targets far from the frontline.

Kyiv said it hit the Taneco refinery in the city of Nizhnekamsk, about 750 miles (1,200km) from the Ukrainian border. Footage circulating online appeared to show smoke rising from the refinery.

Ukraine’s general staff said the raid was part of a campaign to reduce the “military potential of the Russian aggressor”.

Russian investigators claimed civilian and industrial sites in the city had been hit. The head of the Tatarstan region, Rustam Minnikhanov, said a Ukrainian drone hit a hostel, killing nine people. He posted images showing a badly damaged building.

If the death toll is confirmed, the strike would be among the deadliest Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory since the full-scale invasion began in 2022, underscoring the growing reach of Kyiv’s strikes deep inside Russia.

The Uzbek consulate said in a Telegram post that seven of the victims were Uzbek citizens. Minnikhanov declared a day of mourning and Russian prosecutors opened a criminal case into alleged terrorism.

Local video footage showed Ukrainian drones buzzing above the city’s skyline, flying low over grey and box-like Soviet-era apartment blocks. Two plumes of black smoke could be seen rising above an industrial zone on the wooded outskirts of Nizhnekamsk.

The site is home to Taneco, one of Russia’s biggest and most technologically advanced oil refineries, owned by Tatneft. It also houses a plant that produces rubber and petrochemical products. Ukraine also bombed the area in June.

In an address on Sunday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said “long-range sanctions” against the Kremlin and its war machine would continue. In recent months Ukrainian drones have wreaked havoc on Russia’s oil export industry, even hitting refineries in Siberia, 1,500 miles from the frontline.

The governor of the Tyumen region in western Siberia said on Monday that several Ukrainian drones had fallen on an industrial facility and that emergency services were dealing with a fire.

There have been several strikes on warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s equivalent of Amazon, as well as on oil tankers in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea. Ukraine’s long-term goal is to slowly strangle the Russian economy so Moscow can no longer fund its war.

Zelenskyy described his country’s remote bombing campaign as “entirely justified”. “Every Russian strike [on Ukrainian towns and cities] will be met with our response. Russia’s war will be felt more and more at their own home – in Russia,” he said on social media. “The only reason this is still continuing is Russia’s unwillingness to end this war.”

Russia’s defence ministry said it had intercepted 456 Ukrainian drones flying above Russian territory and annexed Crimea. Ukraine says it is knocking out its opponent’s air defence systems more quickly than they can be replaced, creating air corridors or “doors” it can exploit.

Kissing in public: will it make your relationship stronger?

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 16:04:16 GMT

Public displays of affection are widely mocked online and off, but they have a positive side – and now science has proved it

Name: Kissing in public.

Age: Kissing is 17m-21m years old – probably older than the notion of privacy.

Appearance: Romantic, uninhibited.

Sounds horrible. Actually, I think attitudes tend to vary from person to person.

Well, they shouldn’t. When I go to the cinema, I want the orgy to be on the screen. In fact, public kissing is very big right now among celebrity couples.

I think we have amassed enough evidence over the years to establish that celebrities simply don’t know how to behave. Dua Lipa and Callum Turner, Kylie Jenner and Timothée Chalamet, Brooklyn Beckham and Nicola Peltz – they’re all at it, kissing and cuddling for the cameras.

No good will come of this. That’s where you’re wrong: new research suggests that public displays of affection, or PDAs, are strongly linked to higher-quality romantic relationships.

I prefer the private display of affection. Also good for your relationship, according to the research.

What sort of research is this? The study, published in the journal Plos One, looked at 461 people in three countries: Poland, Nepal and Indonesia.

Quite a random selection. These societies all have different, though generally negative, attitudes towards PDAs. Yet subjects who engaged in more PDAs consistently reported higher relationship satisfaction across the three cultures.

Why would that be? “Because affectionate behaviour is one of the ways people communicate closeness, love and emotional connection,” said the leader of the study, Dagna Kocur.

I still think it’s just showing off. And icky. You don’t think it’s ever appropriate to kiss in public?

During a wedding ceremony, maybe, or at the end of a major world war, but otherwise it should remain behind closed doors. Fewer PDAs and more private displays of affection, please! You’re right, in a way: Kocur went on to point out that private displays of affection are even more strongly linked to relationship satisfaction, “so it may be worth making the time to hold hands and kiss at home, too”.

At home, on the bus, in the bread aisle at Morrisons – don’t these people ever get tired of pawing one another? A further study is now planned to include 1,000 people across nine countries.

Good! We’ll finally get proof that a persistent lack of affection builds character. Actually, it can lead to mental health problems.

What sort of mental health problems? A condition commonly known as skin hunger, which may cause anxiety, depression and alexithymia – an impairment of your ability to interpret emotion.

Relax, Casanova – you’re not my type. A case, I think, in point.

Do say: “Physical affection, wherever it occurs, is essential to our wellbeing as humans.”

Don’t say: “Get a room!”

From ticket booking fees to shrinkflation, six other ways Burnham could cut cost of living

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 15:47:19 GMT

The prime minister is promising to crack down on ‘rip-off’ business practices

Andy Burnham has announced he will ban fake discounts and make it easier to cancel unwanted subscriptions in an effort to improve life for UK consumers.

In the long run, these so-called “everyday fixes” may not make as much difference to your wealth as increasing mandatory contributions on pensions or capping rents, but they will get rid of some day-to-day frustrations. Here are six other things he could fix while he is in the mood:

Buying a ticket for an event such as a gig or show doesn’t come with as many hidden costs as previously, thanks to consumer protection laws introduced last year. But the fact the fees are clearer does not make them all more palatable.

In the days when you could choose to go to a box office, or between having your tickets posted or emailed, there may have been a justification for some of the add-ons to cover different costs for the promoter, but when there’s no choice, it sticks in the throat. Retailers do not charge “transaction” or “order processing fees”, so why can they still be slapped on tickets?

You pay your bill by direct debit and have been careful with your usage, so at the end of the winter, you are in credit – and then your provider tells you it wants to put up your monthly cost by £50. Of course, a rising price cap might mean you need to increase what you pay, but if you have already got a cushion, why should you hand over more?

According to the regulator Ofgem, providers held a total of £3.2bn of customers’ money in the year to March, with the average household £135 in credit. Yet some households on fixed tariffs with large balances are still told that their supplier wants to increase their direct debit. Yes, you can refuse, but the onus is on you as a customer to make the effort. Providers could be banned from raising direct debits by more than the price change, or when customers have built up a surplus that covers a set percentage of their bills.

We all know prices have been going up and sometimes a smaller pack for the same price is more welcome than having to shell out more, but when the cuts are sneaky, that’s bad for consumers.

In France and Austria, there are rules designed to make it more obvious to shoppers when they are getting less product for the same – or sometimes even more – money. Demanding a simple “new pack size” message on products would at least alert people to the change and mean they are making informed decisions about what they are buying.

You’ve got a problem with a company and you want to get it sorted – and then you realise you cannot find a number for it anywhere. There are communications companies that have no “contact us” link anywhere to be seen, and energy companies that send you all round the houses looking for a way to get in touch.

One of the recurring themes of Guardian Money readers’ problems is the struggle to find someone to help when something goes wrong. Clearly, once you have published a phone number, you need staff at the other end answering the phone and offering some joined-up thinking, so this is only the start of the solution – but at least customers would not feel like companies were trying to hide from them.

Fines for charging an electric car, debt notices that should never have been sent, fees when you have tried to pay and the app has let you down … Guardian Money has heard from readers encountering all of these things and more when simply entering a car park. The government has promised to sort it out: a code of practice was drawn up several years ago but was not introduced, and a new consultation on it ended last September. Meanwhile plans for a nationwide app that would bring together all of the different parking company apps, making it easier to pay while out and about, were watered down.

Bringing forward and enforcing the planned code, so that drivers are not receiving bills for parking crimes they did not commit, would leave a welcome gap in the Guardian Money postbag.

A lot has been done to improve the experience of renewing your insurance policies. Insurers are supposed to offer existing customers as good a deal as they do new ones, and your renewal letter tells you how much you paid last year so that you can see if the cost has gone up. And yet the annual dance continues: if you don’t call your insurer and query an increase, shop around or threaten to leave, you will probably end up paying more than you need to. It is a system that still penalises those who stay put.

Octopus Energy urges millions of households to use less electricity during solar eclipse

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 15:28:53 GMT

Firm urges customers to avoid running washing machines and dishwashers between 6pm and 8pm on Wednesday

Where in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse?

Great Britain’s biggest household energy supplier is calling on its customers to use less electricity this week during the deepest solar eclipse in almost 30 years.

Octopus Energy has urged customers to avoid running washing machines and dishwashers between 6pm and 8pm this Wednesday as the moon is expected to block up to 95% of the sun over parts of Britain.

The eclipse is expected to knock out the last of Great Britain’s solar power generation for the day, at the same time as the country’s fifth heatwave of the year is likely to increase demand for electricity to run air conditioning, fans and refrigeration systems.

In return for avoiding unnecessary electricity use during the eclipse, the supplier is offering customers who are signed up to its rewards programme a free hour of electricity to use the next weekend. The offer is open to Octopus customers who are signed up to take part in the supplier’s “saving sessions”, when households can earn rewards for using more electricity at times when renewables are abundant or less electricity when wind and solar power are scarce.

Octopus believes that if enough households delay using electricity for a short time during the eclipse, it could reduce the need for Great Britain’s electricity system operator to fire up extra gas-fired stations to replace the lost solar power.

“Household flexibility is one of Britain’s biggest untapped energy resources,” the supplier said. “Octopus estimates homes could provide a whopping 13 gigawatts of flexible capacity to support the electricity system – particularly through smart appliances, EVs and home batteries – yet only a fraction of this potential is currently being used.”

The National Energy System Operator (Neso), which is responsible for running Great Britain’s electricity system, said it had been “planning for over a year” to manage the effects of the eclipse, “one of the most unusual evenings our control room will manage this year”. In addition to a major fluctuation in solar power generation, Neso expects the daily early evening peak in electricity demand to occur later than usual as millions head outdoors to watch the eclipse before returning home to cook, clean and watch TV.

The heatwave forced Neso to issue its first warning notice for electricity supplies during a summer period in late June. Soaring temperatures lifted demand while disrupting electricity supplies owing to low wind speeds and power plant outages across Europe.

In total, the solar eclipse is expected to wipe out 9.7GW of power production across Europe between 7.15pm and 9.30pm during its strongest point. In the UK this could mean losing between 700 megawatts and 1.3GW of solar generation while in Spain, solar power could be reduced by up to 5GW, according to the country’s system operator.

This would “pile pressure” on Europe’s already “tight” power system, according to analysts at RBC Capital Markets. The heatwaves have forced nuclear and coal plants to lower their output or shut down entirely across Europe because of reduced river water levels needed for cooling. The drought has also affected hydropower reservoirs in Norway, a leading exporter of electricity to continental Europe, which have reached their lowest levels in 30 years.

As a gay guy of a certain age, I’ve found that the vast majority of movies and TV shows about gay men I’ve had to sit through have been tragic or whitewashed. In the US, we drag shows out until all the fun has been completely drained out and at the end they’re unrecognisable from where they began. Danny, 57, New York state

The Good Place is an extraordinarily rare gem. It’s a comedy that’s actually funny, with characters that you really care about despite their varied faults. However, the end of the first series immediately sent up the red flag for other series with such a strong opening – where can you go from here?

However, it remained a gem for all four seasons, until the four principal protagonists finally create the heaven they’d always wanted and, one by one, each at their own time, they decide they’ve had enough of everything, are as happy as they could ever be, have experienced everything they’d ever wanted to experience, and that it’s finally the right time to just … go. It’s beautiful and uplifting, and makes me feel happy whenever I think about it. Andy, Japan

Scrubs is an amazing show with some genuine character development. We follow a trio of budding medical interns – JD, Elliot and Turk – as they grow and become well-rounded doctors and human beings.

In a final two-parter, (for season eight, that is, and not the “should-have-been-a-spin-off” season nine, or the recent reboot), JD accepts a job at a new hospital to be closer to his son. And then, on his last day, he goes to painstaking lengths to have the perfect swan song – the constant farewells with his best friend, Turk, finally learning the name of the janitor who tormented him the entire series, and having the perfect final moment with his gruff but ultimately caring mentor, Dr Cox (even if it did take some coaxing).

And then the grand finale: JD realises through a patient that you need to accept the future and all the uncertainties it holds. JD walks through the hospital’s halls, filled with all the people he interacted with right back to the first season, as he stops to watch a giant screen projecting a moving montage of the future, set to Peter Gabriel’s The Book of Love. A pitch-perfect ending. Arjun, 26, London

The ending of Ghosts is moving and life-affirming, and a perfect example of what this show does brilliantly, which is to land its moments (sad and funny) without lingering on them for too long. It might be because I binged it, but it felt like the ending was really made up of the season’s last three episodes. The fifth one has the heartbreaking reveal of the Captain’s backstory, followed by that joyous line dancing scene. Then there’s episode six, which has a well-crafted throwback to the beginning, with Alison finding out that Julian pushed her out of the window. He’s the one who has to persuade her to stay, via a beautiful monologue made all the lovelier coming from him.

And then, just when you think it’s settled and they’re staying – the Christmas special. It’s happy and satisfying and sad. I love Pat teaching the Captain how to do baby talk and the way they all run to the answering machine to hear Mike’s message. The episode gives all of the characters a moment to be truly themselves. You get a sense of how much Alison loves the ghosts and vice versa; it’s incredibly sweet without being saccharine. Emily, Hampshire

Does anyone else remember Sleepers? A post-glasnost spy comedy in which Warren Clarke and Nigel Havers are Soviet agents sent to infiltrate Britain in 1965, and build lives they’re very happy with, thank you, and don’t want to go back to shabby apartments in the Nevsky Prospect. By the end of the series, both have been captured by the hardline KGB officer sent to recover them, and are drugged and shipped out to a waiting submarine. They wake up, and the KGB is returning them to their homes. But while the lead characters are safe, Clarke’s daughter’s cuddly monkey Maurice is missing! Weeks later he appears, wearing a Russian fur hat, having been on an adventure of his own. A perfect show. Nick, 58, Yorkshire

The show I grew up with in the 70s. Beautifully anti-war with top-drawer writing and brilliant characters. The ending is a tear-fest. After the ceasefire is announced, the members of the 4077th throw a party before taking down the camp for the very last time. So many great moments: Hawkeye and BJ saluting Colonel Potter, upper-class Charles leaving in a garbage truck, the death of Henry, and Hawkeye saluting Radar. And the final scene where Hawkeye, who spent the last episode unable to say goodbye, spells it out in rocks that BJ can only view from the air as he lifts off in a chopper. No, you’re crying. Cameron, Ledbury

Everybody dies! But that’s also what makes it such a special ending, because we get to see how every character’s life plays out in vignettes as the weight of the show’s themes are lifted from them. Claire finally escapes her mother’s overbearing influence, without having to destroy their relationship to do so. Rico gets to run his own funeral home, without the Fishers’ influence. David slays his demons and lives happily ever after with Keith when it looked as if they would destroy him. Brenda realises she can be a good mother after all. Then – yes, as everybody dies! – we get surely the greatest closing montage sequence on TV, with an exceptional soundtrack (Sia’s Breathe Me) to accompany it. I think someone’s started chopping onions in here again … Stephen, 47, Solihull

Not only does the finale offer the sheer joy of David and Patrick’s wedding (Moira in her papal mitre and gloves, sobbing her way through the ceremony, the Jazzagals singing Simply the Best, Alexis accidentally dressed as a bride), but the beautiful denouement of the show, as they quietly move on with their lives, back to success but so differently than they imagined in the beginning.

I can’t watch it without sobbing. It is to me the happiest of endings: the guy gets the guy, the girl gets the career, Johnny finally makes it back to business, and Moira? Exactly where she belongs, back to Sunrise Bay, along with a token tennis bracelet. It is a sublime moment that takes such good care of the fans and how invested we are in each of Rose’s (and Stevie’s) journeys. It is so refreshing to give everyone a simple happy ending without compromise or drama. Casey, 34, Brighton

Are Manchester United about to return to relevance under Michael Carrick?

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 15:01:59 GMT

In a mailbag edition of his newsletter, Jonathan Wilson answers questions about Michael Carrick, VAR and the Premier League’s new teams

Sign up for our free newsletter here

Manchester United finally seem to have something that resembles stability in the dressing room under Michael Carrick. I feel with quality signings in defence and midfield, they could mount a decent challenge for the Premier League next season. How do you feel they will fare? – Sterling.

There’s an odd sense that Michael Carrick’s level of achievement last season was at precisely the most awkward level for the board. United didn’t produce indisputably brilliant football under him but equally 12 wins and three draws in 17 games was good enough that they pretty much had to give him the job. But it’s one thing to turn out those kinds of results when the pressure’s off, you’re already out of both cup competitions and you don’t have any European football; it’s quite another to do it in the heat of a full season. United don’t have to have an especially amazing season to play 15 more games this season than they did in 2025-26.

That’s not to say that Carrick won’t be successful. There was much that he did last season that was very impressive. Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans bolster an area of the squad that desperately needed to improve. A left-back seems almost certain to arrive before the end of the month and there’s probably the need for one more high-class experienced central defender. It’s not clear what Marcus Rashford’s future is after his return from loan at Barcelona, but he has two years left on his contract and could add dynamism and finishing to the left side of the attack. It’s probably not a title-winning squad, but it’s certainly one that should qualify for the Champions League.

Two questions remain that will only be answered as the season goes on. First, Carrick himself: can he cope with the churn of two games a week, and operating with a squad that is at least as fatigued as their opponents? And second, where is the club psychologically? Part of the problem for United, a familiar trait of big clubs who have fallen from grace, is that they have got into a routine of failure, that no success can ever quite be trusted, and every setback is seen as a further example of the terminal decline (although just as damaging would be suddenly believing everything is fine if United were to win, say, their first three games of the season). Retaining clarity of thought and making realistic assessments are perhaps the greatest challenges for a club that has known greatness but is struggling to return to those heights.

What do you see the broader impact of the VAR changes that Fifa made this year being? Do you think that other soccer leagues will see the increasingly automated, faster but less human approach taken by Fifa this summer and choose to adopt it? (I am aware that the Premier League has already chosen to reject much of it) – Dennis.

The most notable changes implemented before the World Cup allowed VAR to review and overturn incorrectly awarded corner kicks, certain attacking fouls and clear mistakes relating to red cards given from a second yellow. The only one of these adopted by the Premier League is to allow VAR to overturn a second yellow leading to a red (VAR cannot recommend that a referee should award a second yellow that would lead to a red). If we have to have VAR, that seems reasonable enough; nobody wants to see a team incorrectly reduced to 10 men.

At the World Cup, the corner issue only rarely came up, but it always seemed slightly odd that incorrectly awarded goal kicks could not be turned into corners. Personally, I would scrap VAR, or at least this form of it, but if incorrect decisions can be corrected quickly and unobtrusively then they probably should be. I understand, though, why the Premier League, aiming for a “light touch” – good luck with that – would be resistant.

Greater use of VAR, though, seemed to be the direction of travel. I suspect relatively soon offsides will be almost fully automated, which probably makes sense so long as it’s almost instantaneous. Whatever doubts there may be about margins of error and frame rates, it’s still going to be more accurate than a 40-year-old running the line 30 yards away, peering through a thicket of players.

More significant is probably the Premier League’s adoption of regulations against timewasting: speeded-up substitutions, players who receive treatment having to remain off the field for 60 rather than 30 seconds, an outfield player having to be withdrawn for 60 seconds after a goalkeeper receives treatment, and a five-second clock on throw-ins and goal kicks. All should speed up the game and improve the spectacle. It’ll be interesting as well to see the level of tolerance for grappling in the box, particularly by attacking players, which was an area in which the Premier League seemed out of step with the rest of Europe last season.

Which of the Premier League’s promoted sides have the best chance of staying up, and why? – Nicholas.

Sign up to Soccer Desk

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

The achievements of Sunderland and Leeds last season, finishing seventh and 14th, will have heartened the promoted sides, but the truth is it will be extremely difficult for all three. Both those sides invested heavily in a way that is impossible for Coventry, Ipswich or Hull. It’s very hard to see how Hull, who were promoted unexpectedly, can survive. Coventry, perhaps, with the euphoria of their Premier League return and the Frank Lampard factor can give it a go, but their summer spending has been modest. Ipswich, with recent Premier League experience, have a chance and have made some intriguing signings in Daizen Maeda, Abdul Fatawu, Issa Diop and Chuba Akpom, but they’ve lost the manager who got them up, with Kieran McKenna opting for a break rather than another Premier League campaign. Gary O’Neil perhaps feels he has unfinished business, but if any of the promoted sides are to survive, they need another club to have a dreadful campaign.

A job that changed me: Working at a toy store was my teen feminist awakening

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 15:00:49 GMT

I loved the business of selling toys – it felt like I was selling joy. But my least favourite part was the gendered language

I was 15 when I landed my job at Toys R Us. Before that, my first job was a one-month stint at the local fish and chip shop, where I was paid in $20 bills slotted into Chiko roll packets. After a burn on my forearm (I still have it), I left the gig. That was the end of my hospitality career.

This was 2014. I knew my strengths and weaknesses; I was no good with deep-fry baskets or carrying more than one thing in each hand. I wanted to work in the hallowed halls of retail.

Lucky for me, there was an excess of Christmas casual jobs specifically looking for the youngest workers they could legally pay the least. So I became one of Toys R Us’s checkout chicks, dressed in a blue polo shirt, black pants, a lanyard and my school shoes. I processed transactions, pointed customers in the right direction, counted the end-of-day tills and cleaned up the store once the doors shut. To decompress, I’d play a few rounds of Bop It! in the board games aisle.

I loved being in the business of selling toys. It felt like I was selling joy. As with any job involving children, there were ugly bits. Vomit and urine in aisles weren’t uncommon sights – though it was the floor staff’s job to deal with the clean-up. We also had its subsidiary, Babies R Us, in the store. I found it amusing that 17-year-olds were allowed to advise expectant parents on breast pumps.

As a burgeoning feminist, my least favourite part of the job was the gendered language entrenched in the industry. I took great pleasure in playing dumb – head cocked to one side, brows furrowed – when customers asked where the “girls” or “boys” toys were. If forced to adopt such language, I’d pair it with exaggerated air quotes.

A woman once called to place an order for balloons for her grandson’s birthday. We took down the typical details – how many balloons? When could she pick them up? – but when it came down to the colour, we touched a nerve. “The boy colour!,” she insisted. She arrived and we handed her a bunch of blue balloons. She recoiled. She wanted red. Obviously.

I saw hyper-consumerism on overdrive. I worked an overnight shift during Chadstone Shopping Centre’s 34-hour Christmas trade period, watching on as frantic shoppers raced to purchase plastic that would end up in landfills by the next festive season. I came to understand that retailers employ harsh lighting in windowless stores so shoppers are unaware of the time.

I met dozens of adults hardcore into collectibles, getting us to bring out boxes of Hot Wheels from the backrooms so they could rifle through stock before it hit the shelves. I learned that we’d play Justin Timberlake’s Can’t Stop The Feeling! on the hour, every hour, the year the Trolls movie came out. I knew which toy was hot one month, and which would be the next big thing the month after. It was a short course in capitalism.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Despite the lows, my memories of Toys R Us are extremely fond. I ended up leaving to work in fashion retail around the time I started university. Soon after, Toys R Us Australia entered administration and all stores closed the same year.

When I applied to Toys R Us as a teenager looking for some pocket money, I didn’t realise that – to this day – I’d be entering my longest place of employment. I also didn’t realise a fluorescently garish 78-year-old US toy company would be the one to radicalise me.

Sam Neill on making Hunt for the Wilderpeople: ‘We were attacked by a puppet pig!’

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 14:14:19 GMT

Speaking just before his death, the actor recalled his hostile hunting dog Zag, director Taika Waititi’s comedy genius – and the wild boar scene that left children traumatised Warning: contains spoilers

Taika Waititi’s film Boy is one of my favourites ever, so when I got the Wilderpeople script I was already well disposed to it. Hec is sort of a New Zealand archetype. When I was at university, during the holidays I’d work at cutting hay and shifting sheep and fertiliser. There was always a Hec driving the truck. They were men of very few words, but when they did say something it meant a lot. It was clear I was never going to have many lines in the film.

Hunt for the Wilderpeople is based on Wild Pork and Watercress, a novel by Barry Crump, a legendary figure when I was growing up. A lot of his stuff is very amusing, but not this one – it took Taika to make it funny. Just about every comedian in New Zealand is in the film. I was probably the only non-comedian, but the film has a complexity beyond the humour. A lot of that comes, I think, from Rima Te Wiata. She plays Hec’s wife Bella with such warmth, compassion and empathy that when she dies both Hec and Ricky are suffused with grief. That grief gives a powerful dimension to the remainder of the film.

The Ricky Baker birthday song seems to have become a sort of informal national anthem, but it’s only in the film because the traditional Happy Birthday song wasn’t then in the public domain. The scene was all set up with Rima about to play the conventional version on her little keyboard when the producer came running in and said: “We can’t use that, we don’t have copyright!” Rima, Taika and I had to write something new in 10 minutes, but it was mostly Rima. Sometimes, working under pressure produces the best things.

I didn’t have the best relationship with the canine actor that played Hec’s hunting dog, Zag. I’m a dog guy, but he wasn’t the pal you would expect a dog to be – he had other things on his mind. The wild boar that wounds Zag was realised on screen in a mixture of ways. But on location we were reacting to a couple of guys operating a kind of puppet pig! The finished scene is pretty full-on. A lot of people have to comfort their children after it.

People often stop me and say it’s their favourite film. They remember it with affection, and when something is taken to heart, that’s a wonderful thing to have in your CV. The only thing that irritated me after its release was some people saying Julian stole the film from me. I don’t think there was any theft involved – the film was always his in the first place.

Sam Neill gave this interview in June, a month before his death on 13 July.

I’d worked with Taika before on an anti-drugs advert and didn’t have to audition. Ricky is this broken kid stuck in a system of foster care that’s failing him. I come from a community where that happens a lot with young people – I had cousins who acted like Ricky Baker, I had friends who dressed like him and my brother listened to Tupac.

I knew Sam Neill was big and lots of people liked him, but I didn’t really know who he was. Knowing there were going to be all these scenes of just him and me in the bush, I thought: “Man, I hope he’s not lame …” He turned out to be very young at heart, like an older cousin. I had the best time and loved hanging out with Sam – sometimes it felt like both of us were 12 years old.

I grew up in a religious home and went to Sunday school, and I wasn’t a big swearer like Ricky. When it came to lines like: “Shit just got real!” I was like: “Am I allowed to say this?”

Rachel House, who played the child welfare officer leading the hunt for Hec and Ricky, was also my acting coach. She taught me tricks like recording my lines and listening back to them the night before we shot a scene. I still do that today. The movie is full of pop-culture references from way before I was born which I didn’t get while I was making it, but I see the bigger picture now.

Taika was open to ideas, which often arrived while we were all practising our lines in a hot tub. In the scene where Ricky and Hec are trying to come up with an escape plan with Rhys Darby’s character, Psycho Sam, there was a line in the script about an underground bunker. I said: “Wouldn’t it be funny if Sam opened the door and realised he hadn’t dug the tunnel yet?” That ended up in the movie.

The big car chase at the end was shot on the ancestral land of the Ngāti Rangi tribe, who were really welcoming and helpful, as were the army, who use some of their territory as a training ground. We had to travel in a truck with army people when we went from the filming base to the location. I guess they’d lost some of their mines or something – they’d be like: “If you see metal things sticking out of the ground, just let us know.” If anything was spotted, someone would come over with bright pink spray paint and draw a circle around it, like some people do to draw attention to dog poo.

The 10th anniversary release of Hunt for the Wilderpeople in 4k is in cinemas and on digital platforms now, with UHD and Blu-ray editions on 17 August.

From M&S pants to fancy skincare: the celebrity shopping recommendations you loved the most

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 14:00:46 GMT

Whether it’s expensive regrets or brilliant bargains, we celebrate the stars’ shopping secrets – and the products that tempted you

Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Like snooping in someone else’s supermarket trolley, discovering other people’s shopping habits satisfies a certain nosiness. And never more so than when it comes to celebrities – there’s nothing more human than knowing Kim Cattrall loves fish and chips, or that Henry Holland is a Skims guy.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

And as celebrities often have the inside track – or perhaps we just think they do – on everything from coffee machines to skincare, their recommendations in our biweekly How I Shop column have inspired more than a few of your own retail habits. In some cases, however, such as David Gandy’s £2,500 Cobra Fortis lawnmower, the price was a little too out of reach.

Beauty products have proved particularly inspiring, from author Nussaibah Younis’s favourite Chanel foundation, which she buys “on repeat”, to the Marvis whitening toothpaste that TV presenter Ben Fogle has been using “for decades”. Perhaps unsurprisingly, given her expertise as a beauty pro, Caroline Hirons’ Vieve skin dew was also popular (she likes to mix hers with Chanel primer for a glowy look).

Even the £1,999 cost of Dawn O’Porter’s Lyma laser kit didn’t put some of you off: “The price tag is OUCH,” O’Porter agreed, noting she was given hers as a gift, but said it has dramatically cut down on the amount of Botox she gets around her eyes: “A device like this goes deep and definitely works,” she said.

We always ask our celebs about coffee. Their answers generally fall into two camps: obsessed and never-touch-it. Some of you were inspired by Patrick Grant’s favourite Bialetti coffee maker, while others decided to invest in other kitchen gadgets, such as Andi Oliver’s Ninja food processor, perhaps due to her ringing endorsement about its durability: “[This is] the only one that doesn’t die on me.”

But your favourite celebrity-recommended product of all? Perhaps because wedding season is in full swing, or perhaps because you wanted to follow her tip about using it on bed sheets, Jo Malone’s £29.99 Philips clothes steamer proved a bestseller.

And because celebs, they’re just like us, there were a few purchases our celebrities regret. David Gandy thinks that pricey Fortis lawnmower was a mistake – “I should have gone for one of Allett’s petrol mowers,” he said – while Dawn O’Porter says she’s bought “countless” pairs of jeans but never worn them because she “can’t quite [find something] right for my shape”. Nussaibah Younis also regrets buying her Christian Louboutin Miss Z patent leather 100mm stilettos as she “can barely walk three steps in them”.

Andi Oliver also told us about her niche but dangerous habit of “sleep shopping”: “I’m pretty menopausal, so I take sleeping pills. When I’m half falling asleep and lying in bed on my phone, I scroll and shop. I don’t even remember I’ve done it. And then weird things turn up.” Her worst buy? “A weird Tory wife outfit.”

Many of the celebrities we’ve spoken to enjoy finding bargain alternatives to everyday items. Gandy refills posh bottles of hand soap with cheaper versions (don’t we all?), and Hirons counterintuitively drives miles to get cheap petrol. And we’re not afraid to ask personal questions: when we quiz our celebs on where they buy their underwear, there’s been one clear winner: Marks & Spencer, of course.

We’ve found the gifts they buy their loved ones particularly touching, such as the hand-embroidered hankies Patrick Grant gave his dad, the jewellery belonging to her late mother that Caroline Hirons saved for her granddaughter, or Banjo Beale’s DIY engagement ring.

We’re occasionally reminded that these people really aren’t like us at all: Ben Fogle got his kids melted snow from the summit of Mount Everest, poured into vintage silver bottles he found on Etsy, engraved with his summit date. Slightly blows that Star Wars Lego set out of the water, doesn’t it?
