‘It’s very challenging’: how the Duke of Westminster’s farm is taking on the climate crisis

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 14:00:46 GMT

Amid world pressure from heatwaves and fertiliser shortages, billionaire’s business has invested in circular farming and biomethane

There is a distinctive smell of cow manure in the air at the Duke of Westminster’s dairy farm near Chester. It is a world away from the collection of grand West End properties controlled by the duke that form the backbone of his near £10bn fortune, a decade on from becoming Britain’s youngest billionaire.

As part of his 349-year-old Grosvenor empire, Lea Manor Farm on the duke’s Eaton Estate in north-west England has fared better than most dairy farms in recent years.

But it has also been hit by declining milk prices and other challenges faced by British farmers. A series of heatwaves causing drought, with a fifth looming this week – combined with fertiliser shortages triggered by the Iran war, diseases and a scarcity of workers since Brexit – have made farming very difficult.

Milk prices are cyclical; higher farm-gate prices in the UK last year encouraged an expansion of production, and oversupply in the UK and overseas has led to price reductions of up to 50% this year, according to Mark Roach, the managing director of Grosvenor Farms. “I can’t imagine any other industries suffering a 50% reduction.”

Lea Manor has been an arable and livestock farm for centuries, with a focus on potatoes between 1984 and 2002, when it switched to cows after the realisation that growing potatoes on the heavy Cheshire clay was not sustainable.

The farm at Eaton Estate, which is part of Grosvenor’s sprawling portfolio of offices, shops, homes, woods and farmland, has 77 staff and 2,600 Holstein friesian cows; it produces more than 34m litres of milk a year – 13,200 litres a cow – and supplies Müller and Tesco. It is surrounded by fields where animal feed such as wheat, maize, barley and rye is grown, set in 4,685 hectares (11,577 acres) of land.

This year’s heatwaves – supercharged by the escalating climate crisis – have piled more pressure on farmers. When temperatures rise above 25C, cows become more lethargic, eat less and produce less milk. At 36C during the June heatwave, each Grosvenor cow produced up to six litres less milk a day, with the heat partly mitigated by a sprinkler system and the large airy barns.

At some other farms, the milk yield was down as much as 10 litres a day for each cow, Roach says. “It’s very, very challenging for farming.”

Mark Preston, an executive trustee of Grosvenor, says: “Extreme weather in many parts of the northern hemisphere is affecting crop yields and farm economics. Farmers are adapting where they can, but the full impact is likely to become clearer over the next growing season, reinforcing the importance of building greater resilience into the UK’s food production system.”

With almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales officially in drought, wheat half the normal height and the broccoli yield down 50%, the UK is forced to import more food from countries such as Spain to avoid shortages, while global prices are rising.

Rural estates are also grappling with labour shortages post-Brexit, which has meant the flow of new eastern European workers has all but dried up.

Many British farms are lossmaking, while Lea Manor – Grosvenor’s only dairy farm – is profitable, after a big revamp starting in 2012 to improve efficiency using technology. The farming division made a profit before tax of £2.6m in 2024, down from £3.6m the previous year, with turnover of £16.2m. By contrast, Grosvenor made an underlying profit of £88.7m from its UK properties last year, up 14% on 2024. The duke received dividends of £53.7m from the group in 2025.

Despite the differing scale, Roach says that the farm is “not a hobby of the duke, it’s a commercial business”. Hugh Grosvenor is one of the UK’s richest individuals, with an estimated fortune of £9.5bn, who upon the sudden death of his father in 2016 inherited the vast estate his family has owned for centuries.

The bequest was largely shielded from 40% inheritance tax because the estate is held in a series of trusts rather than by the duke personally. Grosvenor says that it pays inheritance tax through a recurring 6% payment on the value of its assets every 10 years, instead of a single payment of 40% upon death.

At Lea Manor, the cows are led three times a day from their open-sided barns to an indoor carousel where they are milked using automated machinery. The milking unit is attached by a farm worker but comes off automatically once the udder has been emptied to prevent overmilking, which can lead to mastitis; two robots clean the teats before milking and disinfect them before the animals step off the carousel. Standing in 60 berths, 360 cows can be milked in an hour.

Three tankers are filled every day, with 29,000 litres pouring into each tanker, plus another part-filled tanker, which then go to a Müller processing plant in Manchester, and the milk is for sale in a Tesco supermarket the following morning.

Sensors in the floor measure how the cows walk, so if they show signs of having a sore foot, they will get a foot bath to prevent rot. Sometimes the cows do not want to get off the carousel and have to be guided out of the door back to their barn.

Recurring bovine tuberculosis is another challenge for dairy farms, with testing often unreliable and no vaccine available. Meanwhile, sheep farmers struggle with bluetongue, an insect-borne virus, as changing weather patterns have led to warnings of new diseases.

The rise in factory-style dairy farming has raised concerns over farms using intensive systems to increase productivity from “battery cows”.

Grosvenor insists that overall its cows are healthy, pointing to its own statistics. “Unhealthy cows do not produce much milk,” Roach says. Though its milk is not classed as organic, the farm feeds cows grass and has no routine antibiotics use.

The group says the barns are larger than industry standards and open on the sides, allowing plenty of natural light and airflow. However, the cows are not put out to pasture and stand on concrete floors (with anti-slip grooves). Only 8% of dairy herds in the UK are housed all year round, according to the RSPCA, which says cows should be allowed to graze some of the time.

Grosvenor says: “The health of our herd, low incidence of disease and minimal antibiotic use gives us confidence that the system is working well. We have welcomed representatives from the RSPCA to the farm, who described it as one of the quietest and most content herds they had seen.”

Grosvenor is building a biomethane plant on the estate to produce energy from cow manure, in an effort to broaden its revenue streams. The 2.4-hectare (six-acre) facility is expected to generate 72 gigawatts of renewable gas a year from up to 170,000 tonnes of manure, enough to heat about 6,000 homes, starting in 2027.

It is not the only such rural family estate to have a reactor. Apsley Farms in Hampshire, which has been owned by the Du Val de Beaulieu family since 1936, operates the UK’s third largest biomethane plant and has been supplying renewable gas to the grid since 2014. It generates 104GWh of green gas a year along with renewable electricity for the local network, supplying 10,000 households.

Manure is also used in Grosvenor’s fields, which means more than 80% of the forage fed to the dairy herd is grown without artificial fertilisers. Grosvenor prides itself on circular farming, a system designed to eliminate waste and reuse resources by turning crop waste into feed and animal waste into natural fertiliser, regenerating soil health. As a result, the group has not bought mined phosphate or potash fertilisers for about 15 years and only buys some nitrogen fertiliser.

The near-total blockade of the strait of Hormuz during the Iran war has led to global fertiliser shortages, a situation described as a “food security timebomb” by the head of the International Rescue Committee, David Miliband. Preston echoed those concerns, warning in May that the knock-on effects on food prices could arrive next year.

“The concerns we raised earlier this year remain very real,” Preston says. “Ongoing disruption to fertiliser supply chains continues to affect both availability and cost.”

The media is infatuated with Gadi Eisenkot, the ‘anti-Netanyahu’. Why?

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 14:00:46 GMT

The challenger to Netanyahu is more of the same. His record makes that abundantly clear

Western media outlets cannot seem to get enough of Gadi Eisenkot.

Israel’s former military chief and the leader of the newly formed Yashar party has been embraced by the international press as he and his party take the lead in the polls in the run-up to October’s elections.

“Will Israel embrace the ‘anti-Netanyahu’ who lost a son in Gaza?” asked the Times of London.

“He lost his son in Gaza. Now he’s coming for Netanyahu,” declared the Daily Telegraph.

“How Netanyahu’s Top General Became His Strongest Challenger,” ran the headline on a lengthy David Remnick profile of Eisenkot in the New Yorker.

“Does Gadi Eisenkot offer Israel a new chance?” wondered the Economist.

It’s a fair question. But perhaps British and American commentators aren’t the right people to answer it.

Why not ask the Palestinians of Gaza?

At the height of the genocide, between October 2023 and June 2024, Eisenkot sat in Benjamin Netanyahu’s war cabinet while Israel waged its barbaric military campaign in Gaza. During that period, Israeli airstrikes leveled entire apartment buildings, hit schools, hospitals and refugee camps, and killed more than 30,000 Palestinians.

Eisenkot eventually resigned from the war cabinet in 2024. But not over the horrific death toll. He left over what he regarded as the government’s strategic failures. Even the New Yorker’s Remnick, in his sympathetic profile piece, noted how the general, who lost his own soldier son Gal in the fighting, “remains reluctant to condemn Netanyahu in any detail for the extraordinary severity and duration of the war in Gaza”.

And Eisenkot has form when it comes to killing Gaza’s Palestinians. As Israel’s chief of staff during the “Great March of Return” in 2018 and 2019, he oversaw the armed response to mass Palestinian demonstrations against the siege of Gaza.

Israeli soldiers, mostly snipers, killed more than 200 Palestinians, including dozens of children. “The Israeli security forces killed and maimed Palestinian demonstrators who did not pose an imminent threat,” concluded a UN commission of inquiry, adding that it “found reasonable grounds to believe that demonstrators were shot in violation of their right to life”.

If the Economist wants to know whether Eisenkot represents “a new chance”, perhaps it should also ask Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Yes, Eisenkot may be opposed to the far-right Netanyahu government’s annexation plan, but he is also opposed to Palestinian self-determination and statehood. “I have never said two states for two peoples,” he proudly declaimed in an interview in June, “because I understand the depth of this religious-national-social conflict, and anyone who talks about ‘peace now’ and two states doesn’t understand the conflict.

“I very much believe in settlement in Judea and Samaria,” he continued, using the biblical term for the occupied West Bank.

So much for Eisenkot’s supposed pragmatism and liberalism. He openly rejects a two-state solution and proudly supports Israeli settlements – settlements that the international court of justice and multiple UN resolutions consider illegal under international law.

Or perhaps journalists should ask the residents of Beirut’s southern suburbs, where hundreds of men, women and children were killed in the 2006 Israeli assault on Lebanon, whether Eisenkot represents a fresh start.

As head of Israel’s Northern Command, he became closely associated with what came to be known as the “Dahiya Doctrine”: an Israeli military strategy of deterrence premised on the widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure.

“What happened in the Dahiya quarter of Beirut in 2006 will happen in every village from which Israel is fired on,” Eisenkot explained to an interviewer in 2008. “We will apply disproportionate force on it [village] and cause great damage and destruction there.”

The use of disproportionate force against civilian targets is, of course, an undeniable war crime.

Netanyahu may be a clear villain – but he can also be a cartoon villain. The danger with Eisenkot is that he is a villain who projects the image of a “moderate”. While Netanyahu has become a lightning rod, thanks to his arrogance and belligerence, and his indictment at the international criminal court (ICC) has made Israel an international pariah, Eisenkot cuts a more sober and reasonable figure; a “humble soldier”, to quote Remnick.

By simply not being Netanyahu, a Prime Minister Eisenkot would neutralize a lot of western liberal critics of Israel and restore the country’s standing in western capitals, while allowing the Israeli military and settlers to pursue the same policies of expansion and destruction in both the West Bank and Gaza.

Nor is Eisenkot unique. The Israeli political scene is filled with wolves in sheep’s clothing. There are Eisenkot’s fellow retired “moderate” generals in the Israeli opposition: Benny Gantz, who once bragged about sending parts of Gaza “back to the stone age”, and Yair Golan, who said after 7 October that Israel should prevent humanitarian aid from entering Gaza and the people there could “starve to death – it’s completely legitimate”.

Then there is Naftali Bennett, who has a long history of vile anti-Arab racism, oversaw the deadliest year on record for West Bank Palestinians when he was last prime minister of Israel in 2022, and is currently threatening both Turkey and Qatar.

The point is not that these Israeli politicians are all identical. They are not. They do differ in terms of tactics, personalities and political coalitions.

The point is that replacing Netanyahu with Eisenkot or any other Israeli opposition leader would not be a fundamental change in direction on the key issues of genocide, apartheid and occupation; it would only be a change in branding and messaging. For Palestinians and Lebanese, among many others in the Middle East, the result would be the same.

So come October, Israel’s most notorious prime minister may finally be voted out of office. If that happens, we can and should all celebrate the end of the Netanyahu era – and hope the ICC gets its man.

But then we’ll meet the new boss of Israel, same as the old boss of Israel.

Mehdi Hasan is Guardian US columnist and the editor-in-chief and CEO of Zeteo.

Gen Z calls it ‘loud budgeting’ – small business owners have been doing it for decades

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 14:00:45 GMT

The practice of openly proclaiming to the world what you can’t afford can lead to lower fees, reduced prices and better deals

Ask any small business owner what has challenged them the most over the past couple of years and you’ll frequently hear about cashflow. It’s no secret that costs have risen dramatically and finding places to save money isn’t easy.

If this describes your situation then I’ve got a solution to your problem. Ever hear of “loud budgeting”? Of course you have! You’ve probably been doing it for years.

Loud budgeting is considered to be a relatively new trend. According to one recent survey from Bank of America, as many as 42% of gen Zers “swear by it”. The concept isn’t hard. It’s basically the practice of openly proclaiming to the world that you can’t afford to do stuff instead of just quietly going along with the crowd and paying for something that you can’t afford. Financial services firm Charles Schwab & Co says it “makes oversharing cool – and effective”. The Economic Times says “it’s the smartest way to build wealth in 2026”.

“Loud budgeting is effectively being upfront about your financial situation and when something doesn’t align with your financial goals, values or capacity,” says Emma Edwards, founder of the Broke Generation who offers millennials financial advice on social media. “We have this belief that our financial situation shouldn’t have to be an inconvenience to others, or we shouldn’t reveal ourselves as being on a budget.”

How does one practice loud budgeting? That’s easy. Just complain a lot about money. Make it clear that you can’t afford to do stuff. Or, to save face among your friends, say that you probably could afford to go to that great restaurant or concert or trip to the lake, but choose not to because you simply don’t want to spend the money. Don’t blame yourself. Blame the economy. Blame the president. Point to the high cost of living and your paltry raise. Just be vocal and transparent about your finances. People like honesty. And they’ll understand. If they don’t – well, that’s their problem not yours.

All of the reports I’ve read about loud budgeting have focused on individuals, particularly younger people grappling with a challenging economic environment. But this strategy certainly isn’t new. In fact, I’ve seen a number of my clients – older, boomer, well-seasoned business owners – practice this behavior for literally decades.

“What? You want $0.02 more per pound for that poly-laminate? I can’t afford that!”

“A 4% price increase? Believe me, I hate doing it, but have you seen what my insurance company is charging me?”

“A 5% raise? Is he crazy? We’re barely able to stay in business and this guy wants a 5% raise. Sheesh!”

“I am certainly not going to pay $200 an hour for your accounting services. You of all people should know we can’t afford that.”

“A holiday party for the staff? Bah. Humbug!”

See what I mean? It’s loud budgeting, but from a business owner’s perspective. For many, this is not easy, because it goes against what we’re taught in business school.

The business gurus want us to be confident. And bold. We’re encouraged to take risks, work hard and relentlessly pursue our goals. “Fail greatly!” they say. “Reach for the stars!” “Push yourself to the limits!” “Be positive!” No one ever says to complain about your costs, gripe about your margins or whine about your money problems.

Loud budgeting turns all that positive-thinking advice on its head. Instead, it’s telling everyone around you – your customers, your employees, your suppliers – that you’re barely holding it together and that the $0.02 increase in poly-laminates is going to put you out of business.

You don’t have to reveal the truth. My clients who complain the most are the ones who are generally sitting on the biggest piles of cash. They’re driving 10-year-old cars, fly economy and eat at Outback Steakhouse. They don’t actually tell anyone that they’ve got enough money to afford more expensive things. That would destroy their ruse. They’re not broke. They just consider paying full price a character defect.

Loud budgeting is part of that ruse. Go ahead, try it. You’ll find that it’s a strategy to constantly remind anyone within earshot of your constrained budget and inevitably people start believing it. You’d be surprised at how many of them offer concessions – lower fees, reduced prices, better deals – out of sympathy or empathy or simply just to stop you from complaining.

You don’t need to be a young adult to understand this. Most successful small business owners do.

And it’s never too late to start. Go ahead: complain about your company’s terrible cashflow. Grumble. Grouse. Moan. Bellyache. Do this in public and do it loud. Make it so anyone will think twice before coming to you with something that’s going to cost more than what you’re already paying. People don’t want to get into fights. More than a few will be forced to come up with better ideas, rather than suffer your protests. Others may abandon their price increases altogether just to keep the peace. The ones that pursue their course of action will learn to really think through their case before presenting it to you.

“Loud budgeting helps take an element of shame away from feeling like you don’t have enough money,” said one financial educator.

Shame? I think shrewd is the better word.

From Dubai luxury to an Irish jail cell: Daniel Kinahan’s drastic lifestyle shift

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 13:54:04 GMT

Only spending outlet for man accused of helping to control a third of Europe’s cocaine supply will be prison tuck shop

It sounds like the penal equivalent of five stars: a private gym and library, daily outings to the exercise yard and a landing cleared of other prisoners.

Daniel Kinahan’s first full day inside the walls of Portlaoise prison on Monday, however, marked a drastic change from his luxury lifestyle in the United Arab Emirates.

The alleged leader of the Kinahan organised crime group is confined to a cell for about 20 hours a day, and instead of presiding over an empire said to be worth hundreds of millions of euros his only outlet for expenditure is the tuck shop.

The facilities, it turns out, are meagre consolation – a treadmill, some free weights and limited reading material. “The so-called gym and library are nothing much,” one source told the Irish Times. “The gym is probably slightly bigger than a box room in a house.”

That is the reality facing Kinahan, 49, for months until his trial – and possibly decades if convicted.

The Dubliner has not been convicted of any crime and remains innocent before the law, but his extradition on Sunday represents a victory for the Irish state and law enforcement agencies across the world.

Kinahan was named a leader of a cartel said to control about a third of Europe’s cocaine supply, along with running criminal sidelines in firearms and racketeering. From his base in Dubai he had appeared impervious to such allegations for almost a decade, while becoming an influential figure in sport through his boxing management company MTK Global, which arranged championship bouts.

That changed after the US offered a reward of up to $5m (£3.7m) for information that led to his arrest or conviction. The US treasury department said the Kinahan group had engaged in a gang war with another group in Ireland and Spain, “resulting in numerous murders”.

The US bounty helped Ireland to secure an extradition treaty with the UAE last year, paving the way for Kinahan’s arrest in Dubai in April on foot of an Irish warrant.

After failing to block extradition, Kinahan was flown in an Irish government jet to Casement aerodrome on Sunday and taken to the criminal courts of justice in central Dublin where he was charged with directing organised crime.

Told by one of the three judges that a bail application would have to be made to the high court, the prisoner was phlegmatic. “I think we know I won’t be getting bail, but thank you,” he said.

Observers at the hearing noted that Kinahan, wearing a black hoodie, black tracksuit bottoms and white trainers, looked older than the photographs that show a smiling, more youthful figure. He was pale, reflecting his incarceration since April.

Crowds lined part of the route to watch as he was driven in a Garda car – not a blast-proof prison van, as originally expected – to Portlaoise, a high-security prison 50 miles (80km) outside Dublin that used to house republican paramilitaries and is now home to drug gang members and others convicted of serious crimes.

Kinahan is the sole prisoner on a landing in A block that usually hosts eight inmates. During visits to the yard, which has wire netting to prevent contraband being dropped in, he will be alone. He will be served breakfast at 8am, lunch at 12.30pm and supper at 4.30pm and have a tuck shop account to buy personal items from the prison shop.

Video calls will afford contact with his wife and children in Dubai. A glass pane will separate him from in-person visitors. Kinahan is scheduled to return to the non-jury court on 5 October.

A consortium including the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, is close to completing a deal for a 30% stake in Liverpool after months of talks with Fenway Sports Group. The investors are led by Amit Bhatia, the son-in-law of the Indian billionaire Lakshmi Mittal and who previously was a shareholder and director at Queens Park Rangers.

The Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is another member of the group who will pay in the region of £1.35bn. The deal is effectively agreed, but may take up to a month to complete.

Bezos has a personal fortune of around $257bn (£190bn), according to Forbes, making him the fourth-richest person in the world, while Saverin is reportedly worth $32bn. This will be Bezos’s first investment in football, but he has previously looked into bidding for NFL franchises. The 62-year-old will receive equity as part of the deal, which Deloitte has advised on.

Bezos is the executive chair of Amazon having relinquished day-to-day control when he stepped down as chief executive five years ago. Under his leadership, the online retailer has diversified into being an entertainment provider and has bought numerous sports rights for its streaming service.

Amazon had live UK rights for 20 Premier League games each season for six seasons until the end of last year and broadcasts the Champions League in several European countries, as well as some NFL games in the US.

FSG bought Liverpool in 2010 and have overseen two Premier League titles. FSG sold 3% of the club to the US private equity firm Dynasty Equity in 2023.

It has been a summer of change at Anfield, with Andoni Iraola replacing Arne Slot as head coach, Mohamed Salah left on a free transfer and has joined Trabzonspor and Michael Edwards departed his role as chief executive officer at FSG.

Is Andy Burnham seriously about to tour Britain like some medieval monarch?

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 13:38:12 GMT

The ‘King of the North’ is on the march – or rather, on a bus. But maybe he’d be better off staying at home and thinking than heading out to press the flesh

Andy Burnham is going on a “listening tour”, travelling the country on a bus to find out what real people are concerned about. I’ve heard commentators rationalise the idea in various ways: apparently it underscores the difference between him and his predecessor, who only ever relaxed when he was out of the country; what else is Burnham going to do in recess, with his cabinet already chosen – organise his Post-it notes?; he’s been out of politics a long time, and many people will be only dimly aware of who he is; his speeches to date have had a very urban focus, and particularly with farming being this season’s crisis sector, he needs to broaden his sphere of interest to take in rural areas. Truly, the prime ministerial honeymoon period is like a one-year-old’s birthday party – all you have to do is stand up and smile, for everyone to clap.

None of the rationalisations are in any way true: an in-person focus group, where you journey to discover a range of concerns you could figure out for yourself with one report from the Institute for Public Policy Research and half a brain, is exactly the kind of thing Starmer would have done, if he’d thought of it. There’s quite a bit to be getting on with, between now and September, since autumn’s looming crises – food shortages, energy price hikes due to the ongoing war in Iran – are plain, and there’s no better time to plan than when you don’t have the leader of the opposition yanking your chain. Burnham actually has tremendous household-level recognition, thanks to a combination of hinterland and eyelashes, as evidenced by the fact that even when contesting Makerfield he got mobbed every time he got out of a car. Now, the conditions devastating farmers, being the direct result of climate crisis, would be better addressed by a long-range strategy on the transition to renewables, not a chinwag.

I’ll meet the road show halfway, though, and accept that the thinking behind it is buried deeper in the squishy collective subconscious than the “marketing strategy for mid-sized building society” strata. This is the living definition of “peripatetic”, an adjective usually attached to kings. Medieval kings travelled around the country in order to collect their taxes by literally eating them from one noble estate to the next. Tax hikes could be exacted by simply adding to your entourage and eating more. King John’s train stretched two miles, bulked up by the mercenaries required to protect the pampered non-warrior class from rebel barons who were sick of having their food eaten. In a pesky feedback loop, the larger your entourage, the more you all ate, the more annoyed the aristocracy became, the more mercenaries you needed and the larger your entourage.

Burnham could be forgiven for thinking he’s more than a match for this death spiral, having the lessons of history right there, but can we forgive him for the emotional leap that put him on his tour bus? His first question seems to have been not “What would the leader of a mature democracy in an embattled period do?” but “What would be the first move of the King of the North?” His kingly role models must all come from the dawn of monarchy, since by the time you get to Henry VIII, he’s only really travelling to escape sewage overflow from his last great palace. But then “King of the North” has always had a very medieval overtone. A sign of the early modern period’s growing governmental sophistication was its ability to distinguish one bit of the north from another.

It is endearing, if also nerve-racking and painful, to consider the faith underpinning this self-fashioning – that leadership is an innate quality more important than sequential thought and planning, and that if the stars light upon a leader who can connect with his people, the nation will come together, good decisions will be made, and the rest is detail. One can but hope that’s the limit of the wishful thinking, and he’s not also banking on some dragons.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

How to feel optimistic in the face of crisis? Ask the kids fighting slug-like aliens

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 13:00:44 GMT

The Animorphs books taught my generation about digging deep in the face of an existential threat. We need that spirit now more than ever

Recently I found myself thinking about slug-like aliens that crawl through people’s ears and into their brains, with the ultimate purpose of global domination. It would explain a lot about what has gone so wrong with the world, wouldn’t it? And it was why I immediately flashed back to the children’s fantasy series Animorphs when Donald Trump’s health secretary and conspiracy theorist, Robert F Kennedy Jr, admitted to having had a worm in his brain.

While visiting my parents in Cleveland, Ohio recently, I realised that a few books from the children’s fantasy series were still sitting on the shelves in my old bedroom. No fewer than 54 Animorphs titles were published between 1996 and 2001, and a total of 35m copies have been sold. “I may have just landed a job thanks to Animorphs,” my childhood friend Clifton texted me with excitement in the mid-2010s, when we were fresh out of college. “It was an interview for a vegan food cart and the last question they asked me was what Animorph I would morph into. I said an orangutan.”

The premise sees five adolescent friends encounter a crashed alien spaceship and then face an intergalactic war against the Yeerks, genocidal slug-adjacent beings that slither into the brains of the host species. The young humans are given the ability to transform into any animals they’ve touched, along with the simple task of defending humanity. My generation were told we could grow up to do anything, that life was a continual arc of progress towards better lives, and that the old ideological battles of the past had been laid to rest. We were empowered by what we found in the pages of Animorphs: that Jake, Cassie, Rachel, Marco and Tobias had been endowed with the power of nature itself to help Earth fend off the existential threat of alien conquest.

Despite the optimism of the 90s, Animorphs was surprisingly dark and morally nuanced for millennial children’s fiction. Foreshadowing the real-world future, the teenagers watch parents and other family members fall under the cognitive control of the Yeerks. Looking back at the series now – and the era that produced it – the Animorphs’ baddies had to be an alien species, because it would have stretched credulity that humanity might destroy the Earth by itself, of its own volition. Now, instead of the Yeerks, we have megalomaniac billionaires and fossil fuel interests that have instilled climate denialism and defeatism into our minds – aided by media they so often control – and stripped us of the ability to even conceptualise our collective agency.

The concept of discrete “generations” might be dubious, but where it holds most firmly is in shared cultural references. What millennials share is the distinct feeling of being a bridge: between the analogue and the digital; between a shared informational reality and the post-truth world; between an optimistic world and a pessimistic one. (This latter point shows up even in scientific analysis of pop music: studies have concluded that pop has become sadder.)

It’s the reflex towards a hopeful worldview, and the subsequent shattering of this optimism, that lie at the heart of millennial nostalgia for the less fraught times of our youth. On social media, it’s been dubbed the “millennial optimism era”. You don’t have to search hard to find the sources of that nostalgia: Akon and Britney Spears coming out of the speakers at my gym, Sum 41 playing at the bougie brasserie around the corner. Meanwhile one huge comeback tour collides into the next. Onscreen, too, everything seems to be getting a remake or a reboot: Toy Story, Scary Movie, Air Bud and, if things go well, Animorphs too, which had a brief, two-season run on TV just before the turn of the millennium. Ryan Coogler, who directed Sinners, is developing a new Animorphs TV series for Disney+.

Across the generational line, millennials and gen Z share the same eco-anxiety: in France, it has been found to be significantly more pronounced among those aged 15-34 than among those over 50. Researchers in India found a similar pattern, just as they did in the US. Hannah Ritchie from Our World In Data writes in her personal newsletter that older generations are actually more likely to say that we’re already feeling the impacts of the climate crisis, because they can compare today’s heatwaves and snowless winters with the climate of their childhoods. But the emotional response is different, she writes: millennials and gen Z are more likely to feel fear, guilt and outrage about it.

There is a cruel irony to the fatalism of the young: those who will most suffer the consequences of the climate emergency are those most resigned to that fate. Similarly, I think there is something that doesn’t show up in data yet, but is there in gen Z’s nostalgia for the “millennial optimism era”. It’s the difference between millennials believing that all of this can and should be fought, and gen Z having no nostalgic point of reference for the plausibility of fighting it at all.

after newsletter promotion

Sinners was an intensely literate movie about history, racism and trauma, forces that sap us of our vitality, and our ability to fight back. So I’m not surprised my fellow millennial Coogler might be turning to Animorphs next. In the end, I suspect that he might circle the following: the threat to all of us is not solely alien, but an alien version of ourselves. That fighting back successfully will mean remembering who we really are. That nature is our ally, and we have to remember how indelibly our future is tied to its state of wellbeing. I can’t think of a more urgent millennial-optimist metaphor to splash on to the big screen.

Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoir Generation Desperation is out now

Prison without hope or end is psychological torture. Burnham doesn’t need another review to tell him that

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 11:51:36 GMT

Political leaders have kicked the can of public protection tariff reform down the road for years – causing hopeless inmates to take their own lives

In January 2015, Tommy Nicol told his family that he was suffering “psychological torture of a person who is doing 99 years”. Nicol had been given an imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentence six years earlier for stealing a car from a garage and injuring the owner. He was already two years beyond his four-year tariff – the minimum time you can serve in prison before being considered for release. Nicol was given another two-year knock-back from the Parole Board and was in despair. If and when he got released, he would be on a lifelong licence. Eight months later, aged 37, Nicol hanged himself at The Mount prison in Hertfordshire, England.

By the time he took his own life, the inhumane IPP sentence had already been abolished for three years. The problem is, it didn’t apply retroactively. Those already serving IPP sentences stayed on them. This, despite David Blunkett, who devised and introduced them as home secretary in 2005, calling it “the biggest regret” of his political career. And this despite UN special rapporteur on torture Alice Edwards agreeing with Tommy Nicol that the sentence was “psychological torture”. Astonishingly, more than 2,000 people are still serving IPP sentences in England and Wales.

Last week prime minister Andy Burnham announced a new review into indeterminate sentences as part of his plan to reduce the prison population. Reviewing a sentence that was abolished 14 years ago seems Kafkaesque. And what exactly is left to review? We all know IPPs are wrong – they are no longer handed down, and those serving them should be resentenced. Review after review has said so. Surely it makes more sense to simply introduce legislation to make that happen?

IPPs were given to people who didn’t merit life sentences, but were regarded as a risk to society. With an IPP, once prisoners have served their tariff, they have to apply to the Parole Board for release. The Parole Board only grants release if satisfied that the offender no longer poses a risk to the public. This means that an IPP prisoner could be detained indefinitely. It was expected that very few prisoners would receive IPPs (an estimated 900 at any one time) and only for serious crimes.

The reality couldn’t have been more different. Between 2005 and 2013 (a handful of people were sentenced after the cut-off of 31 December 2012), 8,711 people were given an IPP sentence. While some had long tariffs, most were on low tariffs for minor crimes. Nevertheless, many never got released. Or if they did, they were recalled to prison for the slightest breaches of their licence, such as being late for appointments with probation officers.

Often the people who were imprisoned on an IPP were already vulnerable. Not surprisingly, many prisoners lost hope, like Nicol did. Ninety-four people had taken their own lives up to March 2025 while serving the sentence in prison. Forty-four people are known to have taken their own lives while out on licence, though these community-based figures have only been tracked since April 2019, so are likely to be higher.

The IPP horror stories are legion, and many concern young people such as Martin Myers, who served 18 years for attempting to steal a cigarette, despite having an original tariff of just 19 months and 27 days when sentenced aged 24; Ronnie Sinclair served 16 years in jail on a three-year IPP tariff for stealing a flowerpot at the age of 17; and Wayne Bell was 17 when he was imprisoned on an IPP for punching a boy and stealing a bike in 2007 on a tariff of one year and 350 days. He is still in prison 19 years later.

Although the lifelong licence was removed for IPP prisoners in 2024, many are still serving the sentence. As of June 2026, there were 2,271 IPP prisoners jailed in England and Wales – 856 unreleased prisoners and 1,415 recalled prisoners.

This proposed review would be the third since 2022 when the cross-party Justice Committee Inquiry concluded IPP sentences were “irredeemably flawed” and recommended resentencing. Nothing was done. Last year the Howard League expert working group recommended fixed-release windows for IPP prisoners. Nothing was done. A private member’s bill sponsored by (Lord) Anthony Woodley urged a comprehensive, retrospective resentencing exercise for all prisoners still subject to an IPP. The bill passed its second reading in the House of Lords and progressed to the committee stage, but the government blocked it.

The campaign group Ungripp fears that any new review will have the same outcome as previous ones. “Each review meant more wasted time, more people on IPP despairing and inevitably, more suicides,” it says. “How can we be confident this will be any different?”

Shockingly, all but three of the 2,271 people serving IPP sentences in prison are past their tariff. With resentencing, these three prisoners would be given a fitting determinate sentence, while the 2,268 remaining IPP prisoners would gradually be released with appropriate social care and housing to ensure they were safe within the community and the community safe with them. The £60,000 a year saved in prison costs would go a considerable way towards paying for this.

So why hasn’t it yet been done? Simple. Political leaders are terrified of looking soft on crime – so they have consistently kicked the IPP can down the road. Yet IPP sentences are universally recognised as unjust. Not a single mainstream politician defends this barbaric sentence.

Last year Keir Starmer said: “It is right that the IPP sentence has been abolished”, but he wasn’t brave enough to resentence IPP prisoners. Andy Burnham must be braver.

The former supreme court justice Lord Brown of Eaton-under-Heywood called IPP “the greatest single stain on our criminal justice system” in a 2020 report for the Prison Reform Trust. If Burnham wants to show he means business, he will not bother with another review and will simply legislate to get this shaming stain removed once and for all.

Resentencing is too late for Tommy Nicol and the many others IPP prisoners who took their own lives, but it’s not too late for those still behind bars, tortured by not knowing whether their imprisonment will ever end.

Simon Hattenstone is a Guardian features writer

Lesbians, latex and $2,000 condoms: why are this summer’s movies so obsessed with sex?

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 11:00:43 GMT

From One Night Only to The Invite, a wave of new movies are a raunchy antidote to gen Z celibacy

The first alarm bells sounded nearly 10 years ago, and since then, a deluge of books, podcasts and roundtables has tried to get at the bottom of the problem: why is gen Z not having sex?

Recently it’s as though culture has been recalibrated to make up for the youth’s apparent frigidity. “Smut” literature is on the rise, prestige TV is now depicting OnlyFans models, and indie films have taken a turn towards kink. This summer, through confused young protagonists and their sexual misadventures, the movies are zeroing in on generational attitudes about sex.

There is a contradiction behind gen Z chastity: despite being the most sexually progressive generation ever, zoomers live under the influence of rampant sexual conservatism. After the 2022 overturning of Roe v Wade, for instance, 16% of single gen Z adults are more afraid to date. This tension is at the heart of One Night Only, a new romcom that imagines a world in which Congress has outlawed premarital sex. For one night of the year, the government lifts the ban, essentially enacting the purge for single people’s sexual freedom. On this night, after a series of missed encounters and wrong turns, Owen (Callum Turner) and Allie (Monica Barbaro) meet cute.

Despite its political tenor, One Night Only’s vision of dystopia is not a comment on America’s rapid hurtle toward authoritarianism. It merely presents obstacles for Allie and Owen to overcome – such as the $2,000 price tag for the condoms Owen attempts to procure – much like the missed connection brought about by a busy phone line in a 90s romcom. We know nothing about what these characters’ lives were like before the ban, which means that Allie’s complaints about the difficulty of finding her “Prince Charming” come off generic, indistinguishable from any number of complaints that I, a married zoomer, have heard from my single friends about dating in the age of apps.

Silly hijinks aside, One Night Only misunderstands today’s sex recession as libidinal, when really, it’s existential. It’s not that zoomers aren’t horny, or can’t find a man: they are the first generation to grow up fully under the influence of the internet, with its attendant alienations; worse, its youngest members came of age during the pandemic. Knowing how to relate to one another is hard enough, let alone how to initiate sex – a process often awkward, if not outright painful, for everyone no matter their age (This much, at least, One Night Only gets right.)

Other films this summer understand that sex can’t solve the fundamental alienation brought about by modern life. It’s loneliness that ails Elliot (Cooper Hoffman), the flush-cheeked studio assistant to the provocative artist Erika Tracy (Olivia Wilde) in Gregg Araki’s I Want Your Sex. For the most part Araki’s characters stay in their boxes, with Erika the worldly provocateur to Elliot’s gullible dork. But in the film’s best moment, a doomed threesome with Elliot’s sexually confused roommate Apple (Chase Sui Wonders), that order is disturbed. The arrival of a third person with her own muddled desires – does Apple want Erika, Elliot, or both? Do they want her? Does she want to be wanted? – leads Erika to lose her grip, and Elliot to rebel against his part. Standing there half naked, they might as well be worlds apart.

I Want Your Sex shares a dynamic with The Invite (in which Wilde also stars, and which she directed) and Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma: a younger and less experienced person (or couple) becomes entangled with an older, sexy woman who shows them the path to self-knowledge through desire. But whereas sex is an all-consuming problem for the characters in The Invite and I Want Your Sex, Camp Miasma presents sex, death and art as intertwined human impulses that are impossible to separate from one another. Tasked with rebooting the Camp Miasma slasher franchise that first prompted her “queer awakening”, 29-year-old film-maker Kris (Hannah Einbinder) has one theme on her mind: “DESIRE”, as she scrawls in her journal, in big block letters.

By letting us into Kris’s process of self-discovery, Miasma addresses generational concerns in more nuanced ways than its counterparts this summer. Through her relationship with her muse Billy Presley (a wonderful Gillian Anderson), Camp Miasma’s original final girl, Kris learns that to arrive at artistic epiphany or sexual climax, one must let go of control, let the movie play out. To Billy, slashers are as elemental as sexual desire: she teaches Kris that sex, like art, is a visceral experience not easily theorized.

While One Night Only plays threats to bodily autonomy for laughs and I Want Your Sex’s Erika rolls her eyes at gen Z’s “wokeness”, Camp Miasma strikes a more sincere tone. Kris is initially drawn to reboot the Camp Miasma films to correct the franchise’s transphobia, but only discovers a physical and emotional experience of art when she learns to stop overintellectualizing slashers. It’s only then that she can really connect with Billy, and it’s only through their connection that she can make a film that is true.

These movies don’t exactly present zoomers with a model for how to be a young person who has sex; if anything, they’re more like cautionary guides showing what kinds of behavior to avoid. But that’s precisely where their value lies. After decades of unrealistic depictions of sex on screen and a few worrisome years when it seemed likely that sex would disappear from the movies altogether, it’s a relief to see sex return to screen – messy awkwardness and all.

Stuff of nightmares? Meet the bootlace worm – super-long, super-elastic, and it fires toxic slime

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 11:00:43 GMT

Its mucus, which can kill crabs and cockroaches, could be the basis of new insecticides

It’s the shuddery stuff of nightmares for some, but for a select group who admire extending ladders, giraffes and the Odyssey, one of the longest animals in the world is bound to appeal.

This creature is nneither the blue whale, nor a lion’s mane jellyfish but the humble bootlace worm, Lineus longissimus, one of the most remarkable marine invertebrates of them all.

It can stretch out longer than an Olympic swimming pool. In fact, one worm, found washed ashore after a storm at St Andrews, was recorded at an incredible 55 metres in length. Worm-sceptics suggest it may have been stretched out, because the species is also very elastic. A more usual length is a mere 15 metres. Its width is just 5–10mm.

This slender, super-long superworm has a second superpower: it can fire toxic slime. When threatened, the blackish-brown bootlace worm discharges a poisonous mucus which may remind you of the smell of sewage if you pick up a beached worm.

Although the Swedish archbishop and naturalist Olaus Magnus first noted its toxic slime back in 1555, it wasn’t until 2018 that the worm’s toxins were fully described by (Swedish) scientists. Its mucus was designed to paralyse and kill crabs.

Researchers have discovered the toxins, known as alpha-nemertides, can also kill cockroaches but have little impact on mammals, leading to the possibility that they could be the basis for new insecticides. There are likely to be many more useful chemicals and medicines still to be discovered within the invertebrate world.

The bootlace worm is one of many little-known nemerteans – ribbon or proboscis worms. The phylum contains more than 1,250 described species of worms which are found everywhere from intertidal zones to great ocean depths – a little-heralded but rich and vital branch of the tree of life.

This record-breaking and yet rather overlooked worm is a voracious and extremely effective predator, enjoying nothing more than swallowing annelids (soft-bodied, segmented worms) whole. It was nominated by a reader who says it is “a neglected but quite amazing branch on the tree of life. The longest of all wormy creatures (up to 15m?!) and only a few mm wide.” He loves “a worm that can stretch and stretch and stretch” and argues that it is one of the “many amazing creatures contributing to Britain’s coastal heritage”.

Record 230 people cross Channel to UK as smugglers turn to ‘mega-dinghies’

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 10:55:55 GMT

Crossing in larger vessel highlights changing tactics despite increased enforcement on French coast

A dinghy carrying a record 230 people has arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel in the early hours of Monday.

It is the clearest indication yet that people smugglers in northern France are adapting their business model and escalating their so-called taxi boat strategy to evade enforcement by UK and French authorities.

The development is likely to be a blow to the prime minister and home secretary. Andy Burnham has vowed to be “relentless” and “bring back control”, while Shabana Mahmood has said the government is “bearing down” on small boat crossings.

French authorities told the Guardian that before an incident last week, in which a mega-dinghy carrying 173 people capsized after its engine caught fire, there had been nine mega-dinghy crossings of the Channel so far this year.

Although the number crossing the Channel this year has fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year, the increasing use of larger vessels demonstrates how quickly people smugglers have adapted to stronger enforcement by French police on beaches in northern France.

The UK government has struck a deal with Germany to increase seizures of traditional dinghies and engines “upstream”.

Last year, 106 people were reported to have crossed the Channel in a single dinghy in August and 125 in September. The emergence of mega-dinghies coincided with the announcement in July 2025 of the UK-France “one in, one out” deal, under which a person arriving in the UK from France by small boat can be returned in exchange for another person being brought legally to the UK to claim asylum.

On 12 July this year, a mega-dinghy carrying 128 people arrived in the UK, followed by another carrying 165 people on 23 July. On 4 August, a dinghy carrying 173 people capsized after the engine caught fire. All those onboard are believed to have been rescued, with 11 sustaining minor injuries and three taken to hospital in Boulogne.

The use of mega-dinghies poses an even greater risk to life than smaller vessels, which have recently carried an average of between 50 and 60 passengers, according to NGOs working with asylum seekers crossing the Channel. When small-boat crossings began in 2018, only a handful of people typically travelled in each dinghy.

While there have been “green days” this year, when adverse weather has made conditions too dangerous for smugglers to launch dinghies, NGOs say many continue to wait in northern France for an opportunity to cross the Channel. They include some who have been returned to France under the one-in, one-out scheme and hope to reach the UK for a second time.

Hannah Marwood, the head of legal access at Care4Calais, which delivers emergency aid to refugees, said: “Deterrence doesn’t stop people seeking safety, it just pushes them towards greater danger and greater exploitation. We’ve worked with people who were returned to France only to face violence, exploitation and unsafe conditions, leaving them with no option but to risk another dangerous journey.

“Politicians keep promising that another tough policy will solve this but the evidence keeps proving them wrong. If the government is serious about stopping dangerous journeys, it needs to stop recycling failed gimmicks and create safe routes to claim asylum. When people have a safe way to reach protection, they don’t have to risk their lives to find it.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “This latest incident demonstrates the reckless and dangerous tactics employed by the criminal gangs facilitating these crossings, who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people on to unseaworthy vessels. “We are making progress, with the number of small-boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020. But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches.”

Roman shipwreck with 500 amphorae found off coast of Sicily

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 10:44:54 GMT

Discovery of 2,100-year-old vessel hailed as ‘one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years’

A 2,100-year-old Roman shipwreck carrying about 500 amphorae has been discovered 3 miles off the coast of Mazara del Vallo in Sicily.

Italy’s Carabinieri cultural heritage protection squad investigated the wreck with the help of divers and underwater cameras after receiving a tip-off from fishers. The vessel was found at a depth of about 46 metres (151ft) and was carrying hundreds of amphorae – ancient two-handled ceramic jars with a narrow neck – thought to have been used mainly to transport wine.

The wreck, measuring about 21 metres long and 6 metres wide, was described by Italy’s culture minister, Alessandro Giuli, as “one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years”.

Giuli said the wreck offered “precious fragments of our history” and provided further evidence of the trade routes and exchanges that made the Mediterranean “a crossroads of civilisations”.

The divers Giacomo De Mola and Igor Bisulli described how they came across the wreck.

“Visibility wasn’t the best … I got closer. And my heart stopped. Below me was a vast expanse of amphorae,” De Mola said in an Instagram post accompanying video footage of the discovery.

“This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life,” he said. “It’s hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again.”

Most of the ship’s cargo consisted of Dressel 1A amphorae, widely used to transport wine and particularly valuable to archaeologists because they can help reconstruct the commercial networks that linked Italy with other parts of the Mediterranean between the second and first centuries BC.

Over the coming months, Sicily’s superintendency of the sea is expected to carry out a new phase of scientific documentation and research at the site. Archaeologists will seek to establish more precisely the date of the wreck, the origin and intended destination of its cargo, and the condition of the surviving material, while also drawing up measures to protect what officials have described as a site of exceptional archaeological significance.

The discovery is the latest in a series of important Roman wrecks found in Italian waters.

In 2021, another Roman vessel dating from the second century BC was discovered off the coast of Palermo. The wreck lay 92 metres beneath the sea near Isola delle Femmine and images taken by an underwater robot showed it carrying a large cargo of wine amphorae.

Before that, an almost intact Roman vessel dating from the second century BC was discovered in 2013 off the coast of Liguria. The ship, carrying about 50 valuable amphorae, was located by police divers about a mile off Alassio at a depth of about 50 metres.

In that case, police were alerted to the wreck during a year-long investigation into archaeological artefacts believed to have been looted and sold on the black market in northern Italy.

Italian police recover hundreds of illegally removed ancient Roman amphorae each year, many of them found in the homes or warehouses of collectors and art dealers.

The waters surrounding Sicily are regarded as one of the Mediterranean’s richest areas for underwater archaeology. The island’s strategic position along the ancient maritime routes linking Greece, the Middle East, north Africa and Europe means its seabed is believed to contain some of the most significant surviving wrecks from the ancient world.

Uefa, Concacaf and AFC push for Infantino to quit and discuss rival competitions

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 10:02:37 GMT

Confederations write open letter damning Fifa president

Concacaf president Montagliani seen as top contender

Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf will push for Gianni Infantino to resign after writing an open letter calling for “leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it”.

In a dramatic escalation of the war that has threatened to tear football apart since details emerged of the Fifa president’s failed Football Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, the three governing bodies accused Infantino of “trust broken through deception” and condemned his failure to acknowledge that the proposal should not have been unilaterally launched.

The three confederations have started preliminary discussions about the organisation of new competitions along with Uefa’s repeated threats to boycott Fifa events. As things stand, the under-20 women’s World Cup next month could take place without European teams and alternative options are being sought.

The letter is signed by the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, his AFC counterpart, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, and the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani. Efforts to unite around a suitable candidate to replace Infantino have stepped up since his privately backed plan was revealed and Montagliani is believed to be among the contenders.

“Leadership in football is not a possession,” the letter reads. “It is not about holding – or demanding – power to be held. It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it. When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned.”

It strongly criticises Fifa’s response to the crisis, when a meeting between a small number of senior staff in Rabat was followed by an apology from Infantino that appeared not to show remorse for the scheme.

“It treats this as a failure of communication, when what football witnessed was a failure of judgment,” the letter says. “It did not acknowledge that the proposal itself was inherently wrong. There remains no recognition that attempting to sell an interest in the Fifa World Cup was a profound failure of judgment – not just a procedural misstep, but a fundamental breach of trust with the very institutions Fifa exists to serve.”

The three presidents also call for an independent review, conducted by a body outside football, into the affair. Fifa had committed previously to presenting a full report to the Fifa Council at its next scheduled meeting.

The letter directly addresses concerns that countries may lose out on financial aid under a different leadership, saying it is “[not] about any member association losing the support it has earned, despite the fearmongering directed at our leadership to suggest otherwise”.

The letter concludes: “There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness … Football’s strength has always been its unity. We call for that unity to be honoured now, with leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it.”

Any candidates for the Fifa election must announce their bid by 18 November. The confederations are understood to consider all options in their push for Infantino to be replaced, provided they fit within Fifa’s statutes and governance framework.

Sign up to Football Daily

after newsletter promotion

While the letter outlines the stances of the three confederations, and particularly their leaderships, the story is more complicated within individual member associations. Few outside Europe have been willing to come out publicly against Infantino and only a small minority have been tempted to recall the letters of support they had sent backing his re‑election next March. The influential African and South American confederations, Caf and Conmebol, have come out backing Infantino in recent days.

A number of larger member associations have written to Infantino asking for a meeting where he would be required to explain his actions around the FFE scheme. No response has been received. Nor has Infantino been in touch with federations to address his leading role in the turmoil.

The confederations’ tripartite statement was followed by another joint release headed by the World Cup hosts US Soccer and Canada Soccer, who along with the Caribbean Football Union and Central American Football Union also called for governance change at Fifa.

The four bodies comprise 40 of the 41 Concacaf members, with the outliers being the third World Cup hosts Mexico, who went public last Friday with their continued support for Infantino.

US Soccer had previously been silent and its willingness to condemn Fifa is significant, particularly as it is bidding to host the 2031 Women’s World Cup and also wants to stage games at the 2029 Club World Cup.

“US Soccer, Canada Soccer, CFU [Caribbean Football Union] and UNCAF [Central American Football Union] stand together, along with our colleagues around the world, in calling for meaningful change that strengthens Fifa’s governance, transparency and accountability,” the statement read.

Vondrousova’s antics put tennis doping tests in spotlight – a far cry from football’s view

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 07:00:38 GMT

Former Wimbledon champion’s suspension comes as Mykhailo Mudryk returns for Chelsea, exposing stark contrast in processes

In the months between the first announcement of Marketa Vondrousova’s doping test refusal and the release of the full reasoned decision after her four‑year ban, the 2023 Wimbledon champion did her best to grab hold of the narrative. Between her social media posts and later interviews, Vondrousova explained that she had serious concerns about her safety during the encounter, that the doping control officer at her door had acted improperly, and that her mental health problems had affected her judgment.

Then came the 58-page document, a summary of the court tribunal process, which was finally released a little over a week ago. Among the ample questionable decisions it showed Vondrousova to have made that evening, the text to her boyfriend shortly after the doping control officer arrived was particularly revealing, an indication that she felt disdain towards the tester rather than fear: “So like here is ringing some cunt from the doping,” she wrote.

On 22 June, the International Tennis Integrity Agency announced that Vondrousova had been suspended for four years after refusing an anti-doping test last December. The 27-year-old had been approached by an anti-doping officer at around 8pm at her flat at a time that fell outside the one‑hour slot players provide to the anti-doping authorities as part of the whereabouts programme for doping control officers to reach her.

The full reasoned decision makes for excruciating reading from Vondrousova’s perspective. The most compelling conclusion is that she was ignorant of basic anti-doping rules, that she acted arrogantly due to her irritation at the 8pm anti-doping call and her decision to sign a document refusing a doping test, despite being told there could be severe consequences, will go down as one of the most ill-advised, self‑sabotaging decisions from any tennis player in history.

Vondrousova seemed to believe that testers should arrive only in her designated whereabouts slot, and her agent was also painfully clueless about the anti-doping rules, and she acted on those incorrect assertions. Aside from this, the only other compelling theory would be that she knew what was in her system and deliberately did not want to be tested.

Once the seriousness of her situation became clear after the refused test, Vondrousova even distastefully invoked the horrific stabbing of Petra Kvitova by a home intruder in Czechia when explaining her apparent fearfulness on social media. Despite that, Vondrousova still felt safe enough to walk out of the apartment building to take her dog for a walk, while the doping control officer was still at her door.

Even a large part of Vondrousova’s defence was centred on her dire decision making. She argued that she had been suffering from generalised anxiety disorder and acute stress reaction, which impaired her cognitive functions and led to her questionable actions. One point of interest ahead of the reasoned decision was how compelling her evidence would be to support this argument. Of the four written testimonies she put forward from experts, however, two doctors did not attend the hearing for cross‑examination and one confirmed at the hearing that he did not actually diagnose her. The tribunal concluded that, even if they accepted all of Vondrousova’s evidence, her excuse did not meet the high threshold to justify refusing to take a test.

The World Anti-Doping Agency code is gruelling and stressful for athletes, and most are critical of parts of the system, but it is still part of an athlete’s job to understand the rules and ensure, to the best of their ability, that they comply. An appeal to the court of arbitration for sport may follow in the future, but for now the consequences of Vondrousova’s errors are catastrophic. She is suspended until she is 31, a potentially career-ending absence for one of the most talented players of her generation.

On the same day that Vondrousova’s full decision was released, another high-profile sports doping case was resolved with the announcement from the Football Association that Mykhailo Mudryk, the Ukrainian winger who plays for Chelsea, was free to return to competition after his initial four-year suspension following a positive test for the banned substance meldonium had been shortened.

In contrast to the lengthy, detailed document that accompanied Vondrousova’s case and most doping cases in prominent Olympic sports, the Mudryk case, like the few public doping cases in football, has been defined by how little information is available due to the FA’s confidentiality rules. Forget a 58‑page document, the FA never even announced that Mudryk had received a four-year suspension; this information was revealed by Cas in April when Mudryk appealed against the suspension.

The FA then announced on 31 July that it had, along with Wada, come to a case resolution agreement with Mudryk, reducing the length of suspension. The Ukrainian accepted the anti-doping rule violation but was allowed to return to competition. According to the FA’s press release, the low concentration of meldonium in Mudryk’s sample would not have been reported under Wada’s new technical document, which comes into force in January, and there were apparently “other circumstances of the case”, none of which were specified, that led to the resolution. There are no further details.

After this announcement, the swiftness with which the narrative shifted from the doping suspension to how Mudryk could possibly reintegrate in the Chelsea team, to football matters, was fascinating. Little was made of the secrecy that football’s governing bodies operate with when it comes to anti-doping. This is merely one example – the circumstances around Paul Pogba’s doping ban in 2024, for example, were also murky until Cas became involved after his appeal.

Considering the confidentiality with which the FA operates in anti‑doping matters, it is hard not to wonder which other players might have quietly failed doping tests over the years and how other potential cases might have been resolved. Most other sporting governing bodies, including cycling, athletics and more recently tennis have been forced to become more transparent due to the damage inflicted on their reputation by high-profile doping cases.

Football, however, is eternally popular and there have been relatively few significant doping cases despite how high the competitive stakes are in the sport, meaning there is far less pressure on its governing bodies to be more transparent. As a result, the FA continues to manage its anti-doping programme in relative silence.

It’s not just the Odyssey effect: poetry is booming because it’s the only language for these times of violence and chaos

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 07:00:37 GMT

From Homer’s epic to conflicts in Ukraine and Gaza, we can see how poetry fills the gap when ordinary ways of writing or speaking aren’t enough

The biggest sales of poetry since records began are expected this year. The reason? The movies, of course. UK print sales of The Odyssey increased by 1,400% in the four weeks to 25 July compared with the same period last year. In the US, year-to-date sales of The Odyssey are up 76% so far. Christopher Nolan is doing miracles for Homer – whatever problems one might have with the movie (and Emily Wilson, who made the most popular recent translation, has a few).

Strip out the Odyssey factor, though, and poetry is still doing exceptionally well, driven by writers whose work is often mildly denigrated as “Instapoetry”, such as Lucas Jones. His is a kind of versifying that delivers immediate uplifting aphorisms rather than either the kind of dense, allusive play with language that might reward repeated reading; or the sort of limpid, performable music that propels a well-translated Homeric epic. But even so, the poets of Instagram reach for something that can’t quite be expressed through everyday speech. And readers respond to it.

Sales figures are a rough and insubstantial metric, though. They don’t tell us how someone feels when they read a good poem, what it expands for them, what memories it brings, what connections to other times and places. What shiver of alienation it offers; what moment (often) of puzzlement. Poetry can be baffling; it can refuse to unfurl all of itself to the reader. Better, I think, to sink into the sensations that a poem creates than always to worry at it like a puzzle. By its nature, poetry expresses what can’t be said in prose; it can be resistant, you can snag on it. Poetry is needed in an emergency, when ordinary ways of writing or speaking can’t get at the moment, or the feeling, or the thought.

What poetry is not, however, is peripheral to human life. What I have learned by reporting from Ukraine is that when catastrophe hovers overhead rather than looms from a distance, poetry seems more, rather than less, vital. The most rapt poetry reading I have ever attended was in the frontline city of Kharkiv, the border with Russia only 30km away, when one poet described scratching poems into the wall of her Russian prison cell and audience members silently mouthed the learned-by-heart words of writer Serhii Zhadan’s poems as he performed them.

The foreign correspondent Lindsey Hilsum, who has covered wars and humanitarian crises for decades, has long understood this, which is why I Brought the War with Me, her anthology of work by poets across time and geographies, accompanied by her stories, is such a treasure. The poetry emerging from Gaza, and from Palestinian poets scattered across the world – figures such as the young writer Haia Mohammed, or the Palestinian-American poet Fady Joudah – collectively provides the most arresting document of lives lived amid cataclysm: such poetry is composed with an urgency, vividness and compression that no other art form can quite achieve.

It is true, as the Ukrainian poet Halyna Kruk said in 2022, that “no metaphors work against a man with a machine gun … no poetry can save you from a tank”. It is true, as her fellow Ukrainian writer Kateryna Iakovlenko has put it, that the poetry created most obviously by war is asemic, ugly and inscribed into the very land: “Ruins and abandoned houses, devastated forests, burnt land and roads carved up by tanks and armoured personnel carriers began to resemble letters and unwritten sentences.”

And yet, with remarkable speed, and despite its failure either to deflect bullets, or keep its writers and readers physically safe, poetry quickly began to be written in Ukraine after the full-scale invasion. Poetry was the form that could grapple most effectively with the collapse in meaning brought about by the shock of violence, the feeling that time had ceased to carry significance, the future ripped away. Poems could be written relatively quickly, with limited means, and even in inhospitable places (the shelter, the trench).

The novelist Victoria Amelina, who was later killed by a Russian bomb that targeted the restaurant where she was eating, stopped writing novels (which both take time to write and contain time as an ingredient) and started writing poetry. Some of it denied its own status as poetry, as if it were just the shrapnel-hit remnants of language. One poem, Not Poetry, translated by Uilleam Blacker, contains the lines, “But the reality of war / devours punctuation / plot structure / structure …”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Poems were written at the front. The young writer Artur Dron’, who served in the Ukrainian armed forces for more than three years, did not write about bravado or heroism, but made small, delicate memorials for fellow soldiers who had been killed. Or sometimes he built encapsulations of seemingly insignificant moments.

One of his poems is about a child in some unnamed village near the frontline, who becomes the unofficial mascot of the soldiers posted there. At Christmas, they leave the young boy “a bag with our crushed Snickers bars / and tangerines. / The ones with seeds, / but oh so sweet.” It was a fleeting incident: not newsworthy, not impressive, nothing for the history books – but it was material for a poem. Yaryna Chornohuz told me that her work as a soldier poet was the “documentation of feelings”.

In the midst of a cataclysm, poems survive, often stripped back to their most essential forms, which are surely universal and primordial human forms of expression: the lament for the dead, the lullaby for the child, the curse. In the end, humans need those things: those songs, those poems. They are proof of life. They may not be remembered; but poetry has a better chance at survival than much else that humans do or make. They may become memorials more lasting than bronze.

Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writer

Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War by Charlotte Higgins, is published on 20 August.
