Centrist Democrats dismiss Abdul El-Sayed as a freak radical. Do they want to win in 2028 or not?

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 05:00:35 GMT

Americans want someone on their side in the fight against vested interests – that means politicians like the Michigan primary winner and Zohran Mamdani

Abdul El-Sayed’s win in the Michigan Senate primary was a historic breakthrough. Not only because he is a Muslim son of immigrants who broke with almost every single tenet of establishment Democratic party politics. But because he has wiped that complacent sneer at progressive wins off the faces of centrist gatekeepers. Zohran Mamdani? Relax, he’s just a mayor. And it’s New York City. Outside urban and liberal corridors, there is nothing to worry about. Now El-Sayed has won the Democratic party’s nomination in a swing state that is also on the list of presidential nomination states.

There is a lot to be excited about. Not only within the US, but for observers abroad hopeful for the emergence of a truly revolutionary left that is able to weather powerful and well-funded adversaries and prevail. The money raised to defeat El-Sayed was staggering. He was outspent by more than nine to one. It was the most expensive Democratic congressional primary ever. A roll call of cartoon bad guys, such as Chevron and Philip Morris, funded his opponent, Haley Stevens, to the tune of over $60m. Of that funding, nearly half came from a Super Pac backed by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac).

The symbolism of the win is heavy, that of a politics snapping the chains of corporate power and special interest groups whose agendas run counter to voters’. It suggests two things. One, an electorate waking up to the fact that its democracy is captured. Two, features in the past that would have been disqualifying – lack of experience, lack of establishment endorsement – now render a candidate a “clean skin”. Someone untainted by the sordid game that keeps in play expensive healthcare, cruelty to immigrants and the hoovering of tax dollars out of the country.

Israel took up a large role in the campaign, both on the part of El-Sayed and his opponent. But it’s striking how both were talking about different things. El-Sayed’s detractors stuck to repetitive talking points about “Israel having the right to exist”, a question that is not relevant to the average voter. El-Sayed framed Israel as simply a place that has taken too much of Americans’ money. “The question is quite secondary to whether they have a right to our tax dollars.” It was a clear and salient approach.

What El-Sayed’s win isn’t, yet, is a promise that this success can be replicated not only outside primary contests and against Republicans, but across the board among progressive candidates. The Democratic establishment has been hapless in the face of Donald Trump, and new fiery candidates can appear to have the answers that their party so far has not.

But they are up against huge challenges. First, what the Republican party will throw at them: accusations that, as Trump said, “full of shit” candidates like El-Sayed are radical commies who will bring nothing but “death, squalor, poverty” and “a life of hell”. Then there is what the centrist wing of the Democrats can mobilise against them.

A leading centrist group called Third Way has already raised millions to discredit democratic socialists by investing in social media and mobilising activists against candidates like El-Sayed. “We are preparing for the next war that is coming,” said the group’s leader. Their fear, they say, is that the momentum behind democratic socialists will go all the way to the presidential nomination, and then produce a candidate who would be crushed by Republicans. Because, of course, that has never happened before to a centrist Democratic presidential candidate running against Trump.

Still, the portrayals of progressive candidates as radical can go a long way in a country where people think that Trump is more moderate than Kamala Harris or Hillary Clinton. Fighting on a national level, the left can get away with far less in the political imaginary than the right. That is because the very promise of change that gives progressive candidates the edge in certain contests becomes easily framed as a race into the unknown. This becomes an even more resonant threat as progressive candidates do not have the depth and breadth of a long party record behind them, or the familiarity that comes with ubiquity on the political landscape.

It doesn’t have to be this way. Politicians like Mamdani and El-Sayed are modelling something truly unique. They signify a new US in which the politics of outsiders and their cultural and ideological features is fused powerfully with and against the features of their adopted countries. They have opted not for meek total assimilation for mobility, nor have they recused themselves from contests for a country in which they have claimed a stake.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But they and the rest of the US are carrying too much on their shoulders at a time of domestic and global upheaval. Their movement battles with the stubborn entrenchment of a bankrupt Democratic party establishment, the savage culture wars of the right, and, even though some have thus far prevailed, a gargantuan machine of lobbyists and corporate interest groups.

Progressive voters are not simply found, they are made. And constantly remade into coalitions. If the Democrats would rather lose on their own terms than win on the progressive left’s, then fighting these new candidates will establish the impression that they are freak radicals destined to fizzle out. But these candidates have alighted on what seems like the most viable politics right now. Refuse to embrace them wholeheartedly, and you guarantee that Trumpism wins again and again. Back them all the way to 2028. What, after all, do you have to lose that you haven’t lost already?

Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

‘This is asking a lot of the buttocks’: my 23-hour Wagner marathon on a rock hard seat in a heatwave

The Guardian Mon, 10 Aug 2026 04:00:34 GMT

How does it feel to be locked into a venue notorious for its unpadded seating to experience a full-throttle Ring cycle and more? Our critic found out at the 150th anniversary of the mighty Bayreuth festival

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Liszt and Bruckner were there from the start. Debussy, Mahler and Puccini all subsequently made the journey. So did writers from Virginia Woolf and Thomas Mann to WEB Du Bois, not to mention choreographer Sergei Diaghilev, anarchist Emma Goldman, British fascist Diana Mosley (wife of Oswald) and – most notoriously and fanatically – Adolf Hitler.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Culturally and politically, Germany’s Bayreuth festival doesn’t so much have baggage as its own industrial-scale luggage hangar. But it’s also prized as the ultimate place to hear Richard Wagner’s operas. One hundred and fifty years after the composer launched the festival with the premiere of his epic Ring cycle, tickets for this summer’s edition sold out within 90 minutes. No mean feat for a theatre with famously uncomfortable seats, no air conditioning and only one man’s music on the menu. The shortest work lasts two-and-a-half hours without a break.

So perhaps it was inevitable that I had mixed feelings about my own first trip. Admittedly, I’ve taught generations of students about Wagner and Bayreuth and have been aware of the theatre’s acoustic – revered among opera-lovers – since I was myself an undergraduate. Of course I seized the opportunity to experience it in situ. The brief was to review six operas across seven days: intensive, but not off the scale for a critic covering a festival. Then I did the maths. That’s almost 23 hours of Wagner, not including intervals, in a single week. During a heatwave.

“They lock you in, you know,” a friend tells me when I mention that I’ll be reviewing there this year. “And it’s done with a real theatrical flourish!” I block out a terrifying image of being imprisoned by an opera cult and focus instead on remembering his tip: borrowing a cushion is vital. Wagner and his architects modelled the auditorium on the ancient Greek amphitheatre, after all. The idea was to promote a communal artistic experience through unbroken rows of seats stretching in a wide arc from one side of the theatre to the other. There are no private boxes, no restricted-view tickets and minimal padding. This fantasy of democratic opera-going asks a lot of the buttocks.

That’s no excuse for wriggling, it seems. “You mustn’t move in the auditorium,” warns one Bayreuth old hand when we get chatting at Nuremberg airport. “I got told off once when I uncrossed my legs.” My heart sinks. Sure enough, I witness a set-to about someone twitching their walking stick. Rustling attracts pointed stares and jabbing fingers. But even an audience this committed to self-policing can’t hold the modern world entirely at bay. Every evening features the clatter of phones falling from laps on to the wooden floor. Several text messages arrive with a ping. There are even a couple of incoming calls.

So much for Wagner’s struggle to create the ideal conditions for music drama. But there’s much at Bayreuth that hasn’t changed. The original orchestra pit, for instance, which is exceptionally deep and almost entirely covered, descending in steps beneath the stage. Wagner and his collaborators intended the design to create what they grandly called a “mystic gulf”: a seamless, uncluttered view of the stage that would draw the audience fully into the action.

One happy by-product is Bayreuth’s unique acoustic, which gives the orchestral sound both a luminous sheen and a beguiling sense of perspective as the low brass and percussion filter through the strings sitting metres above them. Less welcome is the pit’s oppressive heat. When I’m ushered in ahead of a performance one afternoon, the musicians already in their seats are wearing T-shirts and shorts. It’s the only feasible concert attire, I’m told. In one of the few modifications made since Wagner’s time, a tiny air-con unit has been fitted. But the contraption looks like spare parts for a vacuum cleaner and apparently helps only the conductor.

It says something about the opera world that such discomfort is considered worth enduring for the sake of Bayreuth’s sound. Another legacy of Wagner’s desire for an ultra-immersive operatic experience has more doubtful value: unlike most major opera houses in the world today, Bayreuth has no surtitles. Your grasp of poetic 19th-century German isn’t what it could be? You struggle to pick out the words from the average Wagnerian’s full-throttle delivery? You’re even – horror of horrors – new to opera? Tough. You’ll have to work out what’s going on from the staging.

Good luck with that this year. The new “AI Ring” involves a set of constantly shifting projections, behind which the singers stand – sometimes invisible and all wearing the same costume. I spot people wisely reading the libretto before curtain-up. “Did you know there wouldn’t be surtitles?” one despairing American visitor asks me during an interval partway through the second opera. He has seen the Ring before but is totally, furiously lost here. “I’m off to Munich tomorrow,” he fumes. “There’s no point staying to see the rest of this.”

Needless to say, I stay put. Bolt upright, in fact, which seems to be the only way to survive the Ring’s almost 15-hour span in these seats (slumping is fatal), at least if you want to reach Götterdämmerung’s apocalypse with any sensation left in your lower body. It helps that I am as swept up as ever in Wagner’s mad, miraculous marathon of a score, which yes, sounds even more spectacular in this acoustic. There are moments when the orchestral sound glows, and others when it rises from the pit – thrilling in its power – to break over us like a slow-motion wave. But I’m left dry-eyed through the drama’s betrayals and its meet-cutes, the hope, the fury, the usually heartbreaking self-sacrifice of its heroine. Not even this lineup of world-class singers can persuade me to invest in their characters when they’re hidden behind an avalanche of visual dross. There’s no storytelling here, just an extended spot-the-past-production game for Wagner nerds.

At a time when many opera companies are trying to make the art form more broadly inviting, Bayreuth’s determination to cater purely to insiders stands out. Particularly given that the town’s other theatre – the exquisitely preserved 18th-century Margravial Opera House, now a Unesco world heritage site – boasts an interactive museum that has “accessibility” written all over it. When I pop in, I find a crowd enthralled by a scale model of the theatre’s machinery that allows visitors to move scenery and create waves, wind and thunder.

Yet no other opera house besides Wagner’s has such a dependably loyal audience or such a restricted repertory – just 10 of his mature operas. (Perhaps that’s just as well: this year’s exceptional anniversary-year production of the composer’s sprawling earlier opera Rienzi – Hitler’s favourite, no less – attempts to recast it as a contemporary political thriller. Let’s just say my review isn’t wholly positive.) But no wonder, given the tiny number of works on the roster, that most Bayreuth productions since the 1950s have involved the flamboyant re-imaginings and conceptual gambits of Regietheater (allowing a director free rein). And no wonder complaining about stagings is a major festival pastime.

“I don’t hate it as much as I thought I would,” one woman ventures of Jay Scheib’s staging of Parsifal. She has come with a group of friends, she explains, after one of them “found a cheap schloss”. Perhaps staying in a castle would’ve improved matters for me, too. I dislike the production far more than I had expected and come dangerously close to needing to leave the theatre to escape the stomach-turning gore-fest – filmed in closeup – that dominates its two-hour first act. Another day, when I pass Wagner’s grave en route to the theatre, I find two men in their 50s comparing stories about the worst Wagner stagings they’ve seen. “What the hell?” explodes one in accented English, outraged by the other’s report of inappropriate animatronics, before returning to German. “What does that have to do with Wagner?”

You could ask the same thing of Bayreuth’s tackier side. Interval drinks are available from “Richard’s Spritz Bar”. A balloon labelled “Wagner Mania” flies over the box office and a lifesize cutout of the composer – smiling, improbably – is available for red-carpet photos. Elsewhere, there are statues, a walking trail of mini-Wagners on plinths and gold figurines in shop windows. It takes me several days of waiting at traffic lights near the theatre to notice that the green man holds a baton and wears the composer’s floppy hat.

Call it theme-parkification, call it kitsch. Either way, such homegrown attempts to cash in on or send up Wagner’s image make for a surreal contrast to the earnest aesthetic debates on and off stage at Bayreuth. But both ultimately betray the same preoccupation with itself that characterises the festival today: the ongoing internal tussle over what it is, who it’s for – and how to come to terms with its deeply troubled past.

The Bayreuth festival continues until 26 August

Star Scholar Resigns as Cambridge Announces Investigation Into His Record

The New York Times August 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Jason Arday was hired by the University of Cambridge in 2023 as the youngest Black professor in its history. Doubt has since been cast on his academic qualifications and claims about his life.

By Neil Vigdor and Jennifer Schuessler

Jason Arday, the University of Cambridge professor at the center of a deepening controversy around his academic qualifications, resigned on Wednesday from the same institution that in 2023 celebrated him as the youngest Black professor in its history.

“I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgement,” Arday wrote in a statement.

His resignation came hours after Cambridge announced an investigation into Arday, and six days before the scheduled release of his memoir “Great and Unfortunate Things,” by the Simon & Schuster imprint 37 Ink, in the United States.

A representative of Simon & Schuster, which has so far stood by the book, told The New York Times on Wednesday that the publisher had no comment beyond the statement about Arday it released last week, citing “the professionalism and integrity he has brought to every stage of the publication.”

Arday, a professor of sociology of education, announced his resignation from Cambridge in a statement posted to the Good Law Project, where a petition in defense of him that has gathered more than 16,000 signatures continues to accrue support. A spokesman for the university confirmed to The Times that Arday’s resignation was legitimate.

Earlier on Wednesday, Cambridge released a statement noting that it had begun an investigation into Arday’s academic qualifications.

“The University of Cambridge has begun an investigation following new information about Professor Arday’s academic qualifications and honorary appointments,” the statement said. “In order to ensure a fair process, we will not comment further until this has concluded.”

When allegations of plagiarism and other scholarly misconduct exploded into public view late last month, Cambridge stuck strongly by Arday, and said it had already referred complaints it received about his early scholarship to Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded him his Ph. D., and to some scholarly journals.

But as new questions arose about his qualifications, along with reports that Arday had apparently filed a harassment claim with the police last year against a British journalist who was investigating his work, the university appeared to change its course.

Arday sent a statement to The Times on Saturday disputing the claims, then canceled a planned interview with The Times on Monday. He did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday about Cambridge’s new investigation or on the claims of harassment.

The imminent publication of “Great and Unfortunate Things” has put a spotlight on Arday’s account of how he, the son of Ghanaian immigrants, overcame autism and other disabilities that left him nonverbal until almost age 12 and unable to read or write until age 18, then earned a Ph. D. and achieved the highest scholarly rank at one of Britain’s most prestigious universities.

Ahead of its publication, reports from other academics, independent journalists and a number of British news outlets have cast doubt on both Arday’s scholarship and biographical assertions, including his claim to have once run 30 marathons in 35 days while raising as much as 5.5 million British pounds for charity and that he was visited twice at his office by a masked intruder, once while wielding a knife.

Arday has said previously that mistakes in his early work were the result of his autism and inadequate supervision from professors, and that the current accusations of plagiarism are part of a racist smear campaign. In his note of resignation, he did not acknowledge any wrongdoing, and reiterated his belief that much of the criticism was unfair.

“While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement,” he wrote. “The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love.”

Questions about Arday’s work had circulated quietly in academic circles at least since 2023, when his appointment to Cambridge at age 37 prompted a spate of news media coverage of him and the extraordinary story he has told about his life.

Those questions became public after detailed allegations of plagiarism and research misconduct were published, first in the newsletter of a scholar known for racist views about intelligence and then on Retraction Watch, an online publication that covers academic misconduct and research ethics. They immediately prompted a pitched debate, with conservative commentators mocking Arday as a “diversity poster boy,” while supporters said he was a victim of racism.

In its initial statement on the controversy, Cambridge said Arday was “the victim of a vile campaign to undermine his credibility, which must stop.” But over the past week, social media users and the news media have continued to surface what they said were additional problems in his published work and on his academic résumé.

Before it was taken down on Wednesday, Arday’s faculty page at Jesus College, Cambridge, where he was a fellow, listed past appointments including visiting professorships in the Office of Diversity and Inclusion at the Ohio State University. But a spokesman for Ohio State said by email that it had no record of employment for a person with Arday’s name.

Arday’s University of Cambridge page said he is a visiting professor at Nelson Mandela University in South Africa. But a spokesman for Nelson Mandela University told The Times by email that while Arday had served as an adjunct professor “on a fixed-term association that concluded in November 2025,” he has no current formal affiliation.

As the charges circulated, so did reports that Arday or others had attempted to quash inquiries into his work by other scholars and a journalist by hiring a top law firm and reporting those asking questions to police.

In a statement on Monday, the publication Times Higher Education acknowledged that it had begun to research Arday and his work last year, but did not go forward with a story “following correspondence with Arday’s solicitors.”

In an article published on Wednesday, shortly after Arday’s resignation, Jack Grove, the reporter who worked on that story for Times Higher Education, described how he had been contacted by a police officer in February who told him not to contact Arday again, since his questions were affecting Arday’s mental health.

Grove said he had sent three “polite” emails to Arday over two months, asking about questions raised by multiple scholars about possible plagiarism or data irregularities in one scholarly paper, discrepancies in his résumé and what he said was a lack of evidence to support his claims about running and charity fund-raising.

Arday, Grove said, never replied. All eventual responses, Grove said, came from Cambridge’s press office. Ultimately, Grove said, he submitted 97 pages of evidence in total to Cambridge and Liverpool John Moores for investigation.

“Serious allegations, certainly,” he wrote. “Deeply embarrassing and distressing, definitely.”

“But were my inquiries grounds for a criminal complaint?” he added. “That was hugely troubling to me as a reporter who specializes in examining issues of research integrity and ethics.”

Neil Vigdor covers breaking news for The Times, with a focus on politics.

Jennifer Schuessler is a reporter for the Culture section of The Times who covers intellectual life and the world of ideas.

Is a packed social calendar the new relationship goals?

Credit... Videos by Mila De La Torre, Ayesha Kazim and Lisa Kimura

Supported by

By Sadiba Hasan

Salsa class after work on Monday. Chess club on Tuesday. Boxing on Wednesday.

That was only the first half of Tylo Laidlaw’s week. So when the conversation turns to dating, the answer is simple: Lately, he’s making more time for hobbies than dates.

After his last relationship ended in 2024, Laidlaw realized he’d become stagnant and robotic. Even though he followed the trajectory of graduating from college, getting a job and saving money, “something was missing,” he said. He wasn’t feeling connected to himself.

Laidlaw, 30, started trying different hobbies. For him, it was about staying curious and putting himself in environments he wouldn’t otherwise be in. And now, he feels more well-rounded. Chess, for example, introduced him to new people and taught him life lessons around strategy and accountability.

“I’m so fulfilled in my life that I know the right person will come,” said Laidlaw, a freelancer in creative direction who lives in London. “But I’m not out searching for it.” Even though he’s a relationship kind of guy — “I want to do the boom box outside the house,” he said, referencing a scene from the 1989 classic film “Say Anything” — he’s finding he’s less concerned with dating because he’s enriched in other ways.

“I’m so good with where I’m at,” he said, that “the energy becomes infectious.”

You could call it “hobbyamory”: Laidlaw is among a growing number of singles emphasizing multiple hobbies over dating. Rather than spending hours swiping and messaging on apps, these singles are investing their time, energy and disposable income in passions like rock climbing, cake decorating and cyanotype printmaking. They say their social calendars are packed, their friend groups are expanding and their lives feel rich, with or without a romantic partner.

Young people are prioritizing their well-being and happiness in a way that other generations have not, said Alexandra Solomon, a clinical psychologist and adjunct professor at Northwestern University. “Lots of people in this generation are asking important questions about this capitalist model of working from nine to five,” Dr. Solomon said. “They’re trying to create lives that have some more flexibility and adaptability and that really value the experiences in life that are beyond just earning money.”

They are also a generation feeling disenfranchised by A. I. and disinclined toward drinking, making wholesome, creative and tactile activities all the more appealing. Online, terms like “hobbymaxxing,” the pursuit of as many hobbies as possible, have taken off. According to TikTok, #hobbies has seen an almost 15 percent increase in posts in the U. S. so far in 2026 compared with last year, and #grandmahobbies has grown by more than 400 percent.

“Side quest,” a term originally used in gaming, has taken on a new life online: It describes the activities and adventures in which people partake outside their routines to add whimsy to their lives. According to TikTok, U. S. posts using the term “side quest” increased over 210 percent this year compared with the same time period last year.

Lisa Kimura, a 31-year-old user experience designer in Brooklyn, has mastered the art of the side quest. Early last year, she learned to D. J., inspired by a flourishing music scene in her Bushwick neighborhood that she felt needed more women.

She also took a genealogy class last year and began building her family tree, then picked up Japanese calligraphy. Her most enduring passion, though, is fiber arts. She knits and dabbles in just about every fiber craft she can get her hands on, she said, including crochet, tapestry weaving, rug tufting, embroidery and cross-stitch.

Kimura moved to New York in 2023, excited for the dating scene. But as an introvert, she found the experience draining. She hasn’t been on a date since last summer.

“I realized that it’s really difficult for me to hear my inner voice when I’m in a relationship,” or sometimes just in the presence of a man, she said. “I grew up in a very traditional, very immigrant household where the patriarchy was alive and well.”

Hobbies have helped Kimura feel more secure and find her voice, partly because many of her hobbies end with a finished product, giving her a feeling of accomplishment. Unlike the women in previous generations in her family, whose lives were centered on marriage and raising children, she feels empowered to pursue the activities that bring her happiness.

“I feel like I can design my future,” she said. As for romantic relationships, Kimura said she’s not closed off to dating indefinitely. “I just don’t feel like I’m in such a rush anymore.”

Natalie Mora, a 21-year-old student in Berlin, said, “I’m the single friend who’s always doing everything.” In addition to scuba diving, indoor cycling, bouldering and boxing, “you’ll catch me skydiving, you’ll catch me traveling anywhere, camel riding, horse riding.”

She continued: “I’m young, I don’t have a husband, I don’t have kids. I’m the happiest I’ve ever been: single.”

According to Amy Chan, a dating coach and author of a book called “Unsingle: How to Date Smarter and Create Love That Lasts”: “People have dating fatigue. They are just so disappointed with the apps that some of them are not dating at all.”

For clients who tend to lose themselves in relationships, Chan advises shifting focus away from finding dates and toward building a rich personal life first. “It’s really, let’s build a full life so that you’re not coming from a place of scarcity and you’re not dating like you’re starving,” she said, adding that establishing independence creates a positive ripple effect when they do return to dating.

“There is a collective course correction around dating apps, which have been the centerpiece of dating in the last 10 years,” added Dr. Solomon, the psychologist, and the solution is investing in real-world experiences.

This isn’t necessarily a bad thing, so long as it is not coming from a place of emotional retreat or avoidance, she said: “Putting yourself out in the world with actual humans and actual art projects or creative endeavors or community endeavors — that’s a really healthy adaptation.” And those endeavors could even lead to new romantic prospects who have common interests.

When a relationship ended five years ago, Laura Geaves, who works in marketing in London, hated being single. Over time, as she saw friends go through different stages in their relationships, she thought, “I have so much freedom. I have all my own money to spend, I can go on whatever holidays I want.”

Once she reframed her perspective, she felt lucky. Now, Geaves, 44, said she is thriving in her solo era.

After finishing work at 5 p. m., instead of spending her evening wallowing in bed, as she had sometimes done, she began lighting candles, putting on a movie and crocheting, water coloring, doing puzzles or making pottery. She began looking forward to her activities after work and realized that relationships are not the goal.

“The goal is actually to enjoy your own company, and the best way to do this is to find a hobby that you absolutely love, and you can lose yourself in and get in that flow state,” Geaves said.

Jenneh Kaikai, the owner of Pelah Kitchen, hosts cake decorating classes in New York that are popular for singles. “So many folks join for solo dates and things to do as an alternative to dating apps,” she said. “I think right now, there’s kind of a boom in people wanting to do those sorts of activities — something that’s creative, tactile and also not focused on drinking.”

For Michael Fasulo, who lives in Cambridge, England, and works in marketing, that has included paddle boarding, open water swimming and baking. He took on these activities in January after splitting with a long-term partner. He has two teenage children who have become more independent and developed their own social circles. Those two factors combined left Fasulo, 42, to do a lot of soul searching.

It started with baby steps, he said: “I’m just trying to do things to get my spark back, to lift my mood, to give me something to do.”

“I think where I maybe have gone wrong in the past is I’ve kind of defined happiness by a successful relationship,” Fasulo said. His definition has since changed, though.

“The more confident, the more fulfilled, the more I expand my social network,” he said, “the better partner I will be in the future and the more likely I am to find the right partner as well.”

A lot of the singles I interviewed for this article said stepping outside their comfort zones to pursue new hobbies brought them a deep sense of fulfillment. Once they took the pressure off dating and finding the perfect relationship, they were able to reconnect with themselves.

Sadiba Hasan reports on love and culture for the Styles section of The Times.

A group of homeowners had sued the city, arguing that the introduction of the tax was mishandled. After the judge issued an order pausing the rollout, the city said it would appeal.

By Mihir Zaveri and Mark Bonamo

The fight over a contentious tax on the second homes of wealthy New Yorkers intensified on Monday when a judge ordered a pause on its rollout, and the administration of Mayor Zohran Mamdani vowed to appeal within hours.

The judge, Wayne M. Ozzi of State Supreme Court on Staten Island, issued a temporary restraining order after a group of homeowners sued the city last week, arguing that the rollout was being mishandled.

The tax, proposed by Gov. Kathy Hochul and backed by Mr. Mamdani, was lauded by supporters as delivering on the mayor’s promise to “tax the rich.” It was supposed to generate some $500 million annually for the city, which faces a budget gap. While the judge on Monday was not asked to rule on the legality of the tax itself, his order threw a wrench into those plans, at least for now.

Matthew Rauschenbach, a spokesman for City Hall, said the city was “confident in both the pied-à-terre surcharge and the city’s ability to implement it fairly and effectively.”

He said the city’s Law Department would appeal the ruling immediately, a step that he said would stay the order.

A spokeswoman for Ms. Hochul, Jen Goodman, said the “lawsuit about the administration of the tax is a matter for the city and the courts to work through.” But she added that Ms. Hochul believes “that people who can afford a multimillion-dollar second home in New York City can afford to pay their fair share.”

The homeowners had argued that New York City officials should have worked harder to determine, using existing records, who might have to pay the tax before publishing a data set on the Department of Finance’s website listing homes that “may be subject to the charge.”

That data set contained nearly one million properties. Justice Ozzi’s order requires the city to remove it from the website for now.

The lawsuit also criticized a decision to send letters to the owners of roughly 17,000 properties informing them that they might be taxed. Homeowners were directed to file paperwork with the city by mid-September if they believed they should be exempt from the tax.

In the courtroom on Monday afternoon, the judge, a Democrat, said that the city had created conditions that met the standard of irreparable harm.

“Sending out notices to 17,000 homeowners who might be subject to a surcharge doesn’t satisfy the intent of the legislation,” he said.

“Notices should state what the records show. They are a treasure trove of information,” he added. “I can’t unring the bell, but I can stop any further notices going out.”

The judge’s order will remain in place until at least Aug. 31, when both sides are expected back in court.

Randy Mastro, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs and a longtime critic of Mr. Mamdani, said in a statement that Justice Ozzi’s decision “vindicated the rights of hundreds of thousands of New York City homeowners who were subjected to a process they never should have been a part of in the first place.”

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Mihir Zaveri covers housing in the New York City region for The Times.

Colombia Quake Chases Teenage Venezuelan Brothers From Their New Home

The New York Times August 10, 2026

Earthquakes in Venezuela

Advertisement

Supported by

A pair of brothers who lost their mother and other family members in Venezuela and were profiled by The New York Times have now survived deadly quakes in two countries.

By Julie Turkewitz

Reporting from Bogotá, Colombia

Once again the ground shook. Once again buildings fell. Once again they wondered where they would be safe.

Winder and Deivi Delfín, ages 15 and 17, survived the back-to-back quakes in Venezuela in June that killed thousands, including their mother, younger brother and grandmother. Last month, their 26-day search for the bodies of their loved ones was the focus of a New York Times article. Then the boys moved to Cali, Colombia, where their father lives and works as a barber.

On Monday, when a 7.4-magnitude quake hit not far from Cali, they found themselves once again at the center of a disaster. At 7:34 a. m. their home began to shake. They ran out in a panic, said their father, Deivid Delfín, 44, who was out of the house at the time. He ran, too — toward home.

At first, he could not find the boys. When he finally did, he said, “I started crying and everything, because I was scared of what I had experienced and what my boys had experienced. I don’t want anything to happen to my children.”

Weeks before, Mr. Delfín had said he hoped to give his sons a fresh start, far from disaster. Venezuela and Colombia are neighbors, and the countries have often shared tragedies. For years, victims of Colombia’s internal conflict fled to Venezuela, and then Venezuelan migrants seeking to escape an authoritarian government fled to Colombia.

“Right now we’re outside the house, just sitting here,” Mr. Delfín said on Monday afternoon. They were too scared to go inside, he added. “But we’re OK. We’re here, alive.”

Julie Turkewitz is the Andes Bureau Chief for The Times, based in Bogotá, Colombia, covering Colombia, Venezuela, Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru.

Takeaways From Jason Arday’s Memoir

The New York Times August 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The British scholar resigned from Cambridge after the university, which made him its youngest Black professor in 2023, began investigating his academic qualifications.

By Neil Vigdor

It’s the book release that the academic world can’t stop obsessing over: “Great and Unfortunate Things,” a memoir by Jason Arday, the British scholar who stepped down from his professorship at Cambridge amid accusations that he had plagiarized other scholars and embellished his personal accomplishments.

In his resignation letter, Arday did not acknowledge any wrongdoing, and said, “The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love.”

“Great and Unfortunate Things,” which goes on sale tomorrow, takes Arday from childhood up to his appointment at Cambridge. Here are some takeaways from it.

By his own account, Arday, the son of Ghanaian immigrants who was raised in public housing in southwest London, spent most of his childhood and adolescence struggling with autism and other disabilities that he said left him nonverbal until almost age 12.

“But miraculously, just a few days shy of my 12th birthday, I spoke,” Arday writes, recalling an exchange with his speech therapist. “It was at the start of one of my sessions, and Katrina had just said, ‘Hello, Jason.’ At that moment, I was fiddling with my hearing aid, which was bothering me, and then I took it out of my ear and said hello back to her.”

Not until he turned 18, Arday laments in his memoir, could he read or write.

When he decided to go to college, his girlfriend “wrote out the entire application for me — including my personal statement.” At St. Mary’s University in London, he scored just 9 percent on his first exam. He worked hard, raising his grades so quickly that a professor at the school accused him of cheating.

“When you succeed against pretty much insurmountable odds, it weirdly makes people question your credibility,” he writes.

College and graduate school were slogs. Arday writes that because he had dyslexia, “sometimes it could take me as much as an hour to read and absorb a single page of academic text.”

At one point in graduate school, he realized that his 3-year-old daughter’s reading skills were not that far behind his. She scolded him at story time: “Daddy, you’re not reading all the words.”

According to Arday, at one point he was beaten so brutally by four boys at a bus stop that he developed epilepsy. His attackers were arrested, and when he gave a victim impact statement, Arday writes, he told the court that they should be spared jail time.

Several years later, two of them showed up in one of his classes. “After the case was closed, we weren’t allowed to contact you,” Arday says they told him. “But we really wanted to say thank you for your forgiveness, so maybe it’s fate that we’re getting to meet you now.”

“Both of them gave me a huge hug, which I returned,” Arday writes, adding, “The two men remained in my class for the rest of that semester, proving themselves to be brilliant and diligent students.” Arday says “they often asked me to write job and character references for them, and I would happily oblige,” adding that “one of them … asked me to be the godfather to his child, and I gratefully accepted.”

In 2015, Arday writes, a doctor found a small tumor pressing on the pituitary gland near the base of his brain. It was removed less than five weeks before he was scheduled to conduct the oral defense of his Ph. D. thesis.

During his recovery, Arday collapsed and “was taken to the hospital, where the doctors told me I’d had a transient ischemic attack (TIA) — a ‘mini-stroke,’” he writes, “and now I was dealing with a new problem: I couldn’t access my short-term memory. When I’d try to recall something I’d read or written, I’d draw a blank.”

“I’d worked on my thesis for over 30 months, and now I was reading it as if for the first time,” he continues.

Arday was unprepared, he said, for the “immediate hostility” he encountered at his thesis defense. But after a rough start, he rallied.

“Congratulations, Dr. Arday,” one of the professors told him when it was over. “You have passed with minor amendments.”

One of the parts of Arday’s personal story that has received the most scrutiny involves his claim that he completed 30 marathons in 35 days in 2010 to raise money for charity.

Two-thirds of the way through the challenge, he writes in the book, he had a seizure during a race and collapsed, resulting in a hairline fracture to the fibula in his right leg. Against doctors’ advice, he continued running.

“The next nine marathons were truly an ordeal,” he writes. “It took me well over five hours to complete each one. Even though I used painkillers, I was in agony throughout. My right leg ballooned to twice its size. To this day, I don’t really know how I did it.”

In his last marathon, Arday says, he was buoyed by hundreds of supporters in the final stretch. “Just like the famous scene in ‘Rocky II,’ where Rocky sprints away from the pack and up the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, I forced myself to speed up to a sprint and break away from the rest of the runners. I’ll never forget the crescendo of cheers as I turned the corner towards Piccadilly Circus, like I was being carried along by a wave of sound.”

In the book, Arday’s trials are numerous. His brain tumor returns. He and his wife decide to split. During Covid, he suffers from autistic burnout, is barely able to get out of bed and thinks about ending his life.

But in April 2022, Arday writes, a prestigious university in London reached out to him about a job. “I’d often been head-hunted in academia, both domestically and abroad, but this was my first time being sought out by an elite British institution.”

Shortly after that, he learned about a position at the University of Cambridge. He dithered about applying for it but finally did, even though he was wracked with uncertainty: “What if I have completely overestimated my capabilities? What if my story ends up being a cautionary tale like Icarus about flying too close to the sun?”

Neil Vigdor covers breaking news for The Times, with a focus on politics.

Trump Wants to Move On From the Middle East. It’s Not Letting Him.

The New York Times August 10, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

President Trump is eager to declare success in Iran and Gaza, but he is struggling to impose his will in either conflict.

By Anton Troianovski

Reporting from Washington

President Trump may want to let go of the Middle East. But it won’t let go of him.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump said his new strategy was to be “low-keying it” in Iran, a suggestion that he wants to pressure the country into making a favorable deal without taking major military action. But a stark reminder of the limits of U. S. power in the region came from Israel, where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared Sunday he was “ruling out” Mr. Trump’s peace plan for Gaza.

The two Middle East conflicts have underscored Mr. Trump’s eagerness to declare success and his inability to impose his will on them, despite the enormous military firepower that he has been able to deploy.

Mr. Trump is “clearly trying to find a pathway as the midterms approach to downgrade all of this,” said Brian Katulis, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, a Washington think tank. Instead, Mr. Katulis went on, “reality is slapping him in the face.”

Mr. Trump faces depleted weapons stockpiles, an Iranian regime determined to impose pain on the United States, an Israeli prime minister battling for re-election and American voters reeling from high prices induced by the Iran war. The November midterms keep ticking closer, steadily raising the political costs of the turmoil to Mr. Trump and Republicans.

Mr. Trump laid out his low-key approach to Iran in a brief interview with the news website Axios on Sunday. Rather than make new military threats, he said that “we are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money.” He added: “It will work out. It always works out. It’s like a chess game.”

“Now, can they make trouble? Yeah, they can make trouble,” Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office Monday, acknowledging Iran’s ability to keep harassing commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. “But they’re broke.”

In describing the Iranian regime as suffering from economic pressure, Mr. Trump evoked his own predicament. The average price of a gallon of gasoline remained above $4 this week, more than $1 above the price when the United States and Israel began bombing Iran on Feb. 28. Polls show even Republicans growing disenchanted with the Iran war and Mr. Trump’s political movement has fractured over his decision to launch military action.

“I don’t think the president has very good options,” said Suzanne Maloney, an Iran specialist and vice president at the Brookings Institution in Washington. “The pressure points for the Iranians are, while real, more endurable and bearable than those that are impacting the U. S. economy and the strategic calculus of the administration.”

In Gaza, Mr. Trump trumpeted a “historic breakthrough” on July 30, a multiphase deal under which the militant group Hamas would eventually disarm and Israel withdraw from the Palestinian enclave. Writing on his Truth Social website, in all capitals, he hailed an “amazing development” that “everybody said could never be achieved.”

But in the days after Mr. Trump announced the plan, Gaza saw an increase in deadly Israeli bombings. On Sunday, Mr. Netanyahu, who earlier this year went into the Iran war alongside Mr. Trump, emphatically rejected Mr. Trump’s plan: “I want to be clear here — Israel is ruling out the 15-point document.”

The Gaza episode was, to some analysts, another reminder of diminished American influence in the Middle East in the wake of the Iran war, which has dragged into its sixth month with none of Mr. Trump’s expansive goals appearing close to being accomplished. Many Israelis have seen Mr. Trump’s pursuit of a peace deal with Iran as a betrayal, giving Mr. Netanyahu a political incentive to be seen as standing up for Mr. Trump as he seeks re-election in October.

In both Iran and Israel, Mr. Katulis said, Mr. Trump has “misread the regional power dynamics.” Mr. Katulis also pointed to the new defense pact between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan as a sign of countries looking to hedge their bets amid uncertainty over the future of American power in the Middle East.

In Iran, for all of Mr. Trump’s efforts at finding a way out, a renewed flare-up of violence could come at any moment. The U. S. military has kept up its naval blockade of shipping to Iranian ports and said Saturday it had redirected 53 commercial vessels in recent weeks, along with disabling two ships and boarding two others. Mr. Trump’s enormous buildup of U. S. military force in the region, including two aircraft carrier groups, has remained in place.

“These tools are not low-key,” said Behnam Ben Taleblu, an expert on Iran at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank that is hawkish on Iran, referring to the U. S. sanctions and blockade. “Iran is likely not going to take them lying down.”

The United Arab Emirates on Saturday said an Iranian attack had targeted a tanker belonging to one of its state-owned oil companies as it crossed the Strait of Hormuz, the major artery for oil shipments out of the Persian Gulf. The Houthis, an Iranian-backed militia in Yemen, have threatened to block Saudi oil shipments through the Red Sea.

A senior Iranian official said on Saturday that Iran would reopen the strait only if the United States met a sweeping list of demands, including lifting sanctions and the blockade. The official, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, also demanded war reparations, prompting Mr. Trump to post on Truth Social on Monday that “I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran.”

Iran’s compensation, he said, would need to cover people killed and wounded in Iran’s “many conflicts” as well as Iranian protesters killed by the regime. He said he had instructed officials to seek that compensation in “any, and all, future negotiations.”

Iran and the United States are not known to be negotiating directly, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week that Iran and neighboring Oman were holding talks with U. S. input. Online, some of the loudest supporters of Mr. Trump’s initial decision to bomb Iran continued on Monday to push for new attacks.

“For those here and elsewhere living in a fantasyland, there will need to be further military action,” the Fox News host Mark Levin wrote on X. “Economic pressure alone won’t cut it.”

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting from Washington.

Anton Troianovski writes about American foreign policy and national security for The Times from Washington. He was previously a foreign correspondent based in Moscow and Berlin.

Homeland Security Intensifies Pursuit of Noncitizens on Voter Rolls

The New York Times August 10, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Immigrants who said they inadvertently registered to vote while obtaining or renewing driver’s licenses are increasingly facing deportation under the Trump administration.

By Madeleine NgoNick Corasaniti and Hamed Aleaziz

The Trump administration is making an intense push to identify and deport noncitizens who registered to vote, even if they did so inadvertently or never cast ballots — an unusually aggressive approach that is helping it promote baseless claims that voter fraud is rampant.

State audits and studies have repeatedly found that noncitizen voting is extremely rare, and there have been no instances in which their votes are known to have swayed an election. It is against federal law for noncitizens to register to vote or actually vote, and doing so can carry steep penalties, including jail time and deportation.

In the past, the Department of Homeland Security has not aggressively tried to deport the relatively small number of noncitizens who unlawfully registered to vote, especially if they mistakenly signed up, according to immigration policy experts. But the Trump administration is taking a harder line in hopes of increasing deportations while also building a case that illegal voting has been underestimated.

Homeland security agents are reopening voter fraud cases that had been closed and investigating voter registration efforts in major cities. Customs officers have detained immigrants suspected of being on the voter rolls at border checkpoints, according to immigration attorneys. And green card holders applying for citizenship have been placed in deportation proceedings for registering to vote.

The department’s efforts are part of the Trump administration’s extraordinary attempt to leverage federal agencies to promote the president’s long-running false claims about a broken election system rife with fraud. Those claims have been used by Mr. Trump to justify his push for federal legislation that would require that people show proof of U. S. citizenship to register to vote and severely restrict voting by mail.

The changes are upending the lives of some green card holders who have lived in the United States for years and maintain that they did not vote or even intend to register.

Abdullah Emre Basar first learned that he was on the voter rolls in Washington State when he applied for citizenship and an immigration officer at his interview last year informed him that he was registered, according to a court filing last month.

Mr. Basar later learned that he was registered in 2014 after visiting the local motor vehicle agency to update his address, said Devin Theriot-Orr, his attorney. The government denied him citizenship and placed him in removal proceedings in April, according to the filing.

Mr. Basar maintains that he never voted or asked to register. Ryan Dosch, a manager at the Spokane County elections office, said in an email that a voter registration record under Mr. Basar’s name was canceled and had no history of a ballot cast.

“It brings a lot of worry and uncertainty,” Mr. Basar said in a statement. “It is putting stress on my marriage, as my wife is a citizen and the unknown is very stressful.”

The administration’s actions have involved a close partnership between the Homeland Security Department and the Justice Department, which has sought to investigate and criminally charge noncitizens with illegal voting. Prosecutors have been instructed to file more charges against those individuals, and the Justice Department has sued dozens of states to obtain voter rolls. The department has also seized on revelations by New Jersey officials that a software glitch led to about 6,600 noncitizens being registered to vote between June 2023 and June 2024. Roughly 400 of them later cast ballots.

Harmeet Dhillon, who runs the Justice Department’s civil rights division, has said officials are ready to arrest or deport those who improperly voted in New Jersey. Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, indicated she would resist the Trump administration’s demands to turn over the names of the registrants, who she said ended up on the voter rolls “through no fault of their own.”

Homeland security officials are devoting significant resources to the effort, ordering agents who typically focus on transnational crimes like human trafficking and drug enforcement to hunt for voter fraud, a major shift for an arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement known as Homeland Security Investigations.

In June, agents with the unit accompanied F. B. I. agents during a raid of the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a group that conducts voter registration drives, and actively questioned staff members.

“Conducting voter fraud investigations is a real departure for H. S. I., and is not within the normal scope of their very important criminal investigative work,” said Deborah Fleischaker, a senior ICE official during the Biden administration.

In a statement, a homeland security spokesperson said that ICE was rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it could be found.

The Trump administration has also prodded states to upload tens of millions of voter records through SAVE, a federal immigration verification tool run by the Homeland Security Department that the administration revamped to look for noncitizens on the voter rolls.

But there have been problems with the SAVE tool itself. In October, Jane Nelson, the Texas secretary of state at the time, announced that her office had identified 2,724 potential noncitizens who were registered to vote in Texas. But local election officials who looked into the findings at the county level found that many identified by SAVE were actually citizens. An independent investigation in Travis County, Texas, home to Austin, found that 25 percent of the noncitizen matches were citizens, according to court records.

Homeland security officials have continued to push evidence-free claims of widespread election fraud. Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, said last month that the administration uncovered more than 250,000 cases of noncitizens registered to vote in four states, but provided no evidence to support the finding or details about how officials arrived at that number.

Letters from the Homeland Security Department to some states indicated that the number was probably overestimated, with caveats and based on initial reviews. Some state officials, including in Nevada, have cast doubt on the methods the department used to calculate the estimate.

The intense focus on deporting noncitizens on the voter rolls marks a shift for the Homeland Security Department. Several immigration attorneys said they had clients who were still approved for citizenship under previous administrations if they explained that they mistakenly registered and had no other issues with their cases.

Michael Valverde, who was a senior official at U. S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for more than two decades, said that immigration officers used to have some ability to take into account factors like intent, age and mental capacity in considering whether registering to vote or voting rendered them removable.

“Now officers have very limited discretion, and I am hearing that denials and removal proceedings based on voting are happening more frequently,” Mr. Valverde said.

Attorneys said many of their clients who registered did so inadvertently while obtaining or renewing driver’s licenses, pointing to voter laws that have made it easier for people to register to vote at motor vehicle agencies. Some immigrants lack English fluency and do not realize they are signing registration forms, lawyers said.

Altagracia White, a 61-year-old resident of Woodbury, N. J. who is married to a U. S. citizen, said the federal government was seeking to deport her. Ms. White said she first learned that she was registered to vote after she applied for citizenship and an immigration officer informed her. Ms. White later obtained documents from the state showing that she signed a voter registration application while renewing her driver’s license more than a decade ago.

“I never thought they were telling me to sign to vote or anything like that,” Ms. White said. “At that time, I didn’t even know how to say yes in English.”

The federal government has initiated her deportation to the Dominican Republic, citing her voter registration and claiming she voted in 2020. County records show that Ms. White voted once via mail-in ballot that year. Ms. White denied that she sent the ballot or ever voted.

George Fishman, a deputy general counsel at the Homeland Security Department during the first Trump administration, praised the agency’s efforts to pursue noncitizen voting. Although he said there was a “certain level of unfairness” when it came to noncitizens who inadvertently registered to vote, he thought it was Congress’s responsibility to pass reforms that would prevent them from getting onto voter rolls.

“I think the most vigorous enforcement should be against those who knew they were voting illegally, but the law needs to be enforced,” said Mr. Fishman, a senior legal fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies, an organization that supports lower immigration rates.

Coral Murphy Marcos contributed reporting.

Madeleine Ngo covers immigration and economic policy for The Times.

Nick Corasaniti is a Times reporter covering national politics, with a focus on voting and elections.

How a Counterintelligence Inquiry Into Trump’s Russia Ties Was Derailed

Documents released by the White House shed new light on the demise of an often-overlooked 2017 F. B. I. investigation.

By Michael S. Schmidt

For the last year, the Trump administration’s efforts to seek retribution against intelligence officials and F. B. I. agents who investigated Russia’s 2016 election meddling have been spearheaded by federal prosecutors in South Florida trying to build a criminal case.

But in recent weeks, the White House has added a dimension to its push to rewrite the history of the Russia investigation, releasing a trove of previously classified F. B. I. memos that it says back up President Trump’s claims that a so-called deep state was out to get him.

There is little new of substance in the documents, and nothing that fundamentally undercuts the F. B. I.’s rationale for pursuing the Russia investigation.

But the material does shed new light on an often overlooked aspect of the swirl of events surrounding Mr. Trump in his first months in office in 2017: the bureau’s remarkable decision to open a separate counterintelligence investigation into the president of the United States, and how that inquiry was sidetracked before it had much of a chance to get going.

Mr. Trump has always dismissed as baseless smears suggestions that he was a Russian asset or had extensive financial ties to Russia. And no publicly known investigation into Mr. Trump ever demonstrated that he was acting at the behest of the Russians.

Here is a look at what we know now, based on the new documents and interviews with former federal law enforcement officials, about what happened.

Although the scrutiny of Mr. Trump at the time became known as the Russia investigation, there were actually several distinct inquiries.

During the 2016 presidential campaign, the F. B. I. opened an investigation into whether the Trump campaign was working with the Russian government as the country interfered in the presidential election to hurt Hillary Clinton. That investigation — known as Crossfire Hurricane — was not looking directly at Mr. Trump’s personal conduct or his ties to Russia.

But in May 2017, a week after Mr. Trump fired James B. Comey, the F. B. I. director, senior officials and counterintelligence agents at the bureau decided to move forward with a two-pronged inquiry. It was oddly code-named Oxferd Comma.

One of the investigations was to be criminal. It was to examine whether Mr. Trump, in firing Mr. Comey, broke the law by obstructing justice and interfering with the F. B. I.’s investigation into Russia’s election meddling. It was also to assess whether the Trump campaign conspired with the Russians.

The second was to be a counterintelligence investigation into Mr. Trump’s ties to Russia.

Counterintelligence investigations are different from criminal inquiries. Instead of focusing exclusively on whether the law was broken, counterintelligence investigations look at whether a foreign adversary is undermining the United States.

Counterintelligence investigations are classified, take place in secret and unfold over many years — sometimes more than a decade. Civil liberties watchdogs are critical of them because they often surface embarrassing, but not criminal, behavior by Americans. People are rarely charged in such cases, but the F. B. I. often takes steps, like warning officials and citizens, about how those around them may be trying to influence them.

Referring to the counterintelligence inquiry, one of the declassified memos made public by the White House last week said: “The goal of the investigation is to determine if President Trump is or was directed by, controlled by, and/or coordinated activities with, the Russian Federation in a manner constituting a threat to the national security of the United States and/or a violation of federal criminal statutes.”

According to the memos released by the White House, the F. B. I. had concluded that the Russian government interfered in the 2016 election to help Mr. Trump. The bureau had learned that Russians had offered to help the campaign. And the F. B. I. knew that the Trump campaign had pushed the Republican Party to embrace a far more Russia-favorable position on Ukraine as part of its 2016 platform.

The F. B. I. also knew that Mr. Trump, before firing Mr. Comey, had been pressuring him to end the investigation into ties between his campaign and Russia.

And the F. B. I. was concerned about Mr. Trump’s personal and business history, the memos show.

“Open-source information indicates that President Trump has had a longstanding business and real estate ties to Russia and the former Soviet states, stemming from the 1980s,” the F. B. I. said in the memo opening the investigation. “In 2008, President Trump’s son claimed that Russians made up a ‘disproportionate cross-section’ of many of President Trump’s assets. Open-source information also indicates that President Trump has had business ties in the United States and Russia with named Russian oligarchs.”

Whether that public information justified opening a counterintelligence investigation is at the heart of the long-running dispute between Mr. Trump’s allies and F. B. I. officials who made the decision. Mr. Trump has always asserted that his personal, business and financial links to Russia were minimal.

But F. B. I. agents wanted to conduct a wide-ranging investigation into whether Mr. Trump, in firing Mr. Comey, was trying to stop the Russia investigation and shield any ties he might have had to that country.

“The obstruction itself would hurt our ability to figure out what the Russians had done, and that is what would be the threat to national security,” the F. B. I.’s general counsel, James Baker, testified to Congress at the time.

On the day the Oxferd Comma investigation was opened, the acting F. B. I. director, Andrew G. McCabe, briefed the deputy attorney general, Rod J. Rosenstein, on the bureau’s decision.

The following day, Mr. Rosenstein undertook his own extraordinary decision: He appointed the former F. B. I. director, Robert S. Mueller III, to be a special counsel to investigate Mr. Trump and his campaign.

But what was not known at the time was that Mr. Rosenstein, in appointing Mr. Mueller, had in effect killed the counterintelligence investigation.

When Mr. Rosenstein appointed Mr. Mueller, he authorized the special counsel to conduct criminal investigations into Russia’s meddling in the election and ties between Mr. Trump’s campaign and Russia, and into whether Mr. Trump tried to obstruct that investigation.

But Mr. Rosenstein did not ask Mr. Mueller to conduct the counterintelligence investigation into Mr. Trump, and made clear to Mr. Mueller that he did not want him conducting an open-ended, yearslong investigation. Mr. Mueller interpreted his appointment as one to just investigate crimes.

Although Mr. Rosenstein did not authorize Mr. Mueller to conduct the counterintelligence investigation, responsibility for overseeing it was transferred to the F. B. I. agents working on Mr. Mueller’s team, according to the memos released by the White House.

But since the special counsel’s mandate was to focus on crimes, the counterintelligence focus fell by the wayside and was “limited to activities within the scope of the special counsel’s jurisdiction,” according to one of the memos.

When Mr. Mueller’s report was released in 2019, it said that the investigation had found no evidence that Mr. Trump and his campaign had conspired with the Russians during the 2016 election. But Mr. Mueller declined to make a determination about whether Mr. Trump obstructed justice. The report did not contain a section on Mr. Trump’s personal ties to Russia and whether he was compromised or represented a counterintelligence threat.

Shortly after the report was released, Mr. Mueller testified about it before Congress, acknowledging under questioning that he had not examined whether, for example, Russian oligarchs had laundered money through Mr. Trump’s businesses.

Mr. Mueller, in response to another question that day, acknowledged that he had only looked at crimes, and appeared to leave open the possibility that some counterintelligence investigation could still be underway.

Mr. Mueller delivered that testimony on July 24, 2019. The memos released last week by the White House showed that the counterintelligence investigation had been closed more than three months earlier.

Michael S. Schmidt is an investigative reporter for The Times covering Washington. His work focuses on tracking and explaining high-profile federal investigations.

As Waymo deploys more driverless cars to 15 U. S. cities and counting, its vehicles keep encountering new and unexpected situations that they have no script to handle.

Waymo driverless cars are in San Francisco and 14 other metropolitan areas, including Denver, Las Vegas, San Diego and Tampa. Credit... Jason Henry for The New York Times

Supported by

By Emmy Martin

Reporting from San Francisco

On July 4, more than 100,000 people packed San Francisco’s waterfront for a foggy fireworks show over the Golden Gate Bridge.

When they tried to go home, Waymo got in the way.

With crowds milling around, Waymo’s driverless cars blocked intersections and choked traffic. Some drivers were stuck behind the electric robo-taxis for more than three hours. Several Waymos had to be towed after their batteries died in the gridlock. At least two drove over exploding fireworks, with one catching fire.

Rose Peterson was inside the other. She and her fiancée had ordered a Waymo to return to their hotel. When the car stopped at an intersection, a man ran into the road, set a firework on the street and lit it. The Waymo drove forward, rolling over the firework as it exploded beneath the car.

“We were just in absolute shock,” said Ms. Peterson, 30, who works in insurance in Walnut Creek, Calif. The car smelled like it was on fire, she said, but the Waymo kept going until it stalled at another intersection. She and her fiancée then got out and walked the rest of the way to their hotel, turning what was supposed to be a five-minute drive into an hourlong journey.

What Ms. Peterson experienced is what the driverless car industry calls an “edge case,” which are the unscripted situations that no one trained the robo-taxis to handle. The problem is that edge cases appear to be piling up as Waymo, the leading autonomous car service, rapidly expands.

Owned by Google’s parent Alphabet, Waymo has more than quintupled the number of autonomous cars it has on the road to nearly 4,000 today, up from about 700 early last year. Its vehicles are now in 15 metro areas, having gone fully driverless in Denver, Las Vegas, San Diego and Tampa in the past month alone. Each week, passengers pay for about half a million trips.

Amid that growth, Waymo has issued three federal recalls since December for software problems — including one where the cars drove into flooded roadways — compared with three recalls in the previous 22 months. Some edge cases have drawn headlines, including a December power outage in San Francisco that left nearly 1,600 Waymos frozen for at least two minutes.

More cars in more cities means more chances to meet something the technology has never seen. That’s hard to fix because the cars often do not recognize they are in trouble and so do not request help, said Philip Koopman, a Carnegie Mellon University emeritus professor who specializes in autonomous vehicles.

“This technology struggles to know when it’s in a novel situation,” Dr. Koopman said. “And when it’s in a novel situation, it’s prone to overconfidence and spectacularly stupid failure.” Waymo’s answer has not been to solve the underlying problems, he said, but to hand control of the car to a remote human operator.

Sandy Karp, a Waymo spokeswoman, said the recent recalls were proactive moves and the rate of edge cases was decreasing as the company expands, adding “the ones that do occur inform ongoing improvements.”

The pace of driverless car rollouts has quickened, acknowledged Franklin Trujillo, who leads Waymo’s team that orchestrates expansion into new cities. The company can move faster into cities because the software it developed in one place increasingly works for the next one without having to be retrained for each locale, he said.

Waymo’s goal is for its technology to handle edge cases “regardless if we’ve seen them before,” Mr. Trujillo said. He pointed to the company’s safety record that showed 94 percent fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers, adding, “we’re constantly learning, constantly improving our product.”

For now, Waymo’s incidents have put the company in the cross hairs of officials and regulators.

Bilal Mahmood, a member of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors who walked an hour to get home after the July 4 fireworks, demanded last month that the city’s emergency management, fire and transportation departments explain what went wrong at the event. Mayor Daniel Lurie also wrote to California’s transportation secretary asking the state to set operational standards for driverless cars during major events and emergencies, saying “regulating for typical conditions is no longer enough.”

On July 28, Mr. Lurie backed federal legislation that would require driverless car companies to staff a hotline for emergency responders and direct regulators to write a minimum standard for how emergency medical workers can move a robo-taxi.

Jonathan Morrison, the administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, also wrote in a July 8 letter that the agency had identified “a clear pattern” of autonomous vehicles interfering with police, firefighters and paramedics. “Emergency scenes are not rare or extreme ‘edge cases,’” he wrote.

Mr. Morrison has summoned driverless car companies to meetings to present fixes. His agency has started developing federal safety standards for driverless cars. Sean Rushton, a NHTSA spokesman, said the agency had already met with several driverless car developers.

Waymo’s failures were foreseeable, said Matthew Raifman, who leads research on policy and autonomous vehicles at the University of California, Berkeley. Tens of thousands of people converging at a marathon or a festival is just another normal weekend in a big city, he said.

“Some of the things that we’re calling edge cases are edge cases for autonomous vehicles, but not necessarily edge cases for transportation,” he said.

Elliot Slade, 31, a San Francisco resident, was recently involved in such a case. He and his fiancée were riding in a Waymo back to the city from an event in nearby San Mateo, Calif., in May when the car entered a construction zone that had closed the right lane of the highway.

The car began driving like a “frightened animal,” Mr. Slade said, swerving through traffic cones and accelerating to highway speed in the closed lane. It then wove past a truck and workers as California Highway Patrol officers hit their sirens and shouted, “Stop, Waymo!”

“We were freaking out,” Mr. Slade said, adding that he placed his arm across his fiancée’s chest “just in case we crashed.” He said he pressed a button in the car to call for support but no one answered until the vehicle exited the highway on its own. The couple got out of the Waymo and then took an Uber the rest of the way home.

Weeks later, Waymo recalled the software on some cars for entering freeway construction zones and pulled its vehicles off highways while creating a fix. The company resumed freeway routes late last month in Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix and the San Francisco Bay Area.

For San Francisco’s July 4 fireworks, Waymo had appeared prepared. The company sent an employee to the city’s Emergency Operations Center that evening and agreed to restrict where riders could hail its cars. Waymo also had a team that could take manual control of stuck vehicles, said Dean Crispen, San Francisco’s fire chief.

Yet more than two hours before the 9:30 p. m. fireworks show began, reports of stalled Waymos reached the center. Several of those cars ran out of battery power, but tow trucks were unable to reach them because of the traffic. The Waymos were not cleared for two hours, according to a letter from San Francisco’s emergency management department.

Waymo’s Ms. Karp said the July 4 traffic snafus “were caused by a number of factors” and that Waymos “contributed to congestion” in the Presidio neighborhood of San Francisco, adding that the company’s roadside assistance team worked with local authorities to clear the vehicles.

Waymo’s next major test in San Francisco is in October, when the U. S. Navy’s Blue Angels take over the sky for the annual Fleet Week air show, which is expected to again draw crowds to the waterfront.

Stephen Sherrill, a member of the city’s Board of Supervisors, has called for a Sept. 3 hearing to better coordinate city agencies to preemptively address potential Waymo failures.

“Waymo is terrible at addressing traffic congestion under abnormal driving conditions during these large scale events,” he said in a statement.

Waymo’s Ms. Karp said the company “will be in close contact and coordination” with city officials about Fleet Week.

Emmy Martin is a reporter covering the technology industry from San Francisco and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship class.
