Colombia’s New President Has Been Immediately Put to the Test

The New York Times August 10, 2026

Colombia Earthquake

Advertisement

Supported by

Abelardo De La Espriella had never held public office until his inauguration on Friday. Now, he is at the helm of a major disaster response.

By Annie Correal

Annie Correal has been covering Colombia’s new president.

Colombia’s newest president was sworn in Friday. On Monday, disaster hit.

The president, Abelardo De La Espriella, is a former criminal defense lawyer with no previous political experience. He rose to power on promises to crack down on criminals and on his country’s resurgent armed groups, and was endorsed by President Trump.

Running as an outsider, he also vowed to shrink the government and tackle a huge budget deficit following four years of what many called runaway spending under Gustavo Petro, Colombia’s first leftist president.

Before taking office, Mr. De La Espriella announced he would govern from Colombia’s Caribbean Coast, near where he was raised, and pledged to travel the country tending to Colombians’ needs, instead of remaining ensconced in the capital.

Now, days into his term, Mr. De La Espriella is facing his first big test.

In a brief video posted on social media on Monday morning that appeared to be shot from the presidential plane, he said he had canceled his travel plans and was headed to Bogotá, where he would “personally” lead the disaster response.

Addressing people in the worst-hit areas — around the epicenter in the Chocó region, and in the coffee-growing region known as Eje Cafetero, or Coffee Axis — he said, “You’re not alone.”

A few hours later, he posted more footage, this time from a conference room where he sat surrounded by scores of people, apparently coordinating the disaster response. Dramatic music played over the video.

The earthquake hit less than two months after twin earthquakes devastated Venezuela.

The epicenter of Colombia’s magnitude 7.4 earthquake was in Chocó, a rural region along Colombia’s Pacific Coast that is home to a large Afro-Colombian population and Indigenous communities. Isolated by geography and a lack of passable roads, some coastal communities have long been accessible only by water.

Towns and small cities in the neighboring coffee-growing region, Valle del Cauca, also suffered severe damage, officials said.

Colombia has for decades been mired in conflict that cut off some areas from the government and left armed groups as the de facto authority. Though Colombia’s largest rebel group, the FARC, signed a landmark peace accord a decade ago, the conflict has resumed in recent years.

Armed groups have multiplied and expanded into more of the country, fueled by soaring demand for cocaine and a boom in illegal gold and mineral mining.

As the groups battle for control of drug trade routes and mines, they have brought renewed violence, killing community leaders and forcing hundreds of thousands of civilians to flee.

Chocó, where the earthquake struck near the village of San José del Palmar, has in recent years become a flashpoint for clashes between two of Colombia’s most powerful armed groups: the National Liberation Army, or ELN, a decades-old rebel army with leftist roots, and the Clan del Golfo, or Gulf Clan, which has right-wing paramilitary ties.

The previous president, Mr. Petro, engaged armed groups in peace negotiations that largely failed.

Mr. De La Espriella pledged while campaigning that he would target Colombia’s armed groups with U. S. help. He made clear during his inauguration speech that the option of negotiations with the groups had been “completely exhausted.”

With Mr. De La Espriella in office, the Trump Administration has been seeking to fast-track military cooperation with Colombia as part of its regionwide effort to go after cartels; on Friday, the State Department announced that it would offer Colombia $1 billion in assistance as part of a “new era in U. S.-Colombia relations.”

Experts say Mr. De La Espriella’s iron-fisted message could result in an uptick in attacks by armed groups. Over the weekend, videos circulated online that appeared to show members of the ELN. In one, a fighter can be heard directing himself to Mr. De La Espriella, who adopted the campaign nickname El Tigre, or The Tiger, and saying, “Let’s see who roars louder.”

Earthquake responders could be moving into areas controlled by those same armed groups.

Mr. De La Espriella already faced the challenge of governing a sharply divided country. He won June’s election by less than one percentage point, narrowly defeating Senator Iván Cepeda, a member of the left-wing party Mr. Petro founded and leads, Pacto Histórico.

Mr. Cepeda and his fellow party members in Congress boycotted the inauguration, and Mr. Cepeda has called on his followers to engage in peaceful civil disobedience, pointing to Mr. De La Espriella’s alleged ties to paramilitary figures and to his U. S. citizenship, which he says stands to undermine Colombia’s sovereignty.

A Times investigation found that Mr. De La Espriella — who lived in Miami for more than a decade and whose clients included accused drug traffickers facing extradition — was investigated by U. S. authorities in connection with the movement of funds by a client accused in a major money-laundering scheme linked to the Venezuelan government, Alex Saab.

On Monday, when Mr. De La Espriella posted from the emergency command center in Bogotá, he added a caption.

“Colombia is united and we will move forward together,” it read.

Annie Correal is a Latin America correspondent for The Times.

Italian Diver Discovers ‘Treasure at the Bottom of the Sea’ in Sicily

The New York Times August 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Hundreds of ancient amphorae were found piled up about 150 feet underwater, suggesting the relics came from a Roman shipwreck from about 2,000 years ago.

By Ephrat Livni

An Italian diver and spearfishing champion on a routine foray in the waters off Sicily recently happened upon the remains of an ancient shipwreck, which Italy’s Ministry of Culture has said is “one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years.”

The diver, Giacomo de Mola, was exploring about three miles off the coast of Mazara del Vallo in southwestern Sicily with an assistant when sonar revealed an underwater structure that he initially thought was a rock. Visibility was low, but he pushed on, coming upon what he called in a video on social media “the most incredible discovery of my life.”

“My heart stopped,” Mr. de Mola said, describing what he saw. A close look revealed a pile of hundreds of ancient amphorae — clay vessels with handles that had been used by ancient Greeks, Romans and Phoenicians to store and transport goods.

The mound of artifacts, many apparently still intact, covered an area of about 6 feet by nearly 70 feet, Mr. de Mola said, and presented “a treasure at the bottom of the sea.” Mr. de Mola reached out to an expert, who connected him with the authorities in Sicily who soon visited the site themselves and confirmed that this was indeed a historically significant find.

The newly discovered underwater archaeological site most likely dates back to a shipwreck about 2,000 years ago during the Roman era between the second and first centuries B. C., said Alessandro Giuli, Italy’s minister of culture, in a statement on Saturday.

He said that the initial find had been made by unnamed private citizens, referring to Mr. de Mola, and was later confirmed by various law enforcement teams in Sicily specializing in cultural heritage.

Mr. Giuli said that the Italian authorities would continue to document and study the site of the shipwreck to reconstruct “the archaeological context” and to ensure the necessary protective measures are taken to preserve the illuminating find. Discovered along with the hundreds of amphorae were two lead anchor stocks, or parts of ancient anchors.

Amphorae were used in ancient Mediterranean cultures to store and transport goods like olives, oil, wine, honey, grains and other items. The vessels were usually curved with a long narrow neck and two handles, but their shape varied somewhat depending on use.

Those used for storage typically had a flat bottom, giving the ceramic containers stability and enabling them to stand up. Vessels that were used for transport, however, commonly tapered into narrow pointed bottoms, making them easier to pack on ships without taking up a lot of space.

Most of the amphorae discovered at the new site in Sicilian waters were of the variety with narrow, pointed bottoms, according to Mr. Giuli and based on video from the area released by Mr. de Mola, as well as video shared by the Italian authorities.

“The sea continues to yield precious fragments of our history,” Mr. Giuli said, noting that the find “speaks to us of the people, trade routes and exchanges that turned the Mediterranean into a crossroads of civilizations.”

Ephrat Livni is a Times reporter covering news around the world. She is based in New York.

Shortly after 7:30 on Monday morning, the most powerful earthquake to hit Colombia in a decade sent people fleeing for safety as buildings teetered and then fell.

The epicenter was in a less populous rural area off the Pacific Coast, potentially blunting its effect, but even so, by midafternoon, Colombian officials were reporting that at least 111 people had been confirmed dead.

I Went to Iowa to See the Young Democrat Packing Town Halls. It Felt a Bit Like Obama in 2008.

The New York Times August 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Ben Rhodes

Mr. Rhodes is a contributing opinion writer. He spent several days in Iowa and went to town halls in Fort Dodge, Boone and Newton for this essay.

Iowa has a cancer problem: The state has the fastest growing rate of new cases in the nation. On the margins of a high school gymnasium, I talked to a young man whose father died of leukemia that he attributes to herbicides or pesticides. On local radio, a woman described spending thousands of dollars on a home system to filter nitrates from her drinking water.

Rob Sand, the state auditor, is running for governor with a slogan “Costs, Corruption and Cancer,” and I followed him to several town halls recently. In 2007, I’d spent months idealistically canvassing the state for Barack Obama’s caucus campaign. Now, well into middle age and the Trump era, I still recognized the neighborliness of the people and postcard Americana of the venues. But in addition to the sweltering heat, there was a heaviness in the political air. Young people are moving away. Crops are being replanted on account of tariffs. More Iowans are getting sick.

At each venue, Mr. Sand lamented a government in Des Moines that is so cozy with agribusiness that it gave polluters immunity from penalties. He never said the name Donald Trump. Instead, he talked up his plan to clean Iowa’s water supply while connecting with voters hungering for community. At one stop, he walked into the middle of an audience of hundreds and asked folks to turn their folding chairs to face him in one giant circle.

Just shy of 44 with boyish good looks, Mr. Sand is very much a moderate, but he has a withering critique of the political establishment in this country. He expresses disdain for a system dominated by “two private clubs.” He blames Republicans and Democrats equally for rewarding special interests and making voters “hate the people they love.” And he is unusually specific on how to change a system rigged for politicians and special interests. He supports nonpartisan primaries and approval voting; age and term limits for politicians alongside cognitive and civics tests; a ban on stock trading for public officials, and prison time for the ones who steal from taxpayers.

From North Carolina to Alaska, effective red-state Democrats, such as Roy Cooper or Mary Peltola, often talk down partisanship while emphasizing problem solving (Ms. Peltola’s message is even a similarly alliterative: “Fish, Family, Freedom”). What sets Mr. Sand apart is his youth, discipline (he’s currently on a “100 Town Hall tour”) and relentless determination to connect his critique of the party system to local outcomes. For now, that seems to be working. Mr. Sand holds a narrow lead in a state that hasn’t had a Democratic governor since 2011. His approach could offer a blueprint for how to break the Republican grip on red states.

It helps that Mr. Sand has a near perfect résumé. He turned down Harvard to attend law school at the University of Iowa, served as the state’s chief public corruption prosecutor and has spent two terms as auditor burnishing his reputation as a crusader against waste. An avid bowhunter and churchgoer — his one misstep may have been a brief stint as a men’s wear model in Milan — he speaks with a self-assuredness that could tip into arrogance if he wasn’t assiduously polite. While not the most dynamic speaker, he holds the attention of his crowds through a blend of unabashed earnestness, folksy religiosity (“Jesus was on the side of the little guy”) and common sense; because he’s comfortable in his own skin, his audiences are put at ease.

Those audiences — like the state — are largely old and white. It was easy to see Mr. Sand through their eyes as an ideal son or grandson. He begins his town halls by asking for a show of hands — who is a Republican, an Independent, or a Democrat — with a round of applause for each faction. Then, he asks the audience to sing the first verse of “America the Beautiful.” Gimmicky? Yes. Corny? Definitely. But as the awkwardness subsides, a few hundred voices build into something resembling harmony, and a soft patriotism envelops the room.

Mr. Sand has proposed making town halls mandatory for public officials. “I think that they would be less corrupt,” he told me, “and they would do fewer things that are obviously bad for their constituents, if they knew they were going to have to look their constituents in the eye and defend their own actions.”

The cynic in me worried that he was ignoring the harsh realities of American politics, including the selfishness and immorality of people who choose their own incentives and ignore disincentives; it was in Iowa, after all, where Mr. Trump said he could shoot someone on Fifth Avenue and get away with it.

But cynicism entraps you in the status quo, and I left Iowa believing that Mr. Sand’s message holds an important lesson for Democrats: For all the fights between left and center, the candidates gaining traction are often younger and in touch with the attitudes and concerns of their own communities. America is a big and complicated country. In New York, a socialist like Zohran Mamdani wins by exposing the corruption that drives up rent and prices at a halal cart; in Iowa, a moderate like Rob Sand is focused on getting carcinogens out of the water. What they and other rising Democrats share is a determination to overhaul a broken system so that power solves the people’s problems instead of perpetuating them.

For all our obsession with national politics and policies, the path out of corrupt, one-party government starts at the local level. That’s where you can take advantage of a party that has become lazy in power, build organizing muscle and test approaches that can be repurposed for other states or scaled up nationally.

Iowa is ripe for that kind of effort. After a decade of one-party rule, the state is struggling not just with cancer but also rising health care costs and anemic economic growth. The agricultural sector has been battered by Mr. Trump’s tariffs and a war with Iran that is driving up the price of diesel fuel and fertilizer. Meanwhile, Republicans in Des Moines have followed the national party, demonizing Democrats over immigration, deregulating industry and banning abortion.

Mr. Sand’s agenda focuses on what they’ve ignored. At every stop, he details his plan to clean up the water supply. He wants to reverse the privatization of Medicaid to bring down the cost of health care and reform a wasteful school voucher program. He supports investments in tele-health and remote work for state employees so it’s easier to stay in rural communities. He wants to ban social media for children under 16.

Most of those issues have a nexus to corruption. Lawmakers turn a blind eye as agribusiness pollutes the water and enable the health care industry to pad profits while rural clinics are shuttered. The tech sector has spread plenty of money around to avoid regulation of social media and artificial intelligence.

The Republican nominee is a political operative and entrepreneur named Zach Lahn who edged out a Trump-endorsed opponent in the primary by framing himself as a reformer. Now, he casts Mr. Sand as a closet radical and holier-than-thou hypocrite. When I asked Mr. Sand how he would overcome Republican attacks, he shrugged. “I go everywhere and talk to everybody,” he said. He also likes to remind voters that Mr. Lahn didn’t switch his voter registration to Iowa from Kansas until 2024 (just in time to run for governor).

Mr. Sand also makes a virtue of the fact that if he wins, he will almost certainly be governing with a Republican legislature. Unusually for a politician, he refused to suggest he’d fight for things that won’t have a chance of passing. Instead, he told voters that he simply wouldn’t be able to do something, whether it was restoring reproductive health care or collective bargaining rights. It all feeds into his broader critique of politicians. “I wish they just would have been upfront to begin with,” he told me. “I oftentimes feel like I’m burying the weight of decades of people just expecting lies from politicians.”

In the middle of one town hall, Mr. Sand’s vision of a nonpartisan future was clouded by the present. A retired school nurse recalled paying for her students’ supplies because of budget cuts. Then, her voice broke: “We got to get back to being a state where we help everybody. And I don’t care if they’re an immigrant. I don’t care what color they are.”

After leading the crowd in a round of applause for her public service, Mr. Sand praised Bob Ray, a Republican governor who welcomed refugees to Iowa in the 1970s while expressing support for people who “want to work and follow the rules.” Then, he quickly pivoted from the fraught terrain of migration and race to focus on costs and corruption, criticizing the current government for raising taxes to pay for the profits of private health insurers and wasteful spending on school vouchers. “If you’re being told to be scared of your neighbors,” he concluded, “it’s so that your pocket can be picked.”

While very much on message, something about the exchange felt unsatisfying. Mr. Sand’s questioner was speaking to issues of morality and identity that cast a dark shadow over American politics. Tactically, I understood the impulse to set those issues aside in favor of a conversation about how politics should work; to level with people about what you can and cannot change. But if he manages to win, I’m not sure that changing the incentives and disincentives for politicians, which Mr. Sand focuses on, would be enough to change the vagaries of politics today.

Perhaps mindful of these doubts, Mr. Sand ends each of his town halls with an appeal to values. How is it, he asks, voice lowered and grave, that we have reached this “abyss”? Once again, the antagonist is not Mr. Trump or big business or the cruelty raised by that former school nurse: it is a broken political system where politicians want to turn a state “red or blue.” By contrast, he describes sending his kids to school urging behavior that is missing from politics today. Respect your teachers. Be kind. Listen to everyone.

It was a message I recognized from my time as a speechwriter for Mr. Obama when he campaigned in Iowa. There are no red states or blue states. Special interests have too much power in Washington. A different kind of politics was possible, particularly with a young outsider.

But Republicans never came to the table. By the end of Mr. Obama’s eight years in office, they had fallen in line behind Mr. Trump, and now many Iowa voters — and legislators — consume a steady diet of right-wing media that is pugilistic by design.

Can Mr. Sand’s anti-partisan localism overcome those forces? He connected his own disgust with the system to that of rank-and-file MAGA legislators. “A lot of the people who I get along with best are some of the people who are most ‘Trumpy’ in the legislature,” he told me. “They look at the way the system works, especially after they’ve been there for a little bit, and they’re like: This isn’t what democracy is supposed to be about.”

While I don’t agree with Mr. Sand’s equal apportionment of blame between right and left for the sorry state of our politics, his pox-on-both-parties message may offer Republicans a permission structure to try something new. An earnest, moderate white man at the state level may also be more capable of reaching across the aisle than a Democratic president. And perhaps the wreckage of the Trump era will pull enough voters — and even some politicians — out of the “abyss.” After all, Iowans tried it one way for a decade and got rising cancer rates, rising costs and more young people leaving home to find opportunity.

Rob Sand offers an Iowa flavor of a recipe that has been coming into focus since the Democratic Party imploded in 2024. Instead of nominating candidates who look or sound like the establishment, get behind people running against it and appeal to Trump voters who were drawn to populism. Instead of debating a national platform, get in touch with voters at the local level. Embrace generational change.

Along the way, Democrats must also confront the immorality that brought that school nurse to tears — insisting that everyone be treated with dignity and remaking a system to solve problems instead of just blaming others for them. That’s the only way to become a country where power serves people instead of the other way around.

Ben Rhodes is a contributing opinion writer and the author, most recently, of “All We Say.”

A Nighttime New York Boat Tour Turned Deadly in a Matter of Moments

The New York Times August 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Investigators are focusing on the tour operator and the pilot of the boat that capsized in New York Bay on Saturday, killing a mother and her infant daughter.

By Miles G. Cohen and Christopher Maag

Paula Rivera stood on a dock on Randall’s Island on Saturday evening, excited for her party to begin. It was her 41st birthday. Her husband, Alexander Reyes, had chartered a boat and invited 11 of their friends. They planned to board the boat, stop at a restaurant for dinner, then sail into New York Bay for some late-night sightseeing.

Before the tour began, one of the party guests, Andrés García, used FaceTime to chat with his mother, who lives in Bogotá, Colombia. Mr. Garcia sat with his wife, Sara Sanchez, 27, and their 5-month old daughter, Antonella. They smiled as they told Mr. García’s mother that they soon would board a boat to celebrate a friend’s birthday.

But the boat did not appear. Someone in the party called Zeus Luxury Rental, the boat’s operator. The passengers were told to leave the dock and walk down the shore to a rocky area. There they found a 22-foot boat called City on the Sea, waiting just offshore.

Mr. Reyes had been told the boat could accommodate 13 people plus the captain, he said. Yet the little craft had seating capacity for no more than 10, the Police Department would later say.

The group stepped over a rocky bank and climbed aboard.

What happened next is now part of a federal investigation about how the City on the Sea ended up capsizing, resulting in the deaths of Ms. Sanchez and Antonella.

After the unusual boarding, at around 7:10 p. m., the tour proceeded as planned. The first stop was a restaurant, where the captain took his passengers for dinner. Then they boarded again, sailed down the East River and into Upper New York Bay. As the group approached the Statue of Liberty, Mr. Reyes’s daughter, Sarah Reyes, smiled and took pictures.

It was 10:20 p. m., and a moderate breeze blew from the west at about 16 miles an hour, according to the National Data Buoy Center. The little boat, loaded with 13 passengers and a captain, bobbed in the chop.

The captain turned the wheel, piloting the boat back toward New York City. The bow dipped below the water, sending water over the deck, said Ms. Reyes, 20, one of the passengers.

Then the boat flipped.

Simon Ducroquet/The New York Times

For a moment, everyone was trapped beneath the capsized boat. A dozen people reached the surface, gasped for air, then climbed onto the hull.

Ms. Sanchez and her baby were not among them.

Ms. Rivera called 911 on her phone. The group waited 10 or 15 minutes for the first boat to arrive, she said. That boat rescued 11 people and was operated by Sea the City, a tour and jet ski rental company, said Adam Schwartz, the company’s owner.

The surviving passengers and captain were brought onboard. Minutes later, a helicopter rescue unit arrived at the scene with police divers. Two Coast Guard boats, two boats from the Police Department and four Fire Department boats also joined the rescue effort.

Ms. Sanchez and Antonella were rescued by police divers and taken to nearby hospitals, where they were pronounced dead.

“We are destroyed,” Cristian Martinez, the infant’s uncle, said from his home in Colombia.

Mr. Garcia manages the breakfast service at Il Punto Ristorante in Hell’s Kitchen, said Antonio Russo, the general manager. He is taking time off work since the accident, Mr. Russo said.

Saturday’s deadly incident echoed a similar summertime boating accident in July 2022, when a 27-foot boat capsized in the Hudson River near Midtown Manhattan, leaving two people dead including a 7-year-old boy. Saturday’s tragedy shocked family members and neighbors of the dead, and focused investigators’ attention on Zeus Luxury Rental. Manuel Hernandez, 46, who was the boat’s captain, was arrested and charged with 13 counts of reckless endangerment, the police said.

Coast Guard investigators are looking into whether the tour was an illegal charter operation, according to a news release. The Coast Guard works to “ensure the safety of everyone on our waterways,” and enforces the law if boat operators are found to be navigating illegally, said Captain Doreen McCarthy, head of the Coast Guard’s New York sector.

Representatives for Zeus Luxury Rental did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Before the outing, Mr. Reyes said he asked a representative of Zeus Luxury Rental by phone how many passengers could fit. The boat could take 12 people, he recalled the person saying. He asked if a baby could also come on board. The representative said yes, according to Mr. Reyes.

Chelsia Rose Marcius, Hurubie Meko and Davaughnia Wilson contributed reporting. Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Christopher Maag is a reporter covering the New York City region for The Times.

Netanyahu Walks ‘Political Tightrope’ on Trump’s Gaza Disarmament Deal

The New York Times August 10, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel is trying to satisfy the sometimes competing demands of his right-wing base and President Trump months ahead of a tough election.

By Adam Rasgon and Aaron Boxerman

Reporting from Tel Aviv

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is months away from his first national elections since the Hamas-led attack on Israel, faces an increasingly difficult challenge: how to placate President Trump, his most important ally, without alienating voters in his right-wing base.

That challenge was on full display after Mr. Trump announced last month that his Board of Peace had reached an agreement to disarm Hamas. The deal was quickly met by Israeli skepticism. Then on Sunday, Mr. Netanyahu openly rejected Mr. Trump’s plan in a rare public break with the American president.

The dispute shows how Mr. Netanyahu, who faces one of the biggest political fights of his career to win re-election in October, is being pulled in opposite directions at home and abroad.

Mr. Trump’s plan calls on Mr. Netanyahu to deliver concessions, such as pulling back Israeli troops in Gaza, which would be unpalatable to hawkish members of his constituency. At the same time, political pressure is intensifying on the prime minister as he lags behind in public opinion polls in the run-up to the election.

“He’s walking on a political tightrope,” said Shira Efron, chair of Israel policy at the RAND Corporation, a research group. “On the one hand, he needs to cater to his base and coalition, which he has promised ‘total victory’ over Hamas. On the other hand, he doesn’t want to upset President Trump.”

Mr. Netanyahu attempted a similar balancing act after the United States and Iran signed a cease-fire deal in June, despite Israeli objections to the agreement. At the time, Mr. Netanyahu heeded Mr. Trump’s demand that Israel abide by the truce, while trying to mitigate domestic blowback. It is unclear whether Mr. Trump or Mr. Netanyahu’s base will hold more sway as the Israeli prime minister debates how to move forward in Gaza.

More than ten months after a cease-fire agreement between Israel and Hamas that was brokered by the Trump administration last year, many Gazans are living in tents and rubble, as Israel has barred full-scale reconstruction there as long as Hamas refuses to disarm. Over 1,250 people have been killed in Israeli strikes in that period, according to the Gaza health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

The Israeli leader appears to have made some limited concessions, like holding back on near-daily Israeli airstrikes in the enclave. In the days after Mr. Trump announced the Hamas deal, the Israeli military continued its strikes in Gaza, killing at least 20 people and damaging warehouses full of medical supplies, according to Palestinian officials.

.

On Aug. 2, Mohammed Dahlan, an influential Palestinian exile and a confidant of the president of the United Arab Emirates, wrote on social media that Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, had told him he was “working with the Israeli side to stop the attacks on Gaza.”

The next day, Mr. Netanyahu met with senior officials from the Board of Peace, including Nickolay Mladenov, a veteran Bulgarian diplomat who is the organization’s high representative for Gaza.

Following the pressure, Mr. Netanyahu agreed to order the military to halt its strikes, according to three people briefed on the conversation, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details.

The last Israeli strike on Gaza was last Monday evening, said Mahmoud Basal, an official in Gaza’s civil defense, an emergency response service under the Hamas-run interior ministry. That was the same night when the Board of Peace officials met with Mr. Netanyahu. It was unclear how long the respite in attacks on the enclave would last.

“I think what we’re seeing is Netanyahu flexing his muscles internally, while taking baby steps toward accommodating some of the administration’s demands,” said Nimrod Novik, a former senior Israeli official and now a fellow at the Israel Policy Forum, a New York-based research group.

But as part of the agreement with Hamas, Mr. Netanyahu would have to make further moves with a higher political cost. He has already rejected any retreat of Israeli forces in Gaza before Hamas fully disarms.

Many Israelis are skeptical that Mr. Trump’s Board of Peace can actually disarm Hamas and destroy its tunnels and weapons depots.

“That strikes me and the vast majority of Israelis as an extraordinarily optimistic assumption about Hamas’s cooperation,” said Eli Groner, a former director general of the prime minister’s office.

The deal also stipulates that Israel first uphold its part of the truce agreed last year to halt airstrikes, pull back its forces within Gaza and allow more aid into the devastated Palestinian enclave.

The timing of Mr. Trump’s deal is especially difficult for Mr. Netanyahu’s re-election campaign, given that his opponents have surged ahead in public opinion polls.

Most surveys project that Mr. Netanyahu and his allies would win between 51 and 53 out of 120 seats in the Israeli parliament — below the 61 typically required to form a government. A new political party founded by a former Israeli military chief of staff regularly polls higher than Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud, long the largest single party in the country.

Israelis will head to the polls in late October in the first national vote since the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, the deadliest day in Israeli history. About 1,200 people were killed and some 250 taken hostage in the assault, prompting the devastating Israeli war in Gaza.

Many Israelis hold Mr. Netanyahu responsible for the disaster. Even the prime minister’s supporters concede that despite his promises to decimate Hamas after the attack, the Palestinian armed group still controls parts of the Gaza Strip.

Mr. Trump’s deal with Hamas stops well short of Mr. Netanyahu’s pledge to exact its full surrender. The deal makes no mention of exiling top military commanders and offers pathways for some members of the Hamas-run government to remain employed in the public sector.

Scenes of Israeli troops withdrawing from Gaza could further undermine Mr. Netanyahu’s argument to right-wing voters that he won the war against Hamas.

“This isn’t the kind of victory he was marketing all throughout the war,” said Mr. Novik.

Negotiators from the Board of Peace spent months revising the text during rounds of talks with Hamas leaders. Clauses that explicitly stated that Hamas would not possess any weapons were dropped from later drafts, according to two officials familiar with the negotiations, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

The finished agreement commits Hamas to “decommission and store” its heavy weapons in a process led by a new group of U. S.-backed Palestinian technocrats. But some critical details are still to be negotiated, including the timeline for when Hamas would hand over its weapons and how Israel would withdraw from Gaza.

“Various elements of the plan still have to be worked out,” said Ms. Efron. “And even elements that have already principally been worked out need to be implemented.”

Natan Odenheimer contributed reporting.

Adam Rasgon is a reporter for The Times in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.

One Source of Paxton’s Wealth: A Cell Tower at a Hospital He Knew Well

The New York Times August 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, makes six-figure income from a cellphone tower on the grounds of a hospital where he was a board member.

By Lauren McGaughy

Reporting from Austin and Frisco, Texas.

Over the course of Ken Paxton’s decade-long rise to prominence, through scandal and turmoil, questions about his finances have followed him. Opponents scrutinized his real estate holdings and suggested that he has used his public office to enrich himself personally — allegations that have never been proven.

With Mr. Paxton locked in a close, contentious race for U. S. Senate in Texas, his Democratic opponent has questioned how Mr. Paxton, the state attorney general, has amassed a multimillion dollar real estate portfolio on a public servant’s salary.

Now, Mr. Paxton’s federal financial disclosure forms and additional records obtained by The New York Times shed light on one unusual source of his income: a cellular tower company from which Mr. Paxton made between $100,000 and $1 million about every 18 months.

The company controls at least one tower in a city north of Dallas that was erected around 20 years ago on the property of a hospital where Mr. Paxton was a board member.

Mr. Paxton co-founded the company, Premier Vertical Properties, in 2005; he reported serving on the board of the hospital, Centennial Medical Center, from 2003 to 2013. Records show that Premier signed a deal to lease space on the tower to T-Mobile in 2006; the hospital’s parent company at the time, Tenet Hospitals, was mentioned in the lease agreements.

The terms of any agreement that may have been struck between Mr. Paxton’s company and the hospital are not clear. Tenet did not respond to questions, and the hospital’s current administration said it could not provide information about a deal made before its tenure.

Industry experts said a hospital’s board would need to review and approve a decision to lease land to a cell tower company such as Premier. It is not clear whether Mr. Paxton, as a board member, voted on any contract between the hospital and his company, or whether he had participated in any such discussions.

In a statement provided to The Times, Nick Maddux, Mr. Paxton’s campaign spokesman, did not address questions about Premier’s dealings with the hospital during Mr. Paxton’s time on the board.

“This week, every major publication in Texas covered the overflow crowds at Attorney General Paxton’s Protect the Texas Promise tour, and the Times spent that same week combing through twenty-year-old lease paperwork on a cell tower that Ken Paxton has disclosed publicly for many years,” Mr. Maddux said in the statement. “That is not journalism; it’s a search for a story that does not exist.”

Industry experts expressed surprise that a cell tower in a prime spot — near a highway and a hospital in a busy area — would be snapped up by a cell tower company like Mr. Paxton’s, which had been created only the year before, and not by a larger, more established firm.

“It’s basically like the guy that steps to bat and hits a home run off one swing,” said Hugh Odom, who runs a cell tower consulting firm that exclusively represents landowners.

Mr. Paxton formed Premier Vertical Properties with Richard Sine in 2005, state business records show. The company listed Mr. Paxton’s then-private practice law office in McKinney as the company’s address.

Less than a year later, Premier signed a 10-year agreement with T-Mobile for the wireless network operator to lease space on a cell tower the company controlled in Frisco, according to property records filed in Collin County. The hospital property, owned by Tenet Hospitals at the time, is listed as the location for the cell tower in the T-Mobile agreement, as well as for agreements with Verizon and DISH Wireless that were signed later, after Mr. Paxton left the hospital’s board.

Mr. Sine’s signature is on all three lease agreements. While Mr. Paxton’s is not, the site name on the T-Mobile paperwork is called “Paxton MP.”

Mr. Sine, who has a background in the telecommunications industry, did not respond to multiple inquiries about Premier.

Cell tower companies typically make money by renting property from a landowner, erecting a tower and then leasing space on the tower to mobile network providers. The less the tower company pays to lease the land and the more it gets from the providers, the bigger its profits.

It’s unclear if Premier Vertical Properties operates just this one tower. The company is not listed in a federal tower database that mostly includes towers over 200 feet or in potential aircraft pathways.

Mr. Paxton did not disclose the site of this or any other tower on his state or federal financial forms. The Times located the Frisco tower in county deed records.

Mr. Paxton first disclosed his interest in Premier Vertical Properties on his state ethics form filed in 2006. That year, he reported that the company had assets of less than $5,000. This year, his state ethics form showed that the company had assets of “at least $55,610 or more,” but did not mention the company’s profits.

Last year, Mr. Paxton filed detailed federal candidacy paperwork as part of his Senate run. In these documents, he reported income between $100,001 and $1 million from a cell tower affiliated with Premier Vertical Properties. The cell tower’s value was listed as between $250,001 and $500,000.

Mr. Paxton makes $153,750 as the attorney general of Texas.

Margaret Dylus-Yukins, senior legal counsel in ethics with the Campaign Legal Center, a watchdog group, said it is difficult to ascertain Mr. Paxton’s total wealth from his federal disclosure because the value of some of his investments is shielded in a trust. But she said the cell tower appears to be an important asset.

“It does look like Mr. Paxton’s investment in the Premier Vertical Properties is one of his top sources of income,” she said.

Industry experts said the value of the cell tower is likely even higher. If income was at the low end of the range, around $100,000, the value of the tower should be closer to $2 million, said Ken Schmidt, a cell tower expert.

“The asset valuation seems odd to me,” he said. “There’s a disconnect.”

Mr. Paxton’s assets and investments have come under repeated scrutiny during his decade as the state’s top lawyer. He has been the subject of a bribery investigation over a $100,000 gift he took from a man with business before his agency, and a grand jury investigated his role in a land deal in McKinney. In 2015, months after he assumed statewide office, he was charged with felony securities fraud when he was accused of failing to disclose that he was making commission for recommending a friend’s business.

Those cases were all closed or settled without Mr. Paxton admitting fault or being convicted of a crime.

In 2023, Mr. Paxton was impeached on corruption charges in which he was accused of accepting a bribe from a campaign donor, among other allegations of malfeasance. He was acquitted of the impeachment charges after a trial in the Texas Senate, and has long denied any wrongdoing while in office.

Mr. Paxton’s assets, including a growing real estate portfolio, were investigated during the impeachment proceedings. Last month, The Times reported that he had added three additional condos to that portfolio.

Pooja Salhotra contributed reporting.

Lauren McGaughy is the Texas politics correspondent for The New York Times, writing about the ways that policymakers in the second largest state are changing lives for their citizens and influencing American politics.

The Subway Is Sweltering. Is There a Way to Put That Heat to Good Use?

The New York Times August 10, 2026

Mamdani Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Mayor Zohran Mamdani and state transit officials announced a plan to study a heat-capture system that could cool a notoriously hot train station and help heat city buildings in the winter.

By Stefanos Chen

Summer in the New York City subway, where temperatures can exceed 100 degrees on train platforms, can feel like a sauna — to say nothing of the aromas.

Now, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and state transit officials want to try something new: an underground air-exchange system that could cool stations in the summer and heat nearby buildings in the winter.

On Monday, they announced a study to test the feasibility of the system, called a thermal energy network, at the Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall and Chambers Street station complex in Lower Manhattan. The study is expected to cost $800,000 and will be funded by the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority. If the findings are positive, design work could begin early next year.

Mr. Mamdani, standing on a steamy platform in the complex, compared the space, which serves several train lines, to a “chamber of horrors,” and said the upgrade would be the first of its kind for an American transit network.

“We are bringing that legacy of abandonment to an end,” he said about the Chambers Street station, one of the hottest and least inviting in the century-old subway system. More than 18,000 riders use the station on an average weekday.

The plan would involve digging holes more than 500 feet below an unused station platform to siphon excess heat into a network of pipes connected to municipal buildings nearby, including City Hall and the Surrogate’s Courthouse. Similar geothermal heat-capture systems have been used at St. Patrick’s Cathedral and apartment buildings in New York, and in several European cities.

Janno Lieber, the chief executive of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, the state agency that runs the subway, said the plan could create a model that could be applied elsewhere in the city’s 472-station network.

Previous plans, including for air-conditioning, have produced mixed results because of the porous and complicated layout of stations, which have multiple vents and exits that make them harder to cool. (Subway trains are air-conditioned, but the hot air removed from train cars is vented into stations and tunnels, compounding the problem.)

It is not yet clear how much cooler the heat-exchange system could make the station, Mr. Lieber said, but he noted that lowering the temperature “even a few degrees” would mean “the difference between total misery and merely sweltering.”

Mark Levine, the city comptroller, said the plan could have the added benefit of reducing utility bills for a number of city-owned properties, including the David N. Dinkins Manhattan Municipal Building, which spends roughly $1.5 million a year on heating.

The study comes a week after Gov. Kathy Hochul announced plans to renovate the Chambers Street station, which opened in 1913 and has long been derided as one of the most neglected in the subway.

That project, which does not yet have a timeline but is expected to cost tens of million of dollars, includes new flooring, additional security cameras and lighting, leak mitigation, and the restoration of damaged features, like mosaics, marble trim and terra-cotta details. The M. T. A. said the project would be funded in part with revenue from Manhattan’s congestion pricing toll program.

Stefanos Chen is a Times reporter covering New York City’s transit system.

Will Voters Think Francesca Hong Is Too Radical? Here’s Where She Stands.

The New York Times August 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The democratic socialist is the front-runner to win the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin on Tuesday.

By Julie Bosman

Francesca Hong, a chef and state lawmaker, is the front-runner in the race for the Democratic nomination for Wisconsin governor. If she wins the primary on Tuesday, Ms. Hong, a democratic socialist who has staked out a position to the left of her party, will have triumphed over several candidates considered more moderate, centrist Democrats. Her policy goals and social media rhetoric have raised eyebrows among some Democratic voters, who are questioning whether her views are too extreme to represent Wisconsin’s many moderates and independents.

Here are four of her most provocative positions to date.

In her five years as a Democratic legislator, Ms. Hong has expressed support for reducing funding for police departments and even abolishing law enforcement. She has also said she believes that the police exist to uphold white supremacy.

Ms. Hong has backed away from those statements in recent days. During a televised debate on July 28, she said “no” when asked if she would sign legislation reducing funding for police. And in a podcast interview, she said, “I will not abolish the police.”

“I want to focus on stopping violent crime and giving law enforcement the resources and the training that they need but ensure that we are also holding accountable law enforcement that does not follow the law,” she added.

This year, Ms. Hong introduced a bill in the State Assembly that would create a new income tax bracket of 17.3 percent for individuals making at least $750,000 and for joint filers making $1 million or more. Wisconsin’s current individual income tax rates vary from 3.5 percent to 7.6 percent.

The state is not exactly bursting with millionaires, and critics of her plan have questioned whether it would have a real impact on state coffers — or, instead, scare wealthy taxpayers away. Asked during a candidate debate whether her proposal might drive Wisconsin millionaires to leave the state, she did not answer directly.

“You know, discussing that hypothetical is a little bit — I’m confused about that,” she said.

When federal immigration authorities began a nationwide crackdown in 2025 that also targeted people in Wisconsin, Ms. Hong was outspoken in her opposition to the arrests.

She supports a ban on face coverings for all law enforcement in Wisconsin, including federal agents, and wants to make it illegal for any state or local government official to help detain people solely for immigration violations.

Ms. Hong has also made clear that she does not believe ICE should even exist. “Abolishing ICE isn’t radical — it’s good policy,” she said on social media in January.

Some of Ms. Hong’s most attention-grabbing social media posts have focused on holidays that are cherished by many Americans — and her own distaste for them.

“I do not enjoy fireworks,” she wrote several days before the Fourth of July in 2019. Halloween, she said in 2025, is “not my thing.” Thanksgiving is a “colonizer holiday” that people should not gather to honor, she posted in 2020. Valentine’s Day, she wrote in 2022, brings out “the worst of humanity” on a day “capitalism tells you how to show love.”

Allison Geyer, a Hong campaign spokeswoman, said that the increased scrutiny on Ms. Hong is “what happens when you are emerging as the front-runner,” adding that some of the posts were written during “peak woke back in the 2020s.”

Even Gov. Tony Evers of Wisconsin, a Democrat who endorsed one of Ms. Hong’s opponents, has said that her social media posts would make it difficult for her to beat Representative Tom Tiffany, the likely Republican nominee, in November.

“She has spent her entire campaign dealing not with the issues, but what’s on the Twitter,” he said.

In interviews over the last several days, Ms. Hong has tried to backtrack. Asked what her favorite holiday is, she said with a half-smile, “Thanksgiving.”

“I don’t want to cancel it,” she said in an interview with Politico. “I actually love it.”

She added that she is “kind of a curmudgeon” about holidays in general.

Julie Bosman is the Chicago bureau chief for The Times, writing and reporting stories from around the Midwest.

Weather at the start of the week looks like more of the same: heat and storms across the Eastern United States. But a subtle shift is in the cards.

By Judson Jones

Judson Jones is a meteorologist and reporter for The Times.

Muggy summertime heat continues to grip much of the country, driving temperatures above seasonal averages and increasing the likelihood once again of afternoon thunderstorms. These systems threaten damaging winds and heavy rain into the evening hours across a broad swath of the United States, though a subtle shift in the weather pattern offers impending relief.

Notes: This map indicates risk in up to three tiers: Some, there is at least some chance of extreme weather in the area; Moderate, it is likely that damaging weather will happen in the area; and High, extreme, dangerous weather is expected in the area. Data is as of 3:20 p. m. Eastern on Aug. 10 and is not available for Alaska and Hawaii. Times are Eastern. Source: National Weather Service The New York Times

The sultry, stormy weekend weather in the Northeast endures into the week. The primary corridor to watch for severe storms stretches from the Dakotas through Illinois and eastward into Pennsylvania, pushing close to New York City, where a minimal risk remains Monday evening. In the Southwest, the summer monsoon will trigger similar afternoon activity.

Damaging winds pose the main threat, though a low probability of quick spin-up tornadoes exists across the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic States. Hail is also possible along the northern tier of storms, with the highest risk for large hail focused over the Northern Plains. Across nearly the entire Eastern United States, a broad marginal risk for excessive rain persists. Forecasters have higher confidence that localized flash flooding will actually materialize from Northern Illinois into Ohio through Tuesday morning.

The general pattern from Monday holds, but repeated rainfall over the same areas of the Midwest will lightly elevate the flash-flood risk in Ohio and West Virginia by Tuesday afternoon and evening.

The severe threat area will dip farther south on its eastern flank, moving out of New York and deeper into the Mid-Atlantic, placing Philadelphia and Washington under at least some risk. But that remains primarily focused from Northern Illinois into Ohio, where storms could bring damaging winds, hail and potentially tornadoes.

As these storms slowly press south over the week, they will drag down the core heat along with them. That shift should allow much of the Midwest to enjoy a multiday break, with temperatures dropping to seasonal or even below-average levels. While major cities along the Northeast corridor will wait longer to feel the change, forecasters at the National Weather Service office in New York indicate that relief is in sight for later this week.

Judson Jones is a meteorologist and reporter for The Times who forecasts and covers extreme weather.

The pop-country megastar is still thrilling young audiences and influencing a new generation of musicians.

Credit... Pari Dukovic for The New York Times

Supported by

By Lizzy Goodman

Lizzy Goodman interviewed Shania Twain over the course of three conversations in London.

Just over a month ago, on a steamy night in London, the pop-country megastar Shania Twain finished a performance at Wembley Stadium, changed out of her hot pants and stilettos and retired to a dressing room with her tall, dashing husband. She never eats solid food before going onstage — “Otherwise, I get burpy” — so now she could enjoy a plate of fruit and cheese, pouring Veuve Clicquot into champagne flutes and sharing bits of Cheddar with her Pomeranian, Sapphire.

She was spending a stretch of the summer in London as the opening act for a record-breaking 12-date residency at Wembley. The headliner: Harry Styles, a pop star nearly 30 years her junior. The two met in New York in 2017 and traded numbers, she told me. Styles asked her for a favor: Could she make a happy-birthday call to his mother, a longtime fan? A few years later, when Styles was the big Friday-night headliner at the Coachella festival, he invited Twain to perform two songs with him and, flashing his famous dimples, gave her this introduction: “In the car with my mother as a child, this lady taught me to sing. She also taught me that men are trash.”

Twain has now met both of his parents. “It breaks down the fame element of things — there’s nothing ‘industry,’” she said. Their fan bases intersected, she said, in the form of “the groups of girls” — “Harry really has the groups of girls, you know what I’m saying?”

At Wembley there were indeed gaggles of girls of all varieties: moms and daughters, dads chaperoning bunches of friends, roving packs of glitter-covered teenagers, young professional women in fannish cosplay. I saw plenty of Styles-inspired fashion — heart sunglasses, feather boas and “Respect Your Mother” T-shirts, shorthand for the kind of Forever 21 feminism that’s part of his lingua franca. But there was also plenty of the leopard print that’s a Twain signature. “We cross audiences,” she said. “We definitely do.”

Granted, Twain’s audience is immense: Her 1997 LP, “Come On Over,” remains the best-selling country album of all time and the best-selling studio album by any female artist, ever. Still, you might not expect her to be thrilling young pop audiences at this stage in her career, and at 60 years old. Styles isn’t sharing Wembley with any of the other women who dominated late-1990s radio; teenagers do not seem this excited about, say, Faith Hill or Celine Dion. If you had imagined, 20 years ago, what Twain’s audience would look like today, you might have pictured something more middle-aged — not, say, the 20-something lesbian couple I saw at Wembley, one in a leopard minidress and cowboy hat, one in a leopard ascot and backward baseball cap, going hoarse screaming along to “Any Man of Mine.” Or the scene later described to me by the writer Liana Satenstein: a Manhattan party where the Gen-Z crowd went wild upon hearing a Twain single, not long after a spin of the theme song from “Hannah Montana.”

Part of this is thanks to the younger musicians who have spent years telling fans that Twain is a crucial touchstone. Styles is not alone: Rappers and indie-rockers and pop stars call her an influence, a dream collaborator, even a blush-inducing crush. Post Malone says he primarily listens to Twain before going onstage. Rihanna ranks her alongside Whitney Houston and Mariah Carey in her pantheon of divas. Diplo described meeting her as “face-melting.” The singer-songwriter Maggie Rogers has praised the instincts Twain brought to conceiving her videos, including the indelible image of Twain in a barren desert, in head-to-toe leopard print with matching suitcase, in “That Don’t Impress Me Much” — a song now regularly covered by the pop trio Haim. Sabrina Carpenter, who has also covered Twain, invited her to appear as Mrs. Claus in a 2024 Christmas special. And on July 4, Twain left her final performance with Styles and crossed London to appear with Mumford & Sons at Hyde Park, where Marcus Mumford described her from the stage as “my [expletive] hero”: “You don’t understand. You don’t get it. This is a very big deal for me.”

There’s nostalgia involved: Millennials were children when Twain conquered radio, introducing some of them to pop the same way SpongeBob introduced them to television. There’s also a question of style. Twain and her husband at the time, the hard-rock producer Mutt Lange, made pop-country engineered to cross over to the mainstream — an achievement that has since moved from rare to practically the definition of pop music. (Taylor Swift says it often: Shania Twain paved her way.)

But the most striking reason is cultural: Twain’s young acolytes often see her as a glamorous, self-actualized champion whose songs are explicitly feminist statements. That was the image captured in a 2017 Rolling Stone article about how Twain “empowered an unlikely group of female artists.” It has younger musicians calling her a “feminist icon” (Kalie Shorr) and saying childhood memories of dancing to her music are “among the earliest I have of testing out my own variety of ‘girl power’” (Caitlin Rose). The singer-songwriter Kelsea Ballerini — who has said her own drive to write female authority into every song traces back to Twain — told me the singer was “on the Mount Rushmore of showing women you can be bold, sassy, smart, sexy, strong and soft, all at the same time,” and that her music offered “the most empowered gift in the world.”

There’s only one wrinkle: Shania Twain does not entirely identify with all of this. It’s exciting, she told me, to see new generations embrace her music — to hear stories from fans who, like Styles, first heard her on their mothers’ stereos. Sometimes, she said, she even wonders: “What was I doing when Harry was born?” But she has never felt comfortable with the idea of herself as a feminist hero. She has not always had an easy relationship with being a woman, let alone a liberated superwoman. And when I mentioned Styles’s Coachella introduction — “she also taught me that men are trash” — she laughed, but hastened to correct the record: “I didn’t ever say that.”

Twain explained more fully from a luxurious, velvet-swathed sitting room at her West London hotel, over cups of builders’ tea.

She wasn’t too far from home: She has lived in Switzerland since 1999, when she moved there with Lange. (About a decade later, the two would separate amid a made-for-TV tangle: Lange married Twain’s close friend and assistant, Marie-Anne Thiébaud, while Twain ended up marrying Marie-Anne’s ex-husband, Frédéric Thiébaud.) Along with that Alpine home, where she keeps horses and dogs, Twain has a ranch in Nevada — purchased during a series of Las Vegas residencies — and a mansion in the Bahamas. She still scans, though, more like a tough country girl than a wealthy diva. When I said I heard she’d been out riding for a photo shoot in Hyde Park, she was quick to reject it as not really riding, just “a lovely bridle path.” She was wearing an upscale version of an equestrian’s kit — khaki pants with subtle knee patches, tall brown boots, Thom Browne Oxford shirt, hair pulled back through a tan baseball cap — but apart from the blingy earrings she seemed a lot like the women who ran the stables where I learned to ride as a child: petite, strong eye contact, throaty laugh, nails refreshingly unmanicured.

This was late in June, in the middle of a historic European heat wave. The previous week, Twain had encountered some mild backlash after telling The Sunday Times that she didn’t see herself as a feminist. In about a month, she would release a new album that had her singing directly, for the first time, about her own origins. Its name, “Little Miss Twain,” came from the introduction she used to hear when she was 8 years old, taking the stage at dive bars in Timmins, Ontario. “For once, I just wanted to describe the setting of it so that people could taste it,” she said. “So they could imagine where Little Miss Twain was. It was winter. It’s winter a lot of the time where I’m from.”

She outlined the story. Her mother, Sharon Edwards, moved to Timmins after a divorce from Twain’s biological father, when Shania was 2. Edwards was soon remarried to the man Twain considers her father, Jerry Twain, an Ojibway Indian born into the Mattagami First Nation. The family struggled. In a 2011 memoir, Twain described lining winter shoes with plastic bread bags and getting by on bowls of boiled milk, bread and sugar that her family called “goulash”; she was, she told me, “that kid that went to school with greasy hair because we didn’t have shampoo. I was probably smelly.”

She loved music, and amazed adults with her singing, but had little interest in performing. “My mother really wanted me to be on the stage,” she said. “So she got me up there very, very young. Too young.” Twain would be dragged out of bed so she could perform after the bars’ last call, when children could enter; the money she earned often paid for gas and groceries. Edwards fixated on dreams of her daughter’s stardom, a mental escape from deep depression and a violent home: Twain remembers getting caught in the physical and verbal abuse between her parents, and one gruesome moment in which her father smashed her mother’s head against a toilet basin and tried to drown her.

Twain’s public image has always read as confidently, assertively feminine, but she spent the first decades of her life resenting being a girl. She saw herself as a tomboy or a lone wolf — someone who relished skinned knees, playing football with her brothers and being the only girl working a reforestation service crew with her father. She has said that she did not feel safe being a girl; she has also described being touched inappropriately by a trusted neighbor and by her father. In London, she remembered a conversation she had at 8 years old. One of her mother’s friends asked her: If she didn’t turn out to be a singer, what would she want to be? “And I said, ‘Well, I want to be a bodybuilder.’ I even said, ‘I want to be a man.’ I thought being a girl was a real [expletive] deal.” She wanted, she said, to be the Incredible Hulk, not Wonder Woman. Puberty felt like a threat that would leave her compromised and vulnerable: “If I could have just stayed 8, that would have been perfect.”

As a teenager, she moved to Toronto to build a singing career. But in 1987, when she was 22, both of her parents were killed in a head-on collision with a logging truck, leaving her to care for the three children still at home. She was back in Timmins, overwhelmed with grief and responsibility, when a friend told her that a resort called Deerhurst was looking for a singer. For the next four years, Twain would support herself and her siblings working at a vast lakeside vacation spot for Toronto’s upper middle class. When a Nashville lawyer flew up in 1990 to scout the woman who would make history’s best-selling country album, he found her dressed as a poodle in a revue-style adaptation of “Cats” called “Dogs” — “and it was in French, so I’m singing in French.”

Deerhurst was an accidental combination of boot camp and finishing school. Twain learned the grunt work of show business, performing multiple times a day, on multiple stages, in wildly different genres. She also trained in femininity. “I learned how to walk in stilettos,” she said. “I learned how to work in a gown that weighed 25 pounds. I learned how to wear makeup” — everything down to the ways stage lights played on different fabrics.

The job of being a girl came with as many downsides as preteen Shania had feared, but dealing with them now felt like honing a skill. “Sexism was just rampant around me, which did make me withdraw,” she said. “I was very experienced with it by the time I went to Nashville. I was insulted, I was patronized, all of it. But I was also like: ‘I’m from a life and a place that you guys probably have never even imagined, so you know what? It’s OK. I can handle the insult.’” She went on. “There’s no man in this room — no matter what way you look at me, or even if you touch me inappropriately — that is ever going to make me feel like I don’t belong here.” Also: “You’re not going to intimidate me. That’s not even possible.”

She had spent decades in a state of subtle resistance to her own gender. But in Nashville, as she crafted her songs and her image, something shifted: “I started taking ownership.” It was videos in particular that, as she put it, “freed” her. As she chose her look and wardrobe, she saw how taking charge of her femininity transformed it from a liability to a strength — something she could embrace “without feeling shame or feeling like I have to hide it for the sake of my talent.” From then on, she said, “the songs just because more and more about that liberation, and about making statements with a smile. Because I wasn’t angry at anyone. I was just, like, Wow, it’s time to celebrate being a woman. This is really, actually great.”

Is that a tale of heroic feminism? For Twain, it is not. She agrees with the principles of feminism, she told me, but rejects the label — a common enough framing among women who remember a time when identifying as a feminist felt self-marginalizing. But with Twain it seemed more pointed. Her life was marked by a scrappy optimism. Her music celebrated the idea of a woman being free, triumphant, powerful, playful. Nineties fans received it as obviously liberationist; there was even concern at her record label, she has said, that she would alienate men by seeming too opinionated. (Or alienate women by seeming too seductive.) And her brand of femininity, with its assertive confidence and perfect red lip, almost exactly forecast the aesthetics of millennial pop feminism. Doesn’t it feel possible, I asked her, that she shaped a generation’s idea of what female empowerment looked like?

“You know, it does,” she said, petting Sapphire and nodding. But a few minutes later, she paused and sighed, as if searching in vain for the right words, and said: “I was just somebody standing up for myself.”

At Wembley I kept looking at the “groups of girls” around me and wondering how their worlds compared with Twain’s. One night, just before the chorus of “Man! I Feel Like a Woman!” I watched three young women in jean shorts and cowboy boots — heads together, iPhones outstretched, Instagram Live rolling — lean back to sing along about Twain’s great subject, the performance of femininity: Go totally crazy, forget I’m a lady. Men’s shirts, short skirts. Color my hair, do what I dare. Oh, I wanna be free to feel the way I feel. The song was inspired by a younger Twain’s male friends in Toronto, who taught her the pleasures of dressing up to go dancing at gay bars. She learned early on to perform femininity for a living, but stardom arrived when she started to convey an explosive, celebratory joy and power in it. Some of the fans at Wembley may have had easy paths to experiencing that joy, and others may have been struggling their way there as Twain did — but they all seemed to be looking to her, as much as to anyone in their own generation, for an excuse to revel in it.

Even during the heat wave, the stadium was already surprisingly full whenever Twain took the stage. Her sets — performed against backdrops of mock bedroom walls covered in leopard-print wallpaper and Shania posters — were full of unabashed, Dolly Parton-level camp, but also serious musicianship and vocal power. Twain contracted Lyme disease in the early 2000s and later discovered that it had caused nerve damage to her vocal cords; two stabilizing surgeries, in 2011 and 2018, left her voice more gravelly and, she says, less dependable. “I lost my voice as I knew it,” she says, comparing it to singing “with a limp”: “You never know when it’s going to give out.” She sounded nearly perfect in every show I saw.

In fact, it was at a moment of peak vocal vulnerability that her sets would go from good to great: a cover of Styles’s “Falling,” performed alone on a stool with her guitar, delivering a fragile ballad to 80,000 people with this voice she describes as a “moody friend.” She didn’t always play it; fans never knew for sure whether it was coming. When it did, the crowd rippled in response. Audiences, she said, enjoyed the realism, the intimacy. The song also offered something to her as the opening act. “I’m the guest, right? But I was able to at least just say, OK, I’m just going to take one little moment and indulge in Little Miss Twain.”

Twain’s famous for this kind of indulgence — “the prerogative to have a little fun,” as she famously sang. It’s the driving force behind every smash she’s written, she said, along with the excruciatingly direct songs on her new album. Her megahits, she acknowledged, were about empowerment. And they were also about being a woman. But they were not, for her, about female empowerment: “It wasn’t meant to be a feminist message.”

Among her proudest moments, she said, were those when she’d see men in pickup trucks singing along to “Man! I Feel Like a Woman!” The song wasn’t, as she saw it, some feminist plaint: There was “no anger in it,” she wasn’t “saying it as a sexist person” — men didn’t even have much to do with it. “I was just owning and celebrating what I think I waited too damn long to celebrate,” she said. “People want to celebrate who they are, and what they are, and they don’t want to be criticized for just being themselves. And I think that is a liberty that we all deserve. I certainly waited way too long to give it to myself.”

Lizzy Goodman is a contributing writer for the magazine and the author of “Meet Me in the Bathroom,” an oral history of the rebirth of rock music in New York City from 2001 to 2011.
